This section widens the lens to the whole AI world: the major assistants, how they differ, when to use which, and the techniques that transfer across all of them. What you'll learn Pick the right model for a job without re-learning the field every time Move between assistants — ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok, open models — without losing your technique Run capable models on your own machine, and know when that is worth it Combine Claude with local models and agent frameworks

If you read one page in this section, read this one. Everything below is a branch off it. How to choose a model — a durable framework that outlives any particular release. Then follow whichever thread matches what you are doing.

ЛЛандшафт AI-моделей: как выбрать между Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini и открытыми моделями Устойчивый подход к выбору подходящей AI-модели под задачу — среди Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, Llama, Mistral, Grok и открытых/локальных моделей — плюс то, какие навыки переносятся на все из них. GGemini 4 Argon: The Field Guide for Claude Users (Sep 30, 2026) Google's Gemini 4 generation opens with Argon and one headline number: a 1M-token OUTPUT limit, up from 64K. Context stayed at 1M. What the coverage gets wrong: the independent Artificial Analysis index puts Argon at 53 — five points BEHIND Claude Opus 5.5's 58 — and its cheaper $1.99-per-task cost comes from the rate card, not efficiency, since it burns 62K output tokens per task against GPT-6 Astra's 27K. Plus: a 15% hallucination rate (lowest measured), and why you almost certainly cannot call it yet. CClaude Opus 5.5: The Field Guide Opus 5.5 shipped 22 September 2026 at $4/$20 per MTok — 20% under Opus 5, with cache reads at $0.20 (a 5% tier, not the usual 10%). Four breaking changes 400-error a naive migration, one more changes the response shape without failing anything and makes your UI go quiet mid-task. Thinking can no longer be disabled at all, forced tool_choice is gone, and the default effort dropped from high to medium — while each level now thinks more than it did on Opus 5. CClaude Fable 5.2: The Migration Field Guide Anthropic shipped Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 on November 9, 2026 — the first Claude flagship point release that costs LESS than the model it replaces ($8/$40, down 20%). Four breaking changes, a prefix check that now applies to every account, prompting lines that stop working, and an official benchmark table with two rows the coverage missed. CClaude Fable 5.1: что изменилось и как мигрировать 1 сентября 2026 года Anthropic выпустила Claude Fable 5.1 и Mythos 5.1: цена прежняя, $10/$50, чтение из кеша подешевело до $0,25, появились три ломающих изменения API (ошибка при принудительном tool_choice, односторонние блоки thinking, история только на дозапись) и пять дополнительных бета-функций. Руководство по миграции для всех, кто закрепил claude-fable-5 или claude-opus-5. CClaude Fable 5 и Mythos 5: полевое руководство по флагману Fable 5 был первым флагманом Anthropic класса Mythos — теперь это устаревшая (legacy) модель, ей на смену пришла Fable 5.1. Её API отказывает in-band (HTTP 200, stop_reason: refusal), поддерживает только adaptive thinking и никогда не возвращает сырые рассуждения. Если вы закрепляете модель верхнего уровня, это меняет то, как вы пишете интеграции. Когда выбирать её вместо Opus 4.8, паттерн fallback, сдвиги в промптинге. CClaude Sonnet 5.5: The Field Guide Sonnet 5.5 shipped 28 September 2026 at exactly Sonnet 5's prices — $2/$10 per MTok — and Anthropic still claims up to 30% less per task. The saving is in the token count, not the rate card. Five breaking changes 400-error a Sonnet 5 codebase, a sixth returns 200 and silences your progress UI, thinking can no longer be disabled (only moved between tool calls), and on Terminal-Bench 4.0 the cheap model scores 70.6% against Opus 5.5's 66.4%. CClaude Haiku 5.5: The 100K Price Cliff Haiku 5.5 shipped 7 October 2026 at $0.10/$0.50 per MTok — a 90% cut — and it is the only current Claude model priced by prompt length. One token past 100,000 reprices the entire request 5x. The threshold is measured on the new tokenizer, so it arrives ~23% earlier in text than you expect, and the 90% headline is ~87% in practice below the cliff and ~35% above it. CClaude Opus 5: практическое руководство Opus 5 вышла 24 июля 2026 года — четвёртая модель Anthropic за два месяца: цена та же, $5/$25, что у Opus 4.8, но результат на Frontier-Bench более чем вдвое выше, на ARC-AGI-3 — втрое выше ближайшей модели, плюс новый уровень усилий xhigh/max. Важные бенчмарки, две ошибки 400, ломающие наивную миграцию, и когда Opus 5 заменяет Fable 5 в вашем стеке. CClaude Sonnet 5: The Field Guide Sonnet 5 is Sonnet 4.6's drop-in successor and Claude Code's default on Pro and Team Standard — but three API constraints will 400 you on migration and a new tokenizer produces ~30% more tokens for the same text. The pricing math, the effort re-mapping (Sonnet 5 medium ≈ Sonnet 4.6 high), and the prompting shifts that catch teams out. CChatGPT для пользователей Claude Свободно владеете Claude, но нужно использовать ChatGPT? The details that decide whether that is true for you: a 922K input ceiling inside a 1.05M window, a hard cost cliff at 272K tokens, tool calling that only works on one of the two APIs, and the benchmark row where Sonnet 5.5 still wins by 8.7 points. What each means for a Claude user. What every part actually does, in Claude-user terms. SSign in with ChatGPT OpenAI's new identity layer, three days old. Различия, которые важны — поиск в реальном времени по X/вебу, API, совместимый с OpenAI, и кодинг-агент Grok Build — плюс всё то, что переносится без изменений. What the append-only event log actually buys you, why the contributor tier is 12.5× cheaper than standard, how it stacks up against Claude Code on Terminal-Bench 2.1, and the three bundled skills that are worth stealing regardless of which agent you use. Both models are priced by prompt length, and their cliffs are in different places: Haiku reprices 5x past 100K, Ember 3x past 200K. That leaves a 100K-200K band where Ember costs exactly one fifth of Haiku and a twelfth on cache reads. TThe Third-Party Memory Layer: How claude-mem Actually Works claude-mem has 103,000 GitHub stars and solves the complaint every coding-agent user has: the agent forgets everything when the session ends. Underneath, it is a second model running in a background daemon that reads every tool call you make — and on the hosted path its own cost dataset maps that observer to a DeepSeek model, not Claude. The six hooks, the exit-code contract that can block your session, the three-layer recall that makes the token math work, where the data lands, who pays for the compression, and a checklist for evaluating any memory layer before you install it. Lllama-modchip: a 284B model on 64 GB of RAM, read honestly 483 points on Hacker News for running DeepSeek-V4-Flash on a laptop CPU with no GPU. The mechanism is real and genuinely clever — two new block-64 tensor types with single-instruction SIMD decode, a chess engine's search used as a draftless speculator, and huge pages that cut dTLB misses per token from 18.42M to 0.31M. But it is a 1.69-bit quant, the 'lossless' numbers are measured against the already-1.7-bit file rather than BF16, and in a 208-comment thread nobody reproduced the headline on 64 GB of x86. What it is, what to run, and what to disbelieve. WWhy a 35 KB System Prompt Breaks on a Local Model Moving a big Claude/GPT system prompt to Ollama or another local runtime: the context-budget math, Ollama's silent middle-of-prompt truncation, the failure signals of context exhaustion, and the restructuring that actually works.
Claude is the core here, but the same skills travel. Start with how to choose, then go as deep as you need on any assistant, on running models locally, or on agents.
Устойчивый подход к выбору подходящей AI-модели под задачу — среди Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, Llama, Mistral, Grok и открытых/локальных моделей — плюс то, какие навыки переносятся на все из них.
documents.s: ЛЛандшафт AI-моделей: как выбрать между Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini и открытыми моделями

documents.t: Google's Gemini 4 generation opens with Argon and one headline number: a 1M-token OUTPUT limit, up from 64K. Context stayed at 1M. What the coverage gets wrong: the independent Artificial Analysis index puts Argon at 53 — five points BEHIND Claude Opus 5.5's 58 — and its cheaper $1.99-per-task cost comes from the rate card, not efficiency, since it burns 62K output tokens per task against GPT-6 Astra's 27K. Plus: a 15% hallucination rate (lowest measured), and why you almost certainly cannot call it yet.
documents.s: GGemini 4 Argon: The Field Guide for Claude Users (Sep 30, 2026)

documents.t: Opus 5.5 shipped 22 September 2026 at $4/$20 per MTok — 20% under Opus 5, with cache reads at $0.20 (a 5% tier, not the usual 10%). Four breaking changes 400-error a naive migration, one more changes the response shape without failing anything and makes your UI go quiet mid-task. Thinking can no longer be disabled at all, forced tool_choice is gone, and the default effort dropped from high to medium — while each level now thinks more than it did on Opus 5.

Anthropic shipped Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 on November 9, 2026 — the first Claude flagship point release that costs LESS than the model it replaces ($8/$40, down 20%). Four breaking changes, a prefix check that now applies to every account, prompting lines that stop working, and an official benchmark table with two rows the coverage missed.
documents.s: CClaude Fable 5.2: The Migration Field Guide

documents.t: 1 сентября 2026 года Anthropic выпустила Claude Fable 5.1 и Mythos 5.1: цена прежняя, $10/$50, чтение из кеша подешевело до $0,25, появились три ломающих изменения API (ошибка при принудительном tool_choice, односторонние блоки thinking, история только на дозапись) и пять дополнительных бета-функций. Руководство по миграции для всех, кто закрепил claude-fable-5 или claude-opus-5.
documents.s: CClaude Fable 5.1: что изменилось и как мигрировать

documents.t: Fable 5 был первым флагманом Anthropic класса Mythos — теперь это устаревшая (legacy) модель, ей на смену пришла Fable 5.1. Её API отказывает in-band (HTTP 200, stop_reason: refusal), поддерживает только adaptive thinking и никогда не возвращает сырые рассуждения. Если вы закрепляете модель верхнего уровня, это меняет то, как вы пишете интеграции. Когда выбирать её вместо Opus 4.8, паттерн fallback, сдвиги в промптинге.
documents.s: CClaude Fable 5 и Mythos 5: полевое руководство по флагману

documents.t: Sonnet 5.5 shipped 28 September 2026 at exactly Sonnet 5's prices — $2/$10 per MTok — and Anthropic still claims up to 30% less per task. The saving is in the token count, not the rate card. Five breaking changes 400-error a Sonnet 5 codebase, a sixth returns 200 and silences your progress UI, thinking can no longer be disabled (only moved between tool calls), and on Terminal-Bench 4.0 the cheap model scores 70.6% against Opus 5.5's 66.4%.

Haiku 5.5 shipped 7 October 2026 at $0.10/$0.50 per MTok — a 90% cut — and it is the only current Claude model priced by prompt length. One token past 100,000 reprices the entire request 5x. The threshold is measured on the new tokenizer, so it arrives ~23% earlier in text than you expect, and the 90% headline is ~87% in practice below the cliff and ~35% above it.

Opus 5 вышла 24 июля 2026 года — четвёртая модель Anthropic за два месяца: цена та же, $5/$25, что у Opus 4.8, но результат на Frontier-Bench более чем вдвое выше, на ARC-AGI-3 — втрое выше ближайшей модели, плюс новый уровень усилий xhigh/max. Важные бенчмарки, две ошибки 400, ломающие наивную миграцию, и когда Opus 5 заменяет Fable 5 в вашем стеке.

Sonnet 5 is Sonnet 4.6's drop-in successor and Claude Code's default on Pro and Team Standard — but three API constraints will 400 you on migration and a new tokenizer produces ~30% more tokens for the same text. The pricing math, the effort re-mapping (Sonnet 5 medium ≈ Sonnet 4.6 high), and the prompting shifts that catch teams out.

Свободно владеете Claude, но нужно использовать ChatGPT? Различия, которые имеют значение, что переносится и когда к какому обращаться — включая вывод Custom GPTs из эксплуатации и Plugins, которые их заменяют.

OpenAI shipped the GPT-5.6 family (Sol, Terra, Luna) and ChatGPT Work on 9 July 2026. What actually changed for a Claude user — 1.05M context, a $1 tier, an agent that runs for hours, and the parts of the launch nobody is writing about.
documents.s: GGPT-5.6 & ChatGPT Work for Claude Users

documents.t: OpenAI shipped GPT-6.1 Sol at DevDay on September 29, 2026 with the exact rate card Claude Sonnet 5.5 has — $2/$10 — and a cached-input price half of Sonnet's. The launch line is 'near-Astra intelligence for a fifth of the price'. The details that decide whether that is true for you: a 922K input ceiling inside a 1.05M window, a hard cost cliff at 272K tokens, tool calling that only works on one of the two APIs, and the benchmark row where Sonnet 5.5 still wins by 8.7 points.
documents.s: GGPT-6.1 Sol: The Field Guide for Claude Users

documents.t: On 6 August 2026 OpenAI shipped a mid-cycle update to GPT-5.6 that most write-ups reduced to 'Sol got smarter.' The real story: a six-tier effort control that changes how you price a request, a free-tier Think button, a 272K token pricing cliff that re-prices the whole call, and a Fast mode that only runs on Sol. What each means for a Claude user.
documents.s: GGPT-5.6 August 2026 Update: Effort Slider, Free Think Button & the 272K Price Cliff

documents.t: OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra went GA on September 4, 2026: 1.05M context, $10/$50 per MTok, a Critical cyber classification, and a 'recurrent depth' architecture that hides part of its reasoning. What's confirmed, how it stacks against Claude Fable 5.1 and Opus 5, the four API gotchas, and when a Claude user should reach for it.
documents.s: GGPT-6 Astra: The Field Guide for Claude Users

documents.t: On 7 August 2026 OpenAI shipped Codex CLI v0.147.0 — the release that turns Skills into portable Agent Plugins with a four-tier catalog, ships an --approve-for-me flag that doesn't do what it sounds like, quietly removes --full-auto, and opts you into MCP 2026-07-28. What every part actually does, in Claude-user terms.
documents.s: CCodex Agent Plugins & Catalog Federation (v0.147.0): The Practical Guide

Фреймворк (а не рейтинг) для выбора передовой модели для программирования — факторы, которые действительно важны, и почему оценка на вашем собственном репозитории превосходит любой бенчмарк.
documents.s: CClaude против GPT против Gemini для программирования

documents.t: Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI и открытые терминальные агенты — как обвязка (а не только модель) определяет результат, и как сохранить переносимость конфигурации с помощью AGENTS.md.

Supabase open-sourced a benchmark that runs Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode against real containerized Supabase stacks — not mocks. Here's what it measures, what it found about how models actually use docs and skills, and how to run it locally in an evening.

Apple's third-generation Foundation Models (AFM 3) landed at WWDC 2026 with a 3B dense on-device model, a 20B sparse MoE that runs on iPhone, and a Swift-native framework that now lets you bring your own LLM provider — including Claude. What actually shipped, the non-obvious mechanisms, and how it changes the on-device story for anyone who ships Claude apps.

documents.t: On 13 August 2026, three weeks after 3.6 Flash, Google shipped Gemini 3.7 Flash at half the introductory price with a 16-point DeepSWE jump. The gotchas most write-ups skip: an expiring intro price, a 3× throughput advantage that matters for agent loops but not chat, and where it still trails Claude Sonnet 5.

documents.t: On September 2, 2026, three weeks after 3.7 Flash, Google shipped Gemini 3.8 Flash at the same $0.75 / $3.75 intro price: DeepSWE 73.7 (+8.4), Terminal-bench 2.1 89.4, HLE-Verified 54.9, plus a Cyber variant gated behind the new Fairwind Program. What the append-only event log actually buys you, why the contributor tier is 12.5× cheaper than standard, how it stacks up against Claude Code on Terminal-Bench 2.1, and the three bundled skills that are worth stealing regardless of which agent you use.

documents.t: Meta's Muse Ember shipped 9 November 2026 at $0.10/$0.50 — Claude Haiku 5.5's exact rate card. Both models are priced by prompt length, and their cliffs are in different places: Haiku reprices 5x past 100K, Ember 3x past 200K. That leaves a 100K-200K band where Ember costs exactly one fifth of Haiku and a twelfth on cache reads. Plus the benchmark row Ember loses by 7.7 points, the harness asymmetry in Meta's own footnote, and the verbosity that eats part of the discount.

documents.t: Нейтральная к провайдеру карта основных открытых фреймворков для создания LLM-агентов — LangGraph, LlamaIndex, AutoGen, CrewAI и подход минимального цикла — и как выбрать.

9 июля 2026 года OpenAI выпустила бету мультиагентности в Responses API и Sol Ultra Mode — первый фронтирный вендор, сделавший «модель сама порождает N субагентов и синтезирует их результаты в одном HTTP-запросе» первоклассным примитивом. How AI agents actually pay for things now — the x402 HTTP-402 protocol, the exact/upto/batch-settlement schemes, facilitators, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Payments' Aug 2026 GA (payment sessions, Coinbase Bazar MCP, Stripe Privy, Machine Payment Protocol), and how to add a paywall or a spending agent without inventing a wallet.

documents.t: Перенос промпта между Claude, GPT, Gemini и открытыми моделями — что переносится без изменений, что нужно подстроить под каждую модель, и рабочий процесс миграции.

The design patterns for sending each request to the right AI model — rule-based, classifier, complexity, cascade, ensemble, fallback. When to use each, what breaks, and the recipes that actually ship in 2026.

documents.t: August 3, 2026: Alibaba's Qwen3.8-Max shipped API-only with a 2.4T parameter MoE (95B active), a 1M context, dual OpenAI/Anthropic-spec APIs, and benchmark scores that beat GPT-5.6 Sol Max on OSWorld. What's genuinely new, what 'open weight' actually means when the Hugging Face page is empty, and the sparsity math that makes self-hosting expensive.

documents.t: On Aug 31 2026 DeepSeek open-sourced V4-Flash-Vision-Exp — a 305B MoE that adds native vision to V4-Flash without hurting text agent scores, matches or beats Claude Opus 4.8 on ApexBench / Agents' Last Exam / ZeroBench at a fraction of the price, and ships MIT. The specific numbers, the hard 384-token-per-image cap most guides ignore, and the concrete way to run it.
documents.s: DDeepSeek V4-Flash-Vision: First Native-Vision Frontier Open Weight

documents.t: On September 10, 2026 DeepSeek shipped V4.1-Flash — a 552B MIT-licensed MoE with native vision, a 1M-token window, a KV cache a quarter the size of V4-Flash's, and a 1–100 reasoning-effort dial. It ties Claude Opus 5 on DeepSWE v1.1 (74.2 vs 74.0) at $0.30 per million input tokens, and trails badly on Terminal-Bench. The numbers, the routing change that silently moved every deepseek-v4-pro call, and where Claude still wins.
documents.s: DDeepSeek-V4.1-Flash: A 1M-Context Open Weight That Ties Opus 5 on DeepSWE (Sep 2026)

documents.t: Свободно владеете Claude, но интересуетесь Kimi K2 от Moonshot? Агентная модель с открытыми весами, на которую действительно можно направить Claude Code — потому что Moonshot предоставляет эндпойнт, совместимый с Anthropic. Что по-настоящему отличается, а что переносится напрямую.

Z.ai's 753B MoE (~40B active), 1M-token context, MIT-licensed — closes to within a point of Claude Opus 4.8 on long-horizon coding, at roughly one-sixth the API cost. What IndexShare actually does, how to run it locally, and where it beats Claude Code in the wild.

Mira Murati's Thinking Machines Lab shipped Inkling — a 975B-parameter Apache 2.0 multimodal MoE with a continuous thinking-effort dial. What the launch coverage got wrong, why it deliberately loses benchmarks, and what the effort knob actually does.

Moonshot AI's 2.8-trillion-parameter open-weight model beats Claude Opus 4.8 on many benchmarks and tops the Frontend Code Arena. What makes it architecturally different, when the cache-hit pricing flips the cost math, and whether it's worth reaching for.
documents.s: KKimi K3: World's Largest Open-Weight Model

documents.t: The definitive practical guide to self-hosting Moonshot's 2.8T open-weight Kimi K3 in 2026. What DSpark speculative decoding actually does, minimum hardware (1× DGX B300 or 16× DGX Spark), the exact vLLM serve commands, the prefill/decode asymmetry nobody warns you about, and when hosted inference undercuts your own rack.
documents.s: RRunning Kimi K3 Locally: vLLM, DSpark & the Real Hardware Bill

documents.t: A 1.02T-parameter MoE with 42B active, 1M context, text/image/video/audio input — MIT-licensed on Hugging Face. What the benchmark tables actually say once you check which version was run, why Pro needs 32 GPUs and Flash doesn't, and what the 10x UltraSpeed tier is really selling.

xAI published the full Rust source of its coding agent under Apache 2.0 — the agent loop, tool layer, TUI and extension system. What the crate map teaches you about building agents, why 'open source' here means source-available, and what the data-collector code still in the tree tells you.

What the 8B-active S 2.1 actually beats, why the 3B-active XS 2.1 runs on a MacBook, the first-known RL-in-FP8 training pipeline, and when to reach for it over Claude, GLM-5.2 or Kimi K3.

Same Claude model, 4.7x the precision of a Claude Code review at 1/15 the tokens on its own benchmark — and a best-case recall of 20%. How it works, how to run it with Claude, GPT, Qwen or a local model, delegation mode, CI, and the gotchas.

The license quietly blocks self-hosting in the US/EU/UK/Korea, the open base is 768p (not 2K), and ~13B of 33B params are AdaLN branches you can skip at inference. What H3 actually is, what it costs, and when it beats the closed video APIs.

documents.t: A soft cap emails you. A hard cap blocks the request. This page maps which AI providers do which — and the trap nobody documents: the same event (you hit your cap) returns HTTP 429 with no retry-after on Anthropic's tier cap, HTTP 400 on the limit you set yourself, 429 on OpenAI, and 402 on OpenRouter. Plus why no cap can be exact, where the Custom tier loses its safety net, and how to build a pre-flight killswitch.

documents.t: Every major provider caches your prompt prefix — but explicit vs automatic, 5 minutes vs 24 hours, and a write premium that can make caching cost you more. The portable break-even rule and the five traps when you move a workload.

Agentic runs cost 50–1000x a chat — not because the model is dumber, but because of the context snowball. The mechanism, the surprising numbers, and the four levers that actually cut the bill across Claude, GPT, Gemini, and open models.

documents.t: Every major provider does function calling, and no two agree on a single field name. The four dialects side by side, the arguments-is-a-string bug that breaks every port, the one provider with no correlation ID at all, and why forcing a tool is the pattern that now fails on Claude's newest models and nowhere else.

Anthropic, OpenAI and Google all now keep your conversation on their servers — and shipped three incompatible contracts. One is an ephemeral latency trick you must code a replay path for; two are durable storage that is ON by default, for 30 and 55 days. The axis that actually decides your design.

Render your context into a picture and the vision encoder becomes a compression dial. Measured across Anthropic, OpenAI and Google, an image of code counts 76–87% fewer input tokens than the same code as text — and on Gemini it can cost 6.95x MORE. documents.t: Агент, который может редактировать файлы и запускать команды, мощен и опасен. Минимальные привилегии, песочница, одобрение человеком, защита от инъекций в промпт, лимиты бюджета — как безопасно запускать агентов.
Бюджеты размышления и усилие рассуждения в Claude, GPT, Gemini, DeepSeek и Qwen — когда стоит тратить токены на размышление, а когда нет.
GPT-Live and the new speech-native models listen and talk at the same time. What full-duplex changes, how it works, and the voice-AI landscape now.
documents.s: FFull-Duplex Voice AI: Why Voice Agents Suddenly Got Real

documents.t: Anthropic opened Claude voice to Opus, Sonnet, and connected apps on July 23, 2026 — but kept the turn-based stack. What actually changed, when to switch models mid-call, and how the design bet differs from OpenAI's full-duplex GPT-Live.
documents.s: CClaude Voice with Opus & Sonnet (July 2026): Reasoning-First Voice vs GPT-Live

documents.t: On September 15, 2026 Google shipped gemini-3.8-live and gemini-3.8-live-extended-thinking. The launch post covers benchmarks. This page covers the rest: which model to pick, the migration traps coming from 3.1 Flash Live (async tools are now the default, thinkingLevel errors, proactive audio can't be turned off), the 15-minute and 2-minute session walls, and why a voice session's cost grows faster than its length.
documents.s: GGemini 3.8 Live and Live Extended Thinking: The Builder's Field Guide to Google's New Voice Models (Sep 2026)

documents.t: Anthropic's Sept 2026 open-source blueprint for shopping and merchant agents on Claude — the split-agent shape, the staged-write guardrail, and the patterns you can steal even if you're not building commerce.

Wafer-scale chips and LPUs are serving frontier models at hundreds of tokens per second. What actually limits inference speed, the new hardware race, and why fast tokens change agents, voice and reasoning.
documents.s: TToken Speed: Why AI Inference Suddenly Got 10-15× Faster

documents.t: Mercury 2 answers a full reasoning question in 1.7 seconds at 1,009 tok/s; Gemini Diffusion samples at 1,479 tok/s against Gemini 2.5 Flash's 272.4. Same transformers, different decoding algorithm. The practical guide: why the open-weight pioneer's own README says quality peaks when you use one step per token, the conditional-independence bug that makes parallel decoding wrong, block diffusion as the fix that restored the KV cache, how DiffusionGemma converted an autoregressive Gemma 4 for under 10% of its training budget, and the masked-infill jailbreak that hits 100% on an aligned dLLM.
documents.s: DDiffusion LLMs: The Models That Don't Write Left to Right

documents.t: Claude, GPT and Gemini can all drive a screen now — but each exposes a different action space, coordinate contract and safety gate. What actually breaks, and how to build a loop that survives it.

A new class of browser — best exemplified by ego lite, which hit #1 on GitHub Trending on July 24, 2026 — lets Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and any other coding agent drive an isolated Chromium session that inherits your real logins. What Spaces and semantic snapshots actually solve, why it undercuts Playwright for agent work, and the security cost of sharing session cookies with an autonomous process.
documents.s: SShared-Login Browsers for AI Agents: The ego lite Pattern

documents.t: On August 6, 2026 Cloudflare launched Kitesurf, a stateless, agent-first browser that runs entirely in V8 isolates on Workers. It uses 3-7x less CPU and memory than Chromium on common agent tasks — at the cost of ~1.7x wall-clock time. Written in Rust, using Firefox's CSS parser (Stylo) and the Blitz rendering engine, drop-in compatible with Puppeteer/Playwright via the Chrome DevTools Protocol. This page: what changed, when to reach for it instead of headless Chrome, how to wire it into Claude Code / Codex / your MCP client, and the four things it flat-out can't do yet.
documents.s: CCloudflare Kitesurf: The First Browser Runtime Built for AI Agents (Not Humans)

documents.t: Vercel Labs shipped agent-desktop on 28 October 2026 — accessibility-tree computer use in Rust, Apache-2.0, for macOS/Windows/Linux. The headline is 'AX trees instead of pixels'. The part worth stealing is its correctness model: refs scoped to a snapshot, fail-closed resolution that refuses to guess, tri-state properties, and a retry rule built on DELIVERED vs NOT DELIVERED rather than success vs failure.

One SKILL.md file, thirty-two agents. What the Agent Skills open standard actually is, how progressive disclosure keeps context cheap, what breaks portability, and how to write a skill that runs unchanged in Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI and Cursor.

Colibrì is a pure-C, zero-dependency engine that runs GLM-5.2 (744B), Kimi K3 (2.8T), DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and six other frontier MoE models on a 16–32 GB machine by keeping the dense layers in RAM and streaming the routed experts from NVMe. This page explains the memory hierarchy, the numbers that decide whether it is usable for you (0.05 to 6.8 tok/s), the SSD-wear and speculative-decoding gotchas, and the exact commands to get a first token.
documents.s: CColibrì: Run a 744B MoE From Your SSD (and What It Really Costs You)

documents.t: On September 10, 2026 OpenAI put the Codex harness behind a single API call: the Agents API public beta — durable sessions, hosted or self-hosted sandboxes, automatic compaction, tool search, subagents. Anthropic has run the same shape since April as Managed Agents. Both use the same four primitives; they differ on permissions, secrets, budgets, network policy and what the sandbox costs. The side-by-side, the request shapes, the six gotchas, and when to pick which.
documents.s: OOpenAI Agents API vs Claude Managed Agents: The Hosted Agent Loop, Compared

documents.t: google/ax hit the Hacker News front page on September 20–21, 2026 (507 points). It is not a model, a harness or a hosted API: it is a kubectl-shaped orchestrator that runs agent Tasks in sandboxes on top of Agent Substrate, with Workspaces (git + MCP + skills), Gateways (egress allowlists) and Models (provider + secret) as declarative resources. What the four primitives do, what survives suspend/resume and what does not, the runner contract your image must honour, the GKE requirements, and why the June-era docs no longer match the CLI.
documents.s: AAX (Agent Executor): Google's Open Agent Runtime, Explained for Builders (2026)

documents.t: TypeSafe AI's Jev (out of stealth September 15, 2026) is a model that never writes text: you send it program state plus typed questions and it returns calibrated probabilities for all of them in one parallel pass, 70–500 ms, $0.042 per million input tokens, output free. Two Hacker News front-page stories on September 21 (Kev, an Apache-2.0 recreation on Qwen3.5, and the jev-leftpad joke) made it the week's topic. What a System One model actually does, what the 'cannot hallucinate' claim really guarantees, the vendor numbers next to the one independent test, where a decision model belongs in a Claude agent loop, and how to run Kev or Nimble locally.
documents.s: SSystem One Decision Models: Jev, Kev and the Open Clones, Explained for Builders (2026)

documents.t: Two weeks after Jev made decision models a category, the open stack caught up: Jeff fine-tunes a 0.8B Qwen into a Jev-compatible classifier in ~2 hours on one workstation GPU, and PostHog's Jeeves shows that letting a decision model think first beats Jev on its own benchmark. What the training recipe actually is (cross-entropy over option letters, a separately fitted temperature), where tiny models beat the API and where they get destroyed, the 26-option ceiling, the 20x CPU latency cliff, and the boring embeddings baseline that scored 93.0% and that you must beat before any of this is worth doing.
documents.s: TTrain Your Own Decision Model: Jeff, Jeeves and the DIY System One Stack (Sep 2026)

documents.t: PrismML compressed Qwen3.8-27B to 1.75 bits per weight and 5.95 GB. The practical guide nobody wrote: why stock llama.cpp loads the file and silently produces garbage, why the bigger 7.21 GB file is faster on an H100 but slower on a 4090, why 5.95 GB of weights needs 12 GB of VRAM, and which capabilities the 98.2% retention headline quietly loses.
documents.s: TTernary Quantization in Practice: Bonsai 2 27B in 5.95 GB

documents.t: Unreal Labs shipped an MIT-licensed Go harness that matches Codex's pass rate on Terminal-Bench 4.0 for 39% less money — by never making the model wait for a tool. The event-log mechanism, why turn count is the real cost unit, and the three things they deliberately refused to build.
documents.s: AAsync-First Agent Harnesses: What Unreal Agent Changes

documents.t: The MIT-licensed memory server that topped GitHub trending — retain, recall and reflect, four parallel retrievers fused by RRF, observations that get refined instead of overwritten, and the 83.6%-vs-39.0% result that says architecture beats model size.

Fireworks post-trained Kimi K3 to stop over-thinking and shipped the result as Ember-1 — same price per token, 35–50% fewer reasoning tokens, and it beats K3 at max effort on two of five benchmarks. Why turning effort down is not the same thing, what the '-51.9% / -23.1 USD' column really says, the implied cost per benchmark task, the modality that quietly disappears, and the Kimi K3 licence clause that lets a derivative stay closed.
documents.s: EEmber-1: Kimi K3's Answers for 40% Fewer Tokens (Sep 2026)

documents.t: At DevDay on September 29, 2026 OpenAI shipped dots — persistent agents that each get their own cloud computer and browser, run on GPT-6 Astra, and keep working while you are logged off. The launch coverage stops at the demo. This page covers the mechanism: the five-rung permission ladder, why proactive research is read-only at the tool layer rather than the prompt layer, what the published safety numbers actually measure, and how a dot compares to Claude Managed Agents and Cowork.
documents.s: OOpenAI Dots: The Always-On Agent, and the Permission Ladder Underneath It

documents.t: AMD is paying about $8.2 billion for World Labs, and two very different things are being sold under the same name. Frame generators like Genie keep the world inside the model and cap a session at 60 seconds. 3D generators like Marble hand you Gaussian splats you own, render for free and cannot collide with. The API shapes, the export tiers, the WorldScore evidence, the open weights you can run, and the five jobs a world model will not do.
documents.s: WWorld Models: What You Can Actually Build Today

documents.t: "They nerfed it" is the most-repeated claim in AI and the least-measured. On the Claude API the weights behind a model ID cannot change — every current ID is a pinned snapshot. But seven other things can change under you without a new model, from a published system-prompt update to a harness that silently swaps models mid-session. Here is what can and cannot move, why the most-cited 'GPT-4 got dumber' result was an eval bug, and a measurement protocol you can run in an afternoon.
documents.s: IIs the model nerfed? How to actually tell

documents.t: Pi 1.0 shipped 1 October 2026 and went to #1 on Hacker News. The interesting part is not the TUI — it is the context engineering: a QuickJS/WASM sandbox where tool results never enter the model's context, four MCP exposure modes, a 3,000-token ceiling on inlined tool declarations, and a trick that appends a new system-prompt section to the transcript instead of mutating tool definitions so your prompt cache survives. Plus the deliberate omissions (no sub-agents, no plan mode), the $0.05 cache-warming rule, and the trust gap that loads a cloned repo's AGENTS.md without asking.
documents.s: PPi 1.0: The Minimal Harness, and the Codemode Trick That Fixes MCP Token Bloat

documents.t: DeepSeek Harness (dsh) passed 242,000 stars and shipped desktop installers on 1 October 2026. The headline is 'everything is a plugin' — and unlike most such claims this one is load-bearing: the model adapter, the tool registry, the session log and the agent loop are all replaceable from a YAML patch file. This page covers the three facts that matter to a Claude user (it runs your existing Claude Code hooks.json, it speaks anthropic-messages, and run_code is codemode by default), the three-mode sandbox and the kernel primitives behind it, the append-only session log invariant, and the config override that silently deletes your other providers.
documents.s: DDeepSeek Harness: the agent where the agent loop itself is a plugin

documents.t: Strata runs Qwen3.8-Flash-Next (125B, 6B active) on a 12 GB gaming GPU at interactive speed. This page explains the three architecture facts that make it possible, reads the benchmark table honestly, and prices the quality you give up: 91.3% of SWE-bench Verified against 98.7% of LiveCodeBench, a KV-cache setting that passes needle tests while losing 8-12% perplexity, a speed mode that strips refusal directions, and a measured vision regression on identical weights.
documents.s: SStrata: a 125B MoE at 94 tok/s on a 12 GB Card — and the Exact Bill

documents.t: Every launch post leads with a benchmark number. Almost none of them tell you the three things that decide what it means: which scaffold produced it, how many trials it averages, and whether the model had already seen the answers. A reader's manual for SWE-bench, SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Pro and the arena leaderboards — with the vendor's own footnotes as evidence.
documents.s: HHow to Read an AI Benchmark Without Getting Fooled

documents.t: ds4 is a 23.6k-star, pure-C engine from the creator of Redis that runs DeepSeek V4 Flash, GLM 5.x and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next locally — and refuses to run anything else. This page explains the three mechanisms a general runtime will not give you (asymmetric routed-expert quantization, bounded expert streaming from SSD, KV snapshots that survive a restart), reads its own numbers honestly — the 126 t/s headline is an eight-GPU aggregate across 16 sessions, not your Mac — and prices the real cost of the overfit bet: deliberately disposable model support, 761 open issues, and a main branch that last moved on 20 September 2026.
documents.s: DDwarfStar (ds4) and the Rise of Overfit Inference Engines

documents.t: Europe's trillion-parameter MoE: why 49B active params still need ~525 GB at 4-bit, the 1M context that evaluators measured at ~512K, a 50% launch promo that hides the real cost-per-task, an Intelligence Index of 38 against Opus 5.5's 58 — and the staged weight release where vetted partners get a less-moderated build first.
documents.s: MMistral Large 4 (Le Chonk): the 1.05T open weight you can't download yet

documents.t: Cactus Compute's Whistle fits a multilingual ASR model in 16.9 MB and hits 11.1 ms to first token on a CPU. The size claim is real. This page reads the vendor's own benchmark chart bar by bar — including the three competitor columns it declines to label — and finds the pattern that explains every field complaint: Whistle wins on close-mic single-speaker audio and is the worst of the three on real meeting audio, 4.6 WER points behind a model 8.6x its size. Plus the 30-second architectural wall, the streaming API the launch thread missed, and the one knob that took a tester from 70/170 to 164/170.
documents.s: WWhistle: Speech-to-Text in 16.9 MB — and the Benchmark Bars Nobody Labelled

documents.t: On 20 October 2026 DeepSeek open-sourced DeepInfer, the engine behind its production service — 16.3k stars in a day, 2,251 points on Hacker News. This page covers the four things the headlines missed: it is a vLLM fork, not a from-scratch engine; 'NVIDIA SM100' excludes every H100 and every consumer GPU you own; its decode throughput is published under full-acceptance accounting, which counts drafted tokens whether or not they were accepted; and its genuinely important feature — batch-invariant inference — is mutually exclusive with its own speculative decoder.
documents.s: DDeepInfer: DeepSeek's Own Inference Engine, Read Honestly

documents.t: HybridAgent is the first open-weight agent that does most of its thinking as hidden states instead of tokens — 170-183 latent steps per task against ~300 text tokens, 35.5-54.7% fewer tokens, 2.7-3.7x cheaper. The mechanism (a ~10M-parameter adapter), the reason it loops forever if you load it in llama.cpp, and why 'inspectable latent thoughts' is the most contested claim in the paper.
documents.s: LLatent Reasoning: Agents That Think Without Words

documents.t: claude-mem has 103,000 GitHub stars and solves the complaint every coding-agent user has: the agent forgets everything when the session ends. Underneath, it is a second model running in a background daemon that reads every tool call you make — and on the hosted path its own cost dataset maps that observer to a DeepSeek model, not Claude. The six hooks, the exit-code contract that can block your session, the three-layer recall that makes the token math work, where the data lands, who pays for the compression, and a checklist for evaluating any memory layer before you install it.
documents.s: TThe Third-Party Memory Layer: How claude-mem Actually Works

documents.t: 483 points on Hacker News for running DeepSeek-V4-Flash on a laptop CPU with no GPU. The mechanism is real and genuinely clever — two new block-64 tensor types with single-instruction SIMD decode, a chess engine's search used as a draftless speculator, and huge pages that cut dTLB misses per token from 18.42M to 0.31M. But it is a 1.69-bit quant, the 'lossless' numbers are measured against the already-1.7-bit file rather than BF16, and in a 208-comment thread nobody reproduced the headline on 64 GB of x86. What it is, what to run, and what to disbelieve.
documents.s: Lllama-modchip: a 284B model on 64 GB of RAM, read honestly

Скопировать как Markdown Продвинутый By mid-2026, most non-trivial agent work is done by several agents cooperating — a research agent hands off to a writer, a billing agent talks to a support agent from a different vendor, an orchestrator delegates to a specialist inside another org's cloud. A2A (Agent-to-Agent) is the open protocol that lets those agents find each other, describe what they can do, and hand tasks back and forth — even when they were built on different frameworks by different teams. Where MCP connects an agent to its tools and data, A2A connects an agent to another agent. They compose; they don't compete. What you'll learn State exactly what A2A is for — and where the MCP boundary sits Read an Agent Card and know what a receiving agent will do with it Walk a task through all eight lifecycle states, including the two that are interrupted rather than terminal Choose between SSE streaming and webhook push for long-running tasks Recognize the non-obvious features: signed cards, multi-tenant endpoints, and structured data parts Последняя проверка: 2026-07-20. A2A is stabilizing but the spec still evolves: the v1.0.1 release, new bindings, and SDK feature gaps land regularly. Treat exact method names, error codes, and SDK support claims below as perishable and check the linked spec and the a2aproject/A2A repo before shipping a production integration. Сверьтесь с официальным источником.

Every agent framework — LangGraph, CrewAI, the Claude Agent SDK, the OpenAI Agents SDK, Microsoft's Agent Framework, custom in-house loops — solved tool use by leaning on the model's native tool-calling and, increasingly, on MCP as the universal tool-and-data connector. That gave us agent ↔ tool. What none of them solved on their own was agent ↔ agent across a boundary. Two problems kept coming up: Discovery. How does agent A know that agent B exists, what it can do, how to authenticate against it, and whether it supports streaming? A hand-rolled README is not a protocol. Task hand-off. Once A wants B to do something, how do they exchange the work (not the model's chat) — including files, structured data, progress updates, and the fact that B might need to pause and ask A for input? Framework-specific answers (LangGraph subgraphs, CrewAI crews, subagents inside one runtime) work great inside one process. They stop at the org boundary. A2A is the piece that lets an agent in your product delegate to an agent in someone else's product without either side leaking its internals — Google's Todd Segal calls it "the secure foundation for personal, team, and domain-specific agents to work together seamlessly across any platform." Governance sits with the Linux Foundation, and by April 2026 the project reported 150+ supporting organizations including AWS, Microsoft, Salesforce, SAP, ServiceNow, and IBM.

Both are open protocols. Both use JSON over HTTP. They solve different problems and are designed to compose: MCP = agent-to-tool. An MCP server exposes tools (search, read_file, run_query) and resources (docs, prompts) to a model-driven client. The client is an agent; the server is a passive capability provider. See MCP & connecting to tools for how Claude uses it. A2A = agent-to-agent. An A2A endpoint exposes an agent — an entity with its own reasoning loop that will decide how to solve a delegated task. Both sides are agents; either can call the other. The concrete difference shows up in the wire format. An MCP tools/call returns a result and closes. An A2A SendMessage opens a task — a stateful thing with its own lifecycle that can stream updates, ask for clarification, or run for hours in the background. If your endpoint's answer is always "here's the result of one function," it's a tool — publish it via MCP. If it's "let me think about that and get back to you, and I might need to ask a follow-up question," it's an agent — publish it via A2A. Most serious systems will run both: an agent whose inside uses MCP to reach tools, and whose outside speaks A2A so peers can hand it work.
documents.s: MCP vs. A2A — the mental model

documents.t: An Agent Card is a JSON document served at a well-known URL that tells any potential caller everything they need to talk to your agent. Think OpenAPI + robots.txt, for agents. Every A2A interaction starts by fetching one. The card includes: Identity — id, name, description, provider (org details). Endpoints — the service URLs and which protocol bindings (JSON-RPC, gRPC, REST) are available. Capabilities — feature flags: streaming, pushNotifications, extendedAgentCard. Skills — declared agent functions with input/output schemas (this is what B says it can do). Security schemes — one or more of APIKey, HTTPAuth (Basic/Bearer), OAuth2 (Authorization Code, Client Credentials, Device Code), OpenIdConnect, MutualTLS. The caller reads this to know what credentials to bring before the first call. Signature — an optional cryptographic signature over the card. That last field is the one worth pausing on. A Signed Agent Card lets a receiving agent verify that the card was actually issued by the domain owner — the DNS/PKI equivalent of "yes, this really is agents.acme.com, not something an attacker planted." Combined with mTLS auth, it closes the door on rogue Agent Cards being served from spoofed hosts, which is how you'd otherwise get a prompt injection at the discovery layer: an attacker's Agent Card lying about what tools it exposes and what data it wants.
documents.s: The Agent Card — the piece of the spec that matters most

documents.t: Once you SendMessage to an A2A agent, the work becomes a Task — a first-class object with an ID you can poll, subscribe to, cancel, or list. The task moves through eight states, and it's worth noticing that only five are terminal: SUBMITTED — the server acknowledged the task. WORKING — active processing. INPUT_REQUIRED — interrupted: the agent needs more information from the caller. Not an error; expected in real workflows. AUTH_REQUIRED — interrupted: the agent needs the caller to authenticate (or re-authenticate) before it can continue. COMPLETED — success. Terminal. FAILED — error. Terminal. CANCELED — caller-initiated cancellation. Terminal. REJECTED — the agent declined the task (policy, capability, quota). Terminal. The interrupted states are the point. Legacy RPC assumes one call → one result. Real agent work looks like "start the analysis, come back an hour later, notice I need to ask a clarifying question, wait for the answer, resume, finish." A2A models that natively. Your calling code has to be a small state machine, not a synchronous await.

Long-running tasks need a way to deliver updates. A2A gives you two async models — pick per task, not per agent: Streaming (SendStreamingMessage / SubscribeToTask). Server-Sent Events over the open HTTP connection. Client stays connected, receives TaskStatusUpdateEvent and TaskArtifactUpdateEvent in order. Great for interactive UIs and short-to-medium tasks. Falls over if the client can't hold a connection (mobile, serverless, browser tabs going to sleep). Push notifications (webhook config). The client registers a webhook via CreateTaskPushNotificationConfig. The server POSTs updates to that URL as they happen. The client can be totally offline in between. This is the mode for tasks that outlive an HTTP connection — think "run this overnight" or "call me back when the batch job finishes." Both require the agent to advertise support in its Agent Card (capabilities.streaming: true and/or capabilities.pushNotifications: true). A conforming caller checks first and downgrades cleanly.

An A2A Message is composed of one or more Parts. Each Part can be one of: text — string content (the chat-y part). raw — binary file, base64-encoded in JSON. url — a reference to an external file (avoids inlining huge blobs). data — a structured JSON object or array, with an optional metadata map. The data part is what makes A2A useful for machine-to-machine work. Two agents can exchange typed payloads — an order, a purchase spec, a JSON diff — without pretending to have a natural-language conversation about it. This is also what makes protocols like Agent Payments (AP2) layer cleanly on top of A2A: the payment intent rides in a data part with a known schema.

This one is easy to miss. A single A2A endpoint can host many agents, served through the GetExtendedAgentCard method after authentication. A SaaS vendor can offer one URL and return different, tenant-specific Agent Cards depending on which API key or OAuth scope the caller presents. From the caller's side it looks like one endpoint per agent; from the vendor's side it's one deployment. If you're building agent-serving infrastructure, this is the pattern that lets you scale without one hostname per tenant.
documents.s: Multi-tenant endpoints — one URL, many agents

documents.t: The full protocol has a lot of surface, but the happy-path flow is short: Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Discover⌄ Fetch the Agent Card from a well-known URL. Verify its signature if one is present. Read `capabilities`, `skills`, and `securitySchemes` to decide whether this agent can do what you need and what auth you'll bring. ←PreviousNext→ 2Authenticate⌄ Obtain the credential the card asked for — an API key, an OAuth2 token, an mTLS cert. If you're going to talk to many agents, cache tokens; A2A doesn't dictate a session model. ←PreviousNext→ 3Send the message⌄ Call `a2a.SendMessage` (or `a2a.SendStreamingMessage` for SSE) with a Message composed of Parts. You get back a `taskId`. ←PreviousNext→ 4Track⌄ Choose: hold the SSE stream open, or poll `a2a.GetTask` by ID, or register a webhook via `CreateTaskPushNotificationConfig`. Handle `INPUT_REQUIRED` and `AUTH_REQUIRED` by responding with follow-up messages, not by treating them as failures. ←PreviousNext→ 5Consume the result⌄ On `COMPLETED`, read the `TaskArtifactUpdateEvent` payloads for outputs. On `FAILED` / `REJECTED`, inspect the error code — the spec defines typed errors like `ContentTypeNotSupportedError`, `UnsupportedOperationError`, `VersionNotSupportedError`, and `ExtensionSupportRequiredError`. ←PreviousNext→

Discovery is just an HTTP GET. This is the shape of a request a client would make to inspect a candidate agent before ever sending it work: Fetch and inspect an Agent Card CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ GET https://agents.example.com/.well-known/agent.json Accept: application/json # Response (abbreviated): # { # "id": "acme/support-router", # "name": "Acme Support Router", # "provider": {"organization": "Acme, Inc."}, # "endpoints": [ # {"url": "https://agents.example.com/a2a", "protocol": "jsonrpc"} # ], # "capabilities": { # "streaming": true, # "pushNotifications": true, # "extendedAgentCard": true # }, # "skills": [ # {"id": "route_ticket", "inputSchema": {...}, "outputSchema": {...}} # ], # "securitySchemes": { # "primary": {"type": "oauth2", "flows": {...}} # }, # "signature": {"alg": "EdDSA", "value": "..."} # } Note what's not in the card: nothing about the model behind the agent, its prompt, its tools, or its private state. That opacity is deliberate — A2A treats a peer agent as a black box you delegate work to, not a system you introspect.

Treating INPUT_REQUIRED as an error. It isn't; it's the protocol asking your code to respond. If your caller code only branches on "did it succeed or fail," you'll break every interactive workflow. Ignoring the Agent Card's capabilities. Sending a streaming request to an agent that didn't advertise streaming: true gets you an UnsupportedOperationError. Read the card, downgrade cleanly. Assuming the streaming connection is durable. Mobile clients, serverless runtimes, browser tabs — they all drop the SSE connection. For anything longer than "a chat turn," prefer push notifications. Skipping signature verification because it's optional. If you're consuming Agent Cards from outside your org, verify the signature — otherwise you've created a discovery-layer prompt injection vector. Confusing A2A with MCP. Publishing an A2A endpoint for a stateless single-shot function is overkill; that's a tool, and MCP is the right protocol. Publishing an MCP tool for something that takes minutes and needs to ask clarifying questions is under-engineering; that's an agent, and A2A is the right protocol. Check yourself 0/4

Put together with the rest of the agent picture: Inside an agent, MCP is how you reach tools and data — including remote MCP servers you didn't write. Between agents in one framework, you use whatever the framework gives you — subagents in Claude Code, LangGraph subgraphs, CrewAI crews, etc. This is fastest but locks you to one runtime. Between agents across frameworks, teams, or vendors, A2A is what you reach for. Read Open-Source AI Agent Frameworks for the runtime side; A2A is the wire between those runtimes. The rule of thumb: if the boundary is a process boundary, framework-native handoffs are fine. If it's an org, cloud, or trust boundary, use A2A.
documents.s: Where A2A sits in your stack

Скопировать как Markdown Продвинутый What you'll learn Understand what 'memory' means in this class of tool: not a saved transcript, but observations extracted by a second model that watches your tool calls Learn the six-hook lifecycle and the exit-code contract that decides whether a broken memory layer degrades quietly or blocks your coding session See the detail almost nobody checks: the observer is a separate model on a provider you choose, and claude-mem's own cost dataset maps its hosted observer to a DeepSeek model — your session content does not necessarily go to Claude Follow the three-layer recall that makes the token arithmetic work — a ~50-100-token index hit before a ~500-1,000-token detail fetch — and why that ordering is the whole design Know where the data lands: SQLite with FTS5, a Chroma vector store that indexes every extracted fact separately, and a worker on port 37700 + (uid % 100) Work out who pays for the compression, and why a $30/month hosted tier exists at all Avoid five documented failure modes, starting with the one where the observer's reasoning tokens ate the session's output budget Apply an eight-point evaluation checklist to any agent memory layer before you let it read every file your agent touches Every coding-agent user hits the same wall. You spend an hour establishing context — which module owns what, why the previous approach failed, the one gotcha in the build — and then the session ends and all of it is gone. Tomorrow you explain it again. claude-mem is the most popular answer to that problem by a very wide margin: 103,252 stars on GitHub as of 26 October 2026, Apache-2.0, and shipping fast enough that it went from v13.38 to v15.2.1 in the twelve days before this page was written. It works with Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, OpenCode, Antigravity, Claude Desktop and several others. This page is not an install guide — the README does that well. It is the thing the README does not do: explain what the tool actually is architecturally, what it costs, what reads your code, and what breaks. Most of what follows comes from the repository's own docs/ folder, which is detailed, honest, and almost certainly unread by the large majority of those 103,000 stargazers. Последняя проверка: 2026-10-26. На этой странице приводятся факты, которые меняются со временем — считайте дату выше показателем её актуальности. This project ships multiple releases per week and renames features between majors — treat every specific port, flag, command, default and price here as a snapshot, and check the current release notes before relying on one. The architecture-overview hook table lists Setup plus five lifecycle events; the README describes six hooks including UserPromptSubmit and Stop separately. Where the two disagree, this page follows architecture-overview.md and says so.
documents.s: The Third-Party Memory Layer: How claude-mem Actually Works

documents.t: The first mental model to discard is "it saves my chats". It does not. The unit of storage is an observation: a structured note with a type, a title and a narrative, extracted by a model from what your agent did. The flow, from the repo's own data-flow diagram: You submit a prompt. The session-init handler registers the session and asks the worker for semantically relevant context. Your agent uses a tool. The PostToolUse hook posts that tool usage to the worker, which enqueues it. The worker's SDKAgent — a model session, running in a background daemon — reads the queue and produces observations and summaries. Those land in SQLite, get synced into a Chroma vector store, and get broadcast to a local UI over server-sent events. So the thing watching your work is a second model, and the thing it reads is every tool call: file reads, file writes, command output, search results. That is the price of admission for this entire category of tool, and it is worth saying plainly before any of the rest. What you'll learn A memory layer is not a storage feature. It is a second model with a standing subscription to everything your first model touches. Evaluate it the way you would evaluate adding any model to your pipeline — what it reads, where it sends it, who pays for its tokens, and what happens when it fails.
documents.s: What it stores is not your transcript

documents.t: claude-mem installs as a set of lifecycle hooks, each invoked as a single shell-free command of the form claude-mem hook claude-code <event>. Per docs/architecture-overview.md: Event Handler What it does Timeout Setup version-check.js Sub-100 ms version-marker check; prints a hint to run npx claude-mem repair on mismatch 60s SessionStart worker start + context Starts the worker service and injects prior context 60s UserPromptSubmit session-init Registers the session, starts the SDK agent, semantic injection 60s PostToolUse observation Captures tool usage and enqueues it in the worker 120s Summary summarize Requests a session summary from the SDK agent 120s SessionEnd session-complete Ends the session and drains pending messages 30s Now the part that will matter to you at 2 a.m. The hook orchestrator implements an explicit degradation contract: Transport errors — ECONNREFUSED, timeouts, 5xx from the worker — exit 0. Non-blocking. The worker being down never blocks your coding session. Client bugs — 4xx, TypeError, ReferenceError — exit 2. Blocking, on the stated reasoning that these indicate a bug needing a fix. That is a defensible design, and it has a consequence worth internalising: "the memory daemon is dead" is harmless, but "the memory daemon is answering 400" is not. A malformed request, a schema drift after a partial upgrade, or an expired key that surfaces as a 4xx is in the category the tool deliberately chose to make loud. This is also why the Setup hook nags about npx claude-mem repair after an external plugin upgrade — a version-skewed install is exactly how you reach the blocking branch. Watch out If a coding session starts failing immediately after you updated a plugin, check your memory layer before you debug your agent. The published contract here is that transport failures degrade silently and client-side failures block — so the symptom of a half-upgraded install is a session that will not start, not a session without memory.
documents.s: The six hooks, and the one contract that matters operationally

documents.t: Any memory system can store things. The hard part is retrieval that does not cost more context than it saves — dump twenty remembered notes into every session start and you have made the problem worse. claude-mem's answer, shipped as the default in v15.0.0 on 20 October 2026 under the name Smart memory search, is a three-step search the agent reasons through rather than a single retrieval: Guided walkthrough1 of 3 1Search the compact index⌄ A full-text query (SQLite FTS5, optionally hybridised with Chroma vectors) returns a compact list of hits with observation IDs. The README puts these at roughly 50-100 tokens per result — enough to judge relevance, not enough to be useful on its own. ←PreviousNext→ 2Inspect the timeline around what looks relevant⌄ Given a promising observation ID, fetch the chronological context around it. This is the step that distinguishes 'a note that matches your keywords' from 'the note that matches, plus what happened immediately before and after it'. ←PreviousNext→ 3Fetch full details for the selected IDs only⌄ Only now does the full observation text enter context, at roughly 500-1,000 tokens each. The README's claim for this ordering is about ~10x token savings versus fetching details up front. ←PreviousNext→ The three steps are exposed to the agent as MCP tools — search(query, type, date, project, limit), timeline(observation_id, query) and get_observations(ids[]) — which is why the agent can reason between them instead of the retrieval being a fixed pipeline. The transferable lesson here has nothing to do with claude-mem. Filter on cheap representations, then pay for detail on the survivors. It is the same pattern as reading a search-results page before opening a tab, the same pattern as a database index before a row fetch, and it is the correct shape for any retrieval you bolt onto an agent. If you are designing your own, see context engineering for the general framing and how agent memory actually works for the taxonomy this tool sits inside.
documents.s: The three-layer recall is the actual idea

documents.t: Everything local lands under ~/.claude-mem/. Two stores, with distinct jobs: SQLite (claude-mem.db), with FTS5 for full-text search: Table Purpose sdk_sessions Session lifecycle, and the mapping between the two session IDs observations The extracted notes: type, title, narrative, content hash session_summaries Per-session request / learned / completed user_prompts Your prompt history pending_messages The per-session work queue observation_feedback Usage signals per observation ChromaDB (chroma.sqlite3) for vector embeddings, accessed through chroma-mcp over stdio. The detail worth noticing: each observation produces several documents, not one — obs_{id}_narrative for the main text plus obs_{id}_fact_0, obs_{id}_fact_1 and so on for each extracted fact. Facts are embedded individually, which is why a query about one specific detail can retrieve an observation whose overall summary is about something else. The worker is an Express daemon on a per-user port: 37700 + (uid % 100). If you have seen localhost:37777 in the project's own release notes and docs, that is one uid's port, not a constant — which is a small thing that will cost you ten minutes exactly once. What you'll learn The worker binds a local HTTP API and serves a UI from it. docs/security.md is explicit that the server beta defaults to API-key auth, that keys use a cmem_ prefix and are shown once with only a SHA-256 hash stored, and that the loopback development bypass requires two environment variables set together (CLAUDE_MEM_AUTH_MODE=local-dev and CLAUDE_MEM_ALLOW_LOCAL_DEV_BYPASS=1) and must not be used behind a reverse proxy or on a publicly reachable bind address. Treat that as a hard rule: this daemon holds a searchable index of everything your agents read.

Here is the fact that most surprised me, and the reason this page exists. The observer is a separate model call, and you choose its provider at install time: npx claude-mem install --provider [host|openrouter|gemini|anthropic]. Four options, four different answers to "where does my session content go". The repository's own cost-accounting dataset, in docs/expense-pricing/README.md, documents how to price observer traffic — and in doing so documents what the hosted observer is. Its join recipe says to resolve the model id cmem-observer to deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash on or after 2026-08-08, and to deepseek/deepseek-chat before that. There is an apparent contradiction here worth resolving, because you will hit it if you read the repo yourself: docs/architecture-overview.md labels the observer component SDKAgent (Claude Agent SDK), which sounds like it must be Claude. Both things are true at once. The Agent SDK is the harness — the loop that manages the session and parses responses — and it can be pointed at a non-Anthropic endpoint, which is exactly what the v15.0.2 release notes imply when they describe observer requests going to "OpenRouter, the cmem.ai gateway, and OpenAI-compatible endpoints". The SDK is the client; the provider flag decides who answers. Read the DeepSeek mapping carefully too, because it is easy to over- or under-state. It does not mean the project is hiding anything — the provider is a documented install flag and the dataset is published in the open repo. It does mean that a tool named claude-mem, on its hosted path, has been pricing its observer as a DeepSeek model, and that if your assumption was "this runs on Claude because of the name", the assumption was wrong. If your code cannot go to a third-party inference provider, --provider anthropic or a self-hosted OpenAI-compatible endpoint is the choice you have to make deliberately. The same dataset also tells you the shape of that traffic: the project's own notes treat observer usage as roughly 98% input tokens, which is exactly what you would expect from a process whose job is reading tool output and emitting short notes. Prompt-heavy, output-light. And that is the whole economics of the hosted tier. The paid product, CMEM Pro, is described on cmem.ai as hosted observation and cloud sync at $30/month after a 30-day free trial, with the pitch that hosted observation moves memory generation off your primary agent's subscription. In other words: by default, something has to pay for a second model to read everything your first model does. Either that is your own provider account and plan limits, or it is $30/month to someone else. The site is also careful to say the effect on token use depends on your workload and provider, and that Pro does not change the price or limits of another subscription. What you'll learn Any memory layer has a hidden second bill: the cost of the model that writes the memories. Before you install one, answer three questions. Which model does the extraction? Whose account pays for it? And is the content it reads allowed to go there? For claude-mem the answers are configurable, documented, and not what the name implies by default. The licensing split is also published, in docs/ip-boundary.md, and it is a clean open-core boundary worth knowing if you are planning to build on it: Apache-2.0 covers the memory engine, server, CLI, SDKs, REST schemas, MCP tools, the Claude Code and generic agent adapters and the storage adapters. Reserved commercial areas include hosted Magic Recall, team/org memory sync, the admin dashboard, SSO/SAML/SCIM, enterprise RBAC and audit UI, the DLP/policy engine, managed evals and private connectors. So the engine is genuinely yours to embed; the team and enterprise surface is not.
documents.s: Who pays for the compression — and which model reads your code

documents.t: These are all from the project's own release notes and architecture docs, which is the best possible source for a gotcha list. 1. The observer's reasoning tokens ate the session's output budget. Fixed in v15.0.2 (23 October 2026): observer requests to OpenRouter, the cmem.ai gateway and OpenAI-compatible endpoints now disable reasoning by default, because reasoning tokens were filling the output budget and leaving a session with nothing left to emit. This is the single most instructive bug in the list — it is a pure consequence of putting a reasoning model in a budget-constrained extraction role, and it will recur in anything you build that does the same. 2. Two session IDs that are not interchangeable. contentSessionId comes from the host and is invariant for the session; memorySessionId comes from the SDK agent and changes on every worker restart. The architecture doc calls the conversion between them critical for foreign-key constraints. If you query the SQLite store directly, this is the first thing that will confuse you. 3. Deduplication has a 30-second window. The content hash is SHA256(memory_session_id + title + narrative) truncated to 16 hex characters, and a repeat within 30 seconds returns the existing ID instead of inserting. Useful, and also a reason identical-looking observations can legitimately coexist if they arrived 31 seconds apart. 4. Generator crashes retry three times, then stop. Backoff is 1s, 2s, 4s; after more than three consecutive restarts the worker stops retrying and lets the iterator end. The counter resets when the generator completes work naturally. Pending messages survive restarts and are cleared by the parser path on the next valid response — so a persistently crashing observer means a silently growing queue, not lost input. 5. The install footprint is larger than npm install. npx claude-mem install sets up Bun and uv globally, runs bun install in the plugin cache, and writes a version marker. The README is explicit that npm install -g installs the SDK only and that you must use npx claude-mem install. Two package-manager runtimes installed globally by a memory tool is a reasonable engineering choice and also a supply-chain surface you should know you accepted — vetting agent skills is the general discipline. Watch out Release velocity cuts both ways. Between 13 and 25 October 2026 this project shipped v13.38 through v15.2.1 — two major version bumps in twelve days, with features renamed across them (the viewer, the recall mode, the work views). A tool this active fixes bugs fast and also breaks your notes fast. Pin a version if you are documenting it for a team, and read the release notes before upgrading rather than after.

docs/security.md and the README together give a usable picture: The local engine stores memory on your machine, under ~/.claude-mem/. Cloud sync is opt-in; if you enable it, synced data is also stored by CMEM. The site's own guidance is to read the privacy policy before connecting. CLAUDE_MEM_ONLINE_OPTIN=false skips the sign-in flow. Content wrapped in <private> tags is excluded from storage entirely — not written to the observation store, and not written to profile or project memory. That last one is the control most worth remembering, because it is the only in-band one. Everything else is a configuration decision you make once at install; <private> is the thing you can reach for mid-session when a secret, a customer name or a production hostname is about to pass through a tool call. It is also, by construction, a control you have to remember to use. For the broader question of what an agent ships off your machine in the normal course of doing its job, see what your agent uploads. Inspect what a memory layer has actually recorded about you CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ # Where the local stores live, and how big they have got du -sh ~/.claude-mem/ 2>/dev/null ls -la ~/.claude-mem/ # Which worker port is yours (the formula, not the number in the docs) python3 -c "import os; print(37700 + (os.getuid() % 100))" # Read the observation store directly — it is plain SQLite sqlite3 ~/.claude-mem/claude-mem.db ".tables" sqlite3 ~/.claude-mem/claude-mem.db \ "SELECT type, title, substr(narrative,1,90) FROM observations ORDER BY rowid DESC LIMIT 15;" # Which model actually wrote your memories (the field the cost docs join on) sqlite3 ~/.claude-mem/claude-mem.db \ "SELECT generated_by_model, COUNT(*) FROM observations GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC;" # And your own prompt history, which is stored separately sqlite3 ~/.claude-mem/claude-mem.db \ "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM user_prompts;" What you'll learn Column names come from the schema table in docs/architecture-overview.md and the join recipe in docs/expense-pricing/README.md, which names generated_by_model and created_at on observation rows. A project shipping two majors in twelve days may rename them — if a query errors, run .schema observations and adjust. The point of the exercise is not the exact SQL; it is that you can and should read what a memory layer wrote about you, because it is a local SQLite file and nothing stops you.
documents.s: What leaves your machine, and the one control to know

documents.t: This category is going to keep growing, and the questions generalise. Run these before you install the next one. Guided walkthrough1 of 8 1What is the unit of storage?⌄ A raw transcript, a model-extracted note, or a compiled knowledge artefact? Extraction means a second model's judgement sits between what happened and what you remember — which is usually what you want, and is also a place for errors to become permanent. ←PreviousNext→ 2Which model does the extraction, and whose bill is it?⌄ Ask explicitly. claude-mem makes it a flag with four values and documents its hosted observer as a DeepSeek model in its own cost dataset. If a tool will not tell you, that is your answer. ←PreviousNext→ 3Is retrieval filtered before it is fetched?⌄ A memory layer that injects everything it has at session start is a context tax, not a context saving. Look for a cheap index step before a detail step, and check what the index entry costs in tokens. ←PreviousNext→ 4What happens when it fails?⌄ Find the degradation contract. claude-mem publishes one: transport errors exit 0 and never block, client errors exit 2 and do. A tool without a stated contract will eventually block your session for a reason you cannot see. ←PreviousNext→ 5Can you read and delete the store yourself?⌄ A local SQLite file you can query and rm is a very different privacy posture from an opaque cloud index. Check both the local format and whether sync is opt-in or opt-out. ←PreviousNext→ 6Is there an in-band exclusion control?⌄ You will need to stop one specific thing from being recorded, mid-session, without reconfiguring anything. <private> tags are claude-mem's answer; a tool with no equivalent means your only control is 'do not use it for this work'. ←PreviousNext→ 7What does installing it actually install?⌄ Global runtimes, a background daemon, an MCP server, hooks on every tool call. All reasonable individually; worth counting before you accept them. ←PreviousNext→ 8How fast does it move, and do you need it to?⌄ Fast releases mean fast fixes and fast breakage. If you are rolling this out to a team, pin a version and own the upgrade, rather than letting every developer sit on a different major. ←PreviousNext→ Key takeaways claude-mem is not a transcript store. It is a second model in a background daemon that reads every tool call and writes structured observations — which is the real cost and the real capability of this entire tool class. The observer is a separate model on a provider you select at install time (host, OpenRouter, Gemini, or Anthropic). The project's own cost dataset maps its hosted cmem-observer id to deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash from 2026-08-08, so the name does not tell you where your code goes. Someone has to pay for the extraction. By default that is your own provider account; CMEM Pro's $30/month pitch is explicitly that hosted observation moves memory generation off your primary agent's subscription. Recall is three steps, not one: a ~50-100-token index hit, then timeline context, then a ~500-1,000-token detail fetch for selected IDs only. 'Filter cheap, fetch expensive' is the transferable pattern and the reason the token math works at all. The degradation contract is published and asymmetric: transport failures exit 0 and never block your session, client-side failures exit 2 and do. A half-upgraded install is therefore a session that will not start. Observer traffic is roughly 98% input tokens by the project's own accounting — a reading process, not a writing one. Price it that way. Each observation becomes multiple Chroma documents, one per extracted fact plus the narrative, which is why a query about a small detail can surface a note that is nominally about something else. The v15.0.2 fix is the most instructive bug in the project: a reasoning model in an extraction role spent the output budget on reasoning and left sessions with nothing to emit. Disable reasoning on any model you use as a summariser. Two package-manager runtimes (Bun and uv) get installed globally, a daemon binds 37700 + (uid % 100), and an MCP server joins your agent. All defensible, all worth counting as surface area before you accept them. The one in-band control is the <private> tag, which excludes content from storage entirely. Everything else is decided at install time. Check yourself 0/6
