Скопировать как Markdown Продвинутый For two years agents have been very good at deciding to buy something and very bad at actually paying for it. The workaround was always the same — pre-provision an API key, hand the agent a shared credit card, and hope it doesn't rack up a bill you can't unwind. In 2026 that gap closed. A small stack has emerged around one big idea — use HTTP 402 the way it was always meant to be used — and a real, generally-available AWS service now wraps it in the guardrails an actual business needs. This page is a practical field guide to that stack: how x402 works on the wire, why the upto scheme is the interesting one, what AgentCore Payments actually gives you at GA, and where the sharp edges are. What you'll learn Read a raw x402 challenge and understand the three headers, the two facilitator calls, and the three payment schemes Tell exact from upto and know which one your endpoint should advertise Set a payment session's spend cap and expiry so an agent cannot drain your wallet on a bad prompt Choose between Coinbase Privy (crypto rails) and Stripe Privy (card rails) inside AgentCore Payments Recognize the three real threats: prompt-injection-to-buy, facilitator misbehavior, and 'upto' over-settlement Последняя проверка: 2026-08-27. Numbers here decay fast — settlement volume, supported chains, exact SDK package names, and Bazar catalog contents move week to week. AgentCore Payments GA'd on 2026-08-18. Confirm the payment-session field names and Coinbase / Stripe integration surface against the AWS blog and the x402-foundation repo before you ship, and treat any header capitalization or scheme name as authoritative from the spec, not this page. Сверьтесь с официальным источником.
documents.s: Agent Payments: x402, MPP and AgentCore GA

documents.t: The moment an agent has real spending authority, four things break at once: The API key model was a workaround. Every "agent-friendly" API today asks you to mint a key, top up a balance, and hand the string to the agent. That's the human doing the accounting; the agent is just a client. Anything the agent buys spends the human's pre-committed pool. Cards were designed for one buyer per session. Cards assume there is a person clicking "Pay". Agents want to fan out — buy 200 tiny things across 30 sites in an hour — and each purchase should be atomic, cheap, and reversible. There is no discovery. Human buyers can read a pricing page. An agent needs a machine-readable "here's what this costs and how to pay for it" inline in the response. Guardrails have to be enforced somewhere other than the agent. If the only limit is a prompt saying "spend under $10", the agent will disobey it at some point. The limit has to live in infrastructure the model can't argue with. x402 attacks the discovery problem. AgentCore Payments attacks the guardrail problem. They are complements, not competitors.
documents.s: Why "the agent just pays" is harder than it sounds

documents.t: x402 is an open protocol maintained by the x402-foundation/x402 organisation on GitHub (Apache-2.0, ~6.5k stars at time of writing). Its whole trick is to give HTTP status code 402 Payment Required the semantics people always assumed it had. The full flow is exactly six moves. There is no session, no login, no key. Guided walkthrough1 of 6 11. Client asks⌄ Agent makes a normal HTTP request to a paid endpoint. No auth header, no wallet. ←PreviousNext→ 22. Server challenges with 402⌄ Server responds `HTTP/1.1 402 Payment Required` and sets a `PAYMENT-REQUIRED` header carrying a base64-encoded `PaymentRequirements` object: the price, the accepted token(s), the network, the merchant address, the scheme, and an expiry. That's the machine-readable price tag. ←PreviousNext→ 33. Client signs a payment payload⌄ Agent's x402 client SDK reads the challenge, picks one of the requirements it can pay, and constructs a signed `PaymentPayload` (an EIP-712-style signature, or the equivalent on Solana/Aptos/Stellar). Nothing is on-chain yet — this is an *authorization*, not a transfer. ←PreviousNext→ 44. Client retries with the signature⌄ Same request, this time with a `PAYMENT-SIGNATURE` header containing the signed payload. ←PreviousNext→ 55. Server verifies (via facilitator)⌄ Server hands the payload to a *facilitator* — a small optional service that runs `POST /verify` to confirm the signature and the client's on-chain balance, then, once the server has produced the response, `POST /settle` to actually submit the transfer. The server can also run its own facilitator. ←PreviousNext→ 66. Server returns 200 + settlement proof⌄ Response body carries the paid content; a `PAYMENT-RESPONSE` header carries a base64-encoded settlement receipt so the agent can audit that what it authorised was what actually cleared. ←PreviousNext→ Two design points are worth pausing on. First, the server — not the client — decides when to settle. If the request fails after step 4, the server never calls /settle, so the agent is not charged; the signature was an authorisation with a short expiry and it simply times out. That is the property that makes x402 usable at all for agents: a failed download is a free download. Second, the facilitator never has custody of client funds; the protocol's stated invariant is "all payment schemes must not allow facilitators to move funds outside client intentions." A rogue facilitator can refuse to settle; it cannot over-settle.
documents.s: x402 on the wire — the whole protocol in one flow

documents.t: x402 defines schemes as how the amount is agreed, not what currency is used. The current stable set: exact — the server advertises a fixed price and the client signs for exactly that amount. Best for content with a known cost per read: "$0.02 for this article". Simple, boring, correct. upto — the server advertises a ceiling. The client signs authorising up to that ceiling; the server chooses the actual charge at settlement time, up to the cap. This is the one that unlocks the interesting economics. batch-settlement (EVM) — for high-frequency use. The client posts an escrow deposit once, then racks up many off-chain vouchers that get redeemed in a single batched on-chain settlement. Same trust model, dramatically lower per-request gas. upto is the scheme that makes pay-per-inference and dynamic pricing possible. If you sell inference by the token, you don't know at request time how many tokens the completion will use; you only know at response time. With exact you either overcharge (round up to the ceiling and refund — needs a second on-chain move) or undercharge (the client pays for 4k tokens and you generate 10k). With upto the client signs "charge me for at most 10k tokens' worth", you produce the response, then you settle for the actual usage. The AWS AgentCore Payments GA release specifically highlights this as the pattern their launch enables: "the upto scheme within x402 enables an agent to set a spending ceiling rather than committing to a fixed price." Watch the failure mode: if the server settles the ceiling instead of the actual usage, the client has no on-chain recourse for the difference — the signature covered it. The /settle call's amount parameter is trusted. In practice this is why you want a facilitator you either run yourself or trust; more on that below.
documents.s: The three schemes — and why upto is the interesting one

documents.t: The current x402 monorepo publishes SDK packages for EVM, SVM (Solana), AVM, Aptos, Stellar, TVM, Hedera and Keeta, but the traffic today is heavily concentrated on Base (Coinbase's EVM L2) and Solana, both settling in USDC. In TypeScript the packages you'll actually import are @x402/core, one of the chain modules (@x402/evm, @x402/svm, …), and a client wrapper — @x402/fetch for a drop-in fetch() replacement that transparently handles the 402→sign→retry loop, or @x402/express / x402-hono on the server side. Python has a single x402 pip package; Go has github.com/x402-foundation/x402/go/v2. Cloudflare ships an even shorter path: the agents/x402 submodule inside its Agents package gives you an MCP client with x402 built in, and x402-hono is the paywall middleware for a Worker. So a Cloudflare Worker that turns a route into a paid endpoint is roughly: Turning a Hono route into an x402 paywall CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ import { Hono } from "hono"; import { paymentMiddleware } from "x402-hono"; const app = new Hono(); app.use("/premium/*", paymentMiddleware({ network: "base", facilitator: "https://facilitator.x402.org", routes: { "/premium/summary": { price: { asset: "USDC", amount: "0.05" }, scheme: "exact", recipient: "0xYourMerchantAddress", }, "/premium/inference": { price: { asset: "USDC", maxAmount: "0.50" }, scheme: "upto", recipient: "0xYourMerchantAddress", }, }, })); app.get("/premium/summary", c => c.text("The paid content.")); app.get("/premium/inference", c => c.text("The paid inference result.")); export default app; A caller using @x402/fetch doesn't need to know any of this — the wrapper sees the 402, signs, retries, and returns the eventual 200 response the same way a normal fetch would.
documents.s: The chains and SDKs you'll actually meet

documents.t: x402 alone is a protocol. It gets you how an agent pays. It does not get you whether it should. That is the problem Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Payments — GA on August 18, 2026 after a preview in May — actually solves. The primitive to understand is the payment session. Every payment an agent makes has to run inside one, and a session has exactly two caps: A maximum spend amount in a specified currency. An expiry time. Both are checked deterministically at the infrastructure layer — outside the model, outside the agent framework, outside anything the model can talk itself out of. A request that would push cumulative spend over the cap is rejected before the payment payload is even signed. A request after the expiry is rejected the same way. That is the guardrail. The model does not need to be well-aligned for it to hold; it needs to be well-constrained, and constraint lives in the session. Around that primitive AgentCore GA'd: Coinbase & Stripe Privy wallet integration. The credentials live in AgentCore Identity Secrets Manager; the agent never sees them; a short-lived derived token is what actually authorises wallet operations. End users can top up with a card (Stripe) or with USDC (Coinbase). Quick Create for Coinbase. You provision Coinbase credentials from inside the AgentCore console or CLI without leaving the platform. The Machine Payment Protocol (MPP) — the payment abstraction on top of x402 that lets an agent pay for MPP-compatible services and x402 endpoints with the same session and the same session cap. MPP is where card-rail and stablecoin-rail payments meet. A curated x402-enabled MCP server directory — "Coinbase Bazar" — exposed to the agent through AgentCore Gateway. Discoverability of paid endpoints is ranked on "social proof, metadata richness, description quality, and availability," which is a polite way of saying they're trying not to become a listing of shitcoin drainers. Framework plugins. A Strands Agents plugin and a LangGraph middleware ship at GA, so the payment session context is threaded through your agent loop without you writing an HTTP client for x402 by hand. The Strands wiring is intentionally small — you build a AgentCorePaymentsPluginConfig with the payment-manager ARN, the user ID, the payment-instrument ID and the session ID, and add the plugin to the agent. The session enforcement happens under the plugin. AgentCore Payments — Strands plugin, minimal shape CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ from agentcore_payments import AgentCorePaymentsPlugin, AgentCorePaymentsPluginConfig import os plugin = AgentCorePaymentsPlugin( config=AgentCorePaymentsPluginConfig( payment_manager_arn=os.environ["PAYMENT_MANAGER_ARN"], user_id="test-user-123", payment_instrument_id=os.environ["PAYMENT_INSTRUMENT_ID"], payment_session_id=os.environ["PAYMENT_SESSION_ID"], ) ) # Attach plugin to your Strands agent; the payment session caps # (max spend + expiry) are set when you mint the payment session, # NOT in the plugin config. Every payment attempt emits a CloudWatch log entry and an AgentCore Observability span; the built-in dashboards show success rates, average transaction value, and end-to-end health per agent. This is the observability piece that makes "the agent bought something weird" actually debuggable a week after the fact.
documents.s: AgentCore Payments GA — what AWS actually shipped on 2026-08-18

documents.t: A common misread is that x402 and AgentCore Payments are "crypto for agents". They are not. x402 happens to have shipped first on stablecoins because on-chain settlement is the only rail with true machine-native, permissionless per-request settlement. But AgentCore's MPP abstraction and the Stripe Privy integration mean an agent's session can be funded from a card. What Stripe Privy provides in this context is a card-backed wallet with delegation — the human user hands the agent a scoped, revocable authority to spend against a card, and the AgentCore session enforces the spend cap on top. For businesses that don't want stablecoin custody at all, this is the path. Choosing: Coinbase / Privy (USDC on Base or Solana). Best when you need true per-request, sub-cent settlement; when you want no chargeback; when the counterparty is another agent. Stripe Privy (card). Best when the merchant is a normal business without on-chain rails, when the average ticket is large enough that stablecoin fees don't dominate, when you want the buyer to have card-network dispute rights.
documents.s: Not just crypto — where Stripe fits

documents.t: Autonomous agent payments open a small, specific attack surface. The three you should design against: Prompt-injection-to-buy. A malicious page in an agent's context can instruct it to buy things. The defence is not "make the model refuse" — it's the session cap. Set the smallest spend ceiling that will complete the legitimate task, and set the shortest expiry. If a prompt injection makes the agent try to spend $10,000 and the session cap is $5, the injection fails. This is exactly the same lesson as Cryptographic context injection: Grok — trust boundaries live outside the model. Facilitator misbehavior. The /verify call is honest by construction (a bad /verify can only reject), but a compromised or byzantine facilitator can refuse to /settle after the server has delivered content, silently overcharge in upto mode, or delay settlement past the payload's expiry so the client's signature stops being valid. Defence: prefer facilitators you run yourself for merchant-side use; on the client side use @x402/fetch's built-in receipt check to fail loud if PAYMENT-RESPONSE disagrees with what you signed. upto over-settlement. In upto, the settled amount is server-supplied. A dishonest server can settle at the ceiling regardless of actual usage. The mitigation lives outside the protocol: emit a signed usage receipt in your response body (tokens generated, seconds streamed, bytes served) and refuse to trust a settled amount that isn't consistent with it. Some client wrappers will refuse to accept a settlement if you provide a callback that returns the expected max. These are also the shape of what Cloudflare's WriteGuard is trying to address at the MCP layer — treating "cost money" as a write with attribution and audit — but AgentCore's session cap is the load-bearing control today. Combining a WriteGuard-style write-tier policy at the MCP layer and a payment-session cap at the wallet layer is the belt-and-braces posture that most production deployments will settle into.
documents.s: The three threats worth taking seriously

documents.t: x402 gives an agent a way to transact. MCP gives it a way to reach the endpoints where transactions happen. A2A gives it a way to delegate work to another agent that may itself be paid. In practice you'll see all three composed: an A2A hand-off invokes a peer agent that uses MCP to reach an x402-priced tool, and the caller pays through its AgentCore session. When people talk about "the money layer for agents" this is what they mean — not a single product, but a stack where discovery, capability, and settlement each have a protocol and none of them requires humans in the loop. Check yourself 0/6

Скопировать как Markdown Средний A submission titled "Opus 5.5 is good at explainer videos" sat near the top of Hacker News with 319 points and 175 comments — and reading the thread, the most interesting thing is how many people got the mechanism wrong. They assumed a video model. It isn't one. What is happening is stranger and far more useful: a coding model writes a deterministic animation program, and a separate renderer turns that program into frames. The model never sees a pixel of the output. Which means the whole thing behaves like software — diffable, re-renderable, parameterisable, and debuggable — instead of like a slot machine you re-prompt until it looks right. This page is the practical guide that thread was missing: how the pipeline works, which of the three render engines to pick (and which one the models are measurably bad at), the two failure modes that silently break agent-written animation code, the pacing arithmetic that separates a watchable explainer from an unreadable one, and where the money actually goes. What you'll learn Explain why a coding model beats a video model at explainers — and what it gives up Name the reason Math.random() is banned in a frame-rendered animation, and what replaces it Pick between Remotion, Motion Canvas and Manim on licence and on how well models write them Spot the two traps in agent-written animation code: the Manim fork split and the stale Remotion API Compute a minimum dwell time per slide instead of guessing, so viewers can actually read Predict which line item dominates the bill (it is usually not the LLM) Последняя проверка: 2026-09-25. Volatile here: the Hacker News score, the community-reported per-video costs, the claim that one model is better than another at a specific library, the Remotion version and its package layout (checked at remotion@4.0.529), and the star counts. Re-check any of those before you build a budget or a template on them. Durable: the mechanism (a program rendered frame by frame), the determinism constraint, the licence split between the three engines, and the pacing arithmetic — none of that changes with a model release. Сверьтесь с официальным источником.
documents.s: AI Explainer Videos: The Code-Driven Pipeline

documents.t: Two completely different things get called "AI video". Diffusion video models (the family covered in generative media) take a prompt and emit pixels directly. Excellent for b-roll, a drone shot, a texture, a mood. Bad at anything that must be exactly right: legible text, a correct architecture diagram, your actual product UI, a number that has to say 40%. Code-driven animation goes the other way. A coding model writes source code for an animation — React components, a TypeScript scene graph, or Python — and a renderer executes it. Text is text, so it is sharp and spelled correctly. A diagram is a layout, so it is accurate. Your logo is your logo file. That split explains the HN thread's most common workflow report: the model "creates an HTML page and uses raw JS timed animations", then the frames get captured and assembled with ffmpeg. It also explains what the approach gives up — it cannot invent photographic imagery, so most real pipelines call an image model or a video model for b-roll and composite it in. The consequence worth internalising: your explainer becomes a repository. Change the price on slide 4, re-render, done. Localise the voiceover, re-render twelve languages from the same scenes. That is not a property any prompt-to-video model gives you.
documents.s: The mechanism: the model writes a program, not a video

documents.t: Here is the detail that quietly decides whether your pipeline produces clean video or a flickering mess, and almost nobody writing about this mentions it. A renderer like Remotion does not screen-record your animation. It opens the composition in headless Chrome, sets the clock to frame 0, screenshots, sets the clock to frame 1, screenshots, and so on — and it does this across multiple threads, opening the page multiple times. Frames are produced out of order, in parallel, in separate browser contexts. Everything follows from that: Animation must be a pure function of the frame number. In Remotion that is literally the API: useCurrentFrame() gives you the frame, interpolate() maps it to a value. No timers, no requestAnimationFrame, no CSS transitions driven by wall-clock time. A CSS transition renders whatever it happened to be mid-flight when the screenshot fired. Math.random() is broken by construction. It returns a different value in each thread and each page load, so a "random" particle jitters to a new position every frame. Remotion ships random(seed) — a seeded mulberry32 PRNG — precisely for this: random(1) always returns 0.07301638228818774. Same for spring(), which is a cached pure calculation keyed on (frame, fps, config). Dropped frames stop being possible. A screen recording of a heavy animation drops frames when the CPU can't keep up. Frame-by-frame rendering just takes longer. This is why a 5-minute render on a laptop can produce a video that plays perfectly smoothly. Watch out If you only remember one rule for prompting an agent to write animation code: forbid wall-clock time. No setTimeout, no CSS transition, no Date.now(), no Math.random(). Every visual value must be derived from the current frame number. Models will reach for CSS transitions because that is what the web corpus is full of.
documents.s: Why determinism is the whole trick

documents.t: All three are real, actively maintained, and produce broadcast-quality output. They differ on language, on licence, and — importantly — on how reliably a model writes them. Remotion Motion Canvas Manim Language React / TypeScript TypeScript (generators) Python Repo remotion-dev/remotion motion-canvas/motion-canvas (~19.2k stars) ManimCommunity/manim (~41k) · 3b1b/manim (~94k) Licence Source-available + Company Licence MIT MIT Sweet spot Product/launch video, UI, text-heavy explainer Timeline-precise motion graphics Mathematical and algorithmic visualisation Model-written quality Strong — and it ships official agent skills Decent Weakest of the three (see below) Two things on that table deserve more than a row.

Remotion is not MIT. It is source-available with a two-tier commercial licence, and the threshold is small enough to catch most teams: free for individuals, non-profits, evaluation, and for-profit companies with up to 3 employees; a paid Company Licence for for-profit organisations with more than three. The second split matters more if you are building a product rather than a video: Remotion for Creators — seat-based, intended for low-volume rendering within and for your own company, explicitly not for serving personalised videos to your end users. Remotion for Automators — render-based, which is the tier you land in the moment an agent renders videos for customers. From version 5.0 it carries mandatory telemetry reporting with a license key. So "my agent generates a video per signup" is not a Creators use case. Price it as Automators before you ship it. If that is a dealbreaker, Motion Canvas is MIT and covers a lot of the same ground.
documents.s: Remotion's licence is the gotcha, not the code

documents.t: This one burns people who have never heard of it, and it also explains an observation from the HN thread — that strong coding models write worse Manim than you would expect, with community reports that Gemini currently handles it better than Opus 5.5. There are two Manims: 3b1b/manim — Grant Sanderson's original, the one from the famous videos, ~94k stars, installed as manimgl. ManimCommunity/manim — the community fork, ~41k stars, the one that is actually documented and maintained for general use, installed as manim. They are API-incompatible and both are imported as from manim import *. Every tutorial, StackOverflow answer and blog post in the training corpus is one or the other, unlabelled. So the model writes plausible code that mixes both dialects, and Python raises on a method that exists in the other fork. It is not a reasoning failure; it is a poisoned-namespace failure. The fix is boring and it works: pin the fork in your prompt and in your environment, and give the agent the version's real API surface instead of letting it recall one. Pin the Manim dialect before the agent writes a line CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ Use ManimCommunity Manim (the "manim" package on PyPI), NOT 3b1b/manimgl. Before writing any scene, run: python -c "import manim; print(manim.__version__)" and confirm the version. If a class or method you want is not in that version's API, do not use it — check with: python -c "import manim; print([n for n in dir(manim) if 'Text' in n])" Never mix manimgl APIs (e.g. ShowCreation) with community APIs (Create).
documents.s: The Manim trap: two forks, one import name

documents.t: The same poisoned-corpus problem hits Remotion for a different reason: the library moved faster than the training data. In current Remotion, media components live in @remotion/media, and the trimming props are trimBefore / trimAfter. Preview and render can even use different components deliberately — Html5Audio from remotion while previewing, Audio from @remotion/media when rendering, switched on useRemotionEnvironment(). A model trained mostly on older material writes import {Audio} from 'remotion' with startFrom, which is the old shape. That code may still run. It may also silently do nothing useful, which is worse. This is exactly why Remotion publishes official Agent Skills — a set of twelve skills that hand an agent the current best practices instead of hoping it remembers them. They are designed for Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and friends, and they follow the same open format covered in SKILL.md as an open standard. Install Remotion's official agent skills CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ npx skills add remotion-dev/skills The skills are granular, which is the point — you invoke the one that matches the phase of work: /remotion-create to scaffold, /remotion-markup for animation and typography, /remotion-studio to preview, /remotion-render to render, /remotion-captions for subtitles, plus remotion-best-practices as the umbrella when you are not sure. Vendor-maintained skills are the cheapest available fix for a model's stale knowledge of a fast-moving library: one install, and the agent stops guessing.

The single biggest quality lever is not a better prompt for the whole video. It is splitting the job so the model does judgement work and the renderer does determinism work — with a human-readable artefact in between. Guided walkthrough1 of 7 1Generate a storyboard as data, not as code⌄ Ask for a JSON scene list first: per scene, a title, the on-screen text, the visual intent, and a duration in seconds. This is the cheap, reviewable step. You can read twelve scenes in thirty seconds and fix the narrative before a single component exists — and fixing the story is the edit that most improves the video. Code generated from a reviewed storyboard is also far more consistent than code generated from a paragraph of vibes. ←PreviousNext→ 2Fix the pacing in the storyboard, before any rendering⌄ Do the reading-speed arithmetic below on each scene's text and clamp the durations. Doing this at the data layer costs nothing; doing it after the components exist means re-timing every animation that depends on the scene length. ←PreviousNext→ 3Write the voiceover script per scene, then synthesise it⌄ Script per scene, not per video, so audio boundaries line up with visual boundaries. Synthesise each scene to its own audio file with a TTS API. Then measure the real duration of each clip — the synthesised audio is the ground truth for scene length, not your estimate. ←PreviousNext→ 4Re-derive scene durations from the real audio⌄ This is the step everyone skips and it is why so many AI explainers have visuals racing ahead of the narration. Read each audio file's actual duration, convert to frames, and feed those durations back into the composition as props. Never hardcode a frame count you guessed. ←PreviousNext→ 5Build the components from the storyboard, frame-derived only⌄ Now let the agent write the animation code, scene by scene, against the frozen storyboard. Enforce the determinism rule: every value from useCurrentFrame() and interpolate(), randomness from a seeded helper, no CSS transitions. Preview in the studio — a real preview catches layout errors that no amount of code reading does. ←PreviousNext→ 6Add captions from the audio you already have⌄ Do not ask the model to guess word timings. Transcribe your own voiceover locally and use the token-level timestamps. Remotion ships install-whisper-cpp for exactly this: installWhisperCpp(), downloadWhisperModel(), then transcribe() with token-level timestamps on, and toCaptions() to post-process. Captions are also the cheapest accessibility win available and they are what makes the video watchable muted. ←PreviousNext→ 7Render, then measure the render⌄ Render from the CLI so it is reproducible in CI. Then tune concurrency with a real measurement instead of a guess — Remotion has a benchmark command that runs the same render repeatedly across several concurrency values and compares them. ←PreviousNext→ Render from the CLI, then find your real concurrency CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ # deterministic render, reproducible in CI npx remotion render src/index.ts MyExplainer out/video.mp4 # stop guessing --concurrency: measure it npx remotion benchmark src/index.ts MyExplainer --concurrencies=2,4,8 --runs=3

The most consistent complaint in the HN thread was not that the videos looked bad. It was that they moved too fast to read. Slides appear, text animates in, and it is gone before a human finishes the sentence. This is a bug with a formula, not a matter of taste. Adult reading speed for unfamiliar screen text sits around 200–250 words per minute, and a viewer also needs time to find the new text before starting to read it. So: # minimum dwell time for a text block, in frames words = number of words in the block wpm = 200 # conservative for unfamiliar on-screen text settle = 0.4 # seconds to notice and locate the new text exit = 0.3 # seconds of breathing room before it leaves dwell_seconds = settle + (words / wpm) * 60 + exit dwell_frames = ceil(dwell_seconds * fps) # worked example: a 14-word bullet at 30 fps # 0.4 + (14 / 200) * 60 + 0.3 = 4.9 s -> 147 frames Two notes that make this actually useful: Animate in fast, hold long. The entrance transition should be 200–400 ms; the hold is where the dwell budget goes. Models tend to do the opposite — a long elegant fade, then a short hold. If narration exists, the dwell floor is the narration length. Text must stay up at least as long as the sentence describing it. Which is why deriving scene duration from the synthesised audio (step 4 above) fixes pacing almost for free. Clamp every scene to max(dwell_frames, narration_frames) and a large fraction of the "AI slop video" feeling disappears, with no change to the visuals at all.
documents.s: Pacing: the reason most AI explainers are unwatchable

documents.t: Community reports from the HN thread put a complete generated explainer at roughly $3–$4 in API spend, with the notable detail that the cost was dominated by image-model calls, not by the language model. One commenter reported generating a 5-minute video on an M4 MacBook Air in about 5 minutes of wall-clock time using an orchestrated pipeline. Treat the absolute numbers as perishable, but the shape is structural and worth planning around: The LLM is cheap here. A storyboard plus a few hundred lines of animation code is a small number of tokens. Even at flagship pricing it is cents. See what AI costs across providers. Per-asset generative calls dominate. Every generated image or b-roll clip is a separate paid call, and they multiply by scene count. This is the line item to cap. Compute is yours. Rendering runs on your machine or your CI, so it is time and electricity rather than API spend — until you move it to a serverless renderer, at which point it becomes both. Re-renders are nearly free, which is the whole structural advantage. Fixing a typo on slide 4 costs one render, not one regeneration. Localising into twelve languages costs twelve TTS runs and twelve renders, not twelve videos. The practical budgeting move: generate images once, commit them as assets, and keep re-renders asset-free. A pipeline that re-generates imagery on every render is the one that produces a surprising bill.
documents.s: What it costs, and which line item dominates

documents.t: The sharpest criticism in the thread is the one worth taking seriously: within weeks of these tools spreading, the outputs became recognisable. Same gradient backgrounds, same spring-in cards, same three-word bullets, same brisk voice. Several commenters also flagged repetitive copy and, in one case, a video confidently about the wrong subject entirely — a Twilight Imperium reference site described as an AI data startup. If you use this seriously, the levers that measurably de-generify output: Supply the design system, don't let it be invented. Pass your real palette, type scale, spacing scale and logo as constants the components import. Underspecified prompts are exactly where a model's house style leaks in. Write the copy yourself, or edit it hard. The visuals are the part models are good at. The narrative is the part that reads as generated. Use your own screen recordings as the hero asset. Real product footage composited into a generated scene is the single strongest anti-sameness move, and it also fixes the hallucination risk — the video cannot misdescribe your product if the product is on screen. Verify the claims like documentation. Anything factual in an explainer is a factual claim being published in your name, with none of a text page's easy correction path. Check it before you render, not after it is on YouTube. Break one convention on purpose. One deliberate choice that the default template would not make — an odd aspect ratio, silence where music is expected, a hand-drawn asset — is usually enough to stop the output reading as machine default.

Worth being honest, because the sceptics in that thread had a point: much of what gets produced is an animated slide deck with a voiceover. That is a perfectly good artefact for a changelog, a launch, a release note or an onboarding walkthrough — and a poor substitute for actual teaching, which needs a worked example, a wrong turn, and a reason to care. Reach for the code-driven pipeline when: The content must be exactly right — real UI, real numbers, real diagrams. You will need to change it later, or ship it in several languages. The same template will produce many videos from different data. Reach for something else when the goal is photographic footage (use a video model), or when the value is in a human explaining a hard idea badly and then well — which is still the thing no pipeline produces. Check yourself 0/5

Скопировать как Markdown Средний Once your product talks to more than one model, the direct-SDK approach cracks. Each provider has its own key, its own rate limits, its own outage schedule, and its own bill. An AI gateway is the small piece of infrastructure that sits between your code and every model — Claude, GPT, Gemini, Llama, Kimi, DeepSeek, your local Ollama — and turns "N brittle integrations" into "one endpoint you control." This page compares the four gateways that actually get deployed in production in 2026 — LiteLLM, OpenRouter, Portkey, and Vercel AI Gateway — and shows the killer workflow: point Claude Code at your own gateway so a single proxy handles routing, budgets, logging, and fallback for the whole team. What you'll learn Understand what an AI gateway is and the five problems it solves (many providers, one API; fallback; virtual keys; spend caps; observability) Compare LiteLLM, OpenRouter, Portkey, and Vercel AI Gateway on latency, pricing, self-hostability, and where each shines Wire Claude Code through your own LiteLLM proxy with ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL and a virtual key so the team gets shared limits and logs Configure OpenRouter fallback so a Claude outage silently promotes GPT or Gemini instead of showing users a 5xx Understand the March 2026 LiteLLM supply-chain incident and how to pin versions safely in production
documents.s: AI Gateways: LiteLLM, OpenRouter, Portkey, Vercel

documents.t: The first Claude integration is a two-line change: pip install anthropic, set ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, done. The second — say you want to fall back to GPT-5.4 when Anthropic throttles — is where the abstraction breaks. Now you have two SDKs with different request shapes, two dashboards, two bills, two rotation cadences for API keys, and two sets of retry logic. Add a third for Gemini and a fourth for your local Ollama, and every product decision ("cap this team at $500/month", "log every prompt for review", "let a customer bring their own key") becomes N implementations instead of one. An AI gateway concentrates that plumbing in a single place. Concretely, a production gateway gives you: One request shape for every provider. Most gateways speak the OpenAI Chat Completions API (or Anthropic Messages, or both) and translate to the real provider under the hood. Fallback and routing. Try Claude first; on 429 or 5xx, retry against GPT or Gemini without the caller knowing. Same for latency ceilings and content-moderation rejections. Virtual keys. Issue a per-user or per-service key that maps to a subset of models, its own budget, and its own rate limit — so a rogue script can't drain the whole account. Spend caps and logging. Every request is tagged, priced, and stored. You can revoke a key without touching Anthropic or OpenAI, and you can prove to compliance what was sent where. Caching. Prompt caching (exact-match) and semantic caching (near-match) turn repeat traffic into free hits. Not every team needs all five. But the moment two of them are on your roadmap, running a gateway is cheaper than reinventing them per provider.
documents.s: The problem: one direct SDK per provider does not scale

documents.t: There isn't one "winner" — the four leaders occupy different corners of the design space (self-hosted vs. hosted, open-source vs. proprietary, minimalist vs. control-panel). Gateway Deploy Pricing model Best at Not for LiteLLM Self-hosted (Docker) or SDK Free (OSS); Enterprise tier for SSO/audit Team proxy with virtual keys, budgets, no per-token markup, works with 100+ providers via one config Teams with no DevOps to run Postgres + Redis OpenRouter Hosted only Provider price + ~5.5% credit-purchase fee, no per-request markup Zero-ops access to 300+ models under one key; ideal for products that let users pick a model Compliance shops that need self-hosting or data residency Portkey OSS gateway (npx) or hosted cloud OSS free; cloud has usage tiers Sub-ms gateway latency, semantic caching, guardrails, canary testing — the "control panel" angle Teams who just want the simplest possible key aggregator Vercel AI Gateway Hosted only Provider price, no token markup; free with Vercel plans Devs already on Vercel who want AI SDK v5/v6 + Anthropic Messages + OpenAI Responses APIs unified Non-Vercel infrastructure or air-gapped deployments The important axis to pick on first: self-hosted vs. hosted. If your data cannot leave your VPC (regulated industries, EU residency, enterprise privacy reviews), you need a self-hostable gateway — LiteLLM or Portkey OSS. If you'd rather pay someone to run it, OpenRouter or Vercel AI Gateway is a one-click affair. The second axis: how much control plane you actually need. If you're a one-person product that just wants to try Kimi K3 and Claude and Grok side-by-side without three signups, OpenRouter is the whole story. If you're a 20-person org where finance wants monthly spend by team, security wants virtual keys with rotation, and platform wants Grafana metrics, you're building on LiteLLM or Portkey. Последняя проверка: 2026-07-27. Gateway feature sets and pricing change quickly. Two examples measured on the verification date: OpenRouter charges a 5.5% platform fee on credit purchases (not per request), and Portkey's OSS gateway advertises sub-1ms overhead while hosted OpenRouter typically adds 100–150ms. Confirm against each vendor's current pricing and status page before committing. The categorisation above (self-hosted vs. hosted, minimalist vs. control-panel) is stable; the exact numbers behind it are not. Сверьтесь с официальным источником.

documents.t: The best-kept secret about Claude Code is that it respects ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL and ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN. Set them to your gateway and Claude Code stops talking to api.anthropic.com directly — it talks to your proxy, which forwards to Anthropic (or anywhere else) with the auth you control. For a team, this changes three things at once: One shared virtual key per developer. You issue and revoke keys in the proxy UI. No shared root credentials in .env files. Per-developer budgets and logs. The proxy tags every request, so "who spent the $300 yesterday" is a database query, not an incident. Model aliasing. You can pin claude-sonnet-4-6 at the proxy so a model deprecation is a one-line config change, not a repo-wide grep. Start a minimal proxy in three steps: Guided walkthrough1 of 3 1Install LiteLLM with the proxy extra⌄ In a fresh venv or via uv: uv tool install 'litellm[proxy]'. This pulls in the gateway server (FastAPI + admin UI) alongside the client SDK. ←PreviousNext→ 2Author a config.yaml that lists the Claude models you want to expose⌄ Model IDs on the left are the ALIAS your callers see (whatever you want); the litellm_params.model on the right is the REAL provider route. Put your ANTHROPIC_API_KEY in the env, not the file. ←PreviousNext→ 3Start the proxy and point Claude Code at it⌄ Run litellm --config config.yaml (default port 4000). Then set ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL to the proxy URL and ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN to a virtual key. Claude Code will route every call through the proxy without knowing. ←PreviousNext→ The config file that makes this work: config.yaml — Claude Sonnet/Opus/Haiku behind LiteLLM CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ model_list: - model_name: claude-opus-4-7 litellm_params: model: anthropic/claude-opus-4-7 api_key: os.environ/ANTHROPIC_API_KEY - model_name: claude-sonnet-4-6 litellm_params: model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6 api_key: os.environ/ANTHROPIC_API_KEY - model_name: claude-haiku-4-5-20251001 litellm_params: model: anthropic/claude-haiku-4-5-20251001 api_key: os.environ/ANTHROPIC_API_KEY litellm_settings: master_key: os.environ/LITELLM_MASTER_KEY # Optional: enable exact-match prompt caching cache: true cache_params: type: redis host: os.environ/REDIS_HOST Then, from any developer's shell: Point Claude Code at the proxy (per-developer .env) CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ export ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL="https://llm.internal.example.com" export ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN="sk-team-alice-9f4c..." # a VIRTUAL key issued by the proxy # now every Claude Code call goes through YOUR gateway claude --model claude-sonnet-4-6 The non-obvious win is the virtual key. The master key is admin-only and never ships to laptops. Each developer gets a virtual key that maps to only the models you allow, has its own monthly budget, and can be revoked in seconds without rotating the underlying Anthropic key. If a laptop is lost, you kill one row in Postgres — not the whole team's access. Careful: the same env vars work with Anthropic's Bedrock and Vertex integrations, but there are edge cases with experimental beta features. For Bedrock deployments the LiteLLM docs recommend setting CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_EXPERIMENTAL_BETAS=1 in ~/.claude/settings.json to avoid header-compatibility issues.
documents.s: Killer workflow: point Claude Code at your own LiteLLM proxy

documents.t: If you don't want to host anything, OpenRouter's fallback array is the shortest path to "silently retry another model when Claude 429s". You send an ordered list; OpenRouter walks it top-down and returns the first model that answered. Claude → GPT → Gemini fallback in one request (OpenRouter) CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ import openai client = openai.OpenAI( api_key="YOUR_OPENROUTER_KEY", base_url="https://openrouter.ai/api/v1", ) response = client.chat.completions.create( model="anthropic/claude-sonnet-4.5", extra_body={ # Ordered fallback. If the first model 429s, is down, or is # rejected by moderation, OpenRouter tries the next one. "models": [ "anthropic/claude-sonnet-4.5", "openai/gpt-5.4", "google/gemini-2.5-pro", ], }, messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Explain B-trees in one paragraph."}], ) # 'model' in the response tells you which one actually answered. print(response.model, "->", response.choices[0].message.content) Three things people miss on their first try: Billing follows the model that answered, not the one you asked for. If Claude fails and GPT-5.4 answers, you pay OpenRouter's GPT-5.4 rate for that request. The fallback triggers on more than 5xx. Rate-limiting, provider downtime, context-length validation errors, and content-moderation refusals all promote to the next model. That last one is the sharpest edge — a "moderation" refusal from one provider can silently route to a more permissive one, which may or may not be what you want. Review your fallback list with the same care as an ACL. You cannot mix models with fallbacks. The Anthropic-format Messages endpoint uses a different fallbacks array. Sending both keys in the same request returns a 400. Pick the format your client speaks and stick to it.
documents.s: Killer workflow #2: silent fallback with OpenRouter

documents.t: On 24 March 2026 at 10:39 UTC, two malicious PyPI releases of LiteLLM — v1.82.7 and v1.82.8 — were published by an attacker after they stole the maintainer's PyPI credentials via a prior compromise of Trivy, a security scanner running in LiteLLM's CI/CD pipeline. PyPI quarantined the packages at 13:38 UTC (about three hours later). During the exposure window, tens of thousands of downloads occurred. The payload was an infostealer with a persistence mechanism (a litellm_init.pth file that ran on every Python invocation, harvested credentials, and installed a systemd backdoor). Attribution goes to a group tracked as TeamPCP, which also compromised Trivy and Checkmarx KICS. If you run LiteLLM in any environment, apply this once and then keep it in your platform playbook: Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Pin to a known-safe version⌄ v1.82.6 and earlier are clean. v1.83.0 and later (published via LiteLLM's rebuilt CI/CD v2 pipeline) are clean. Anything in between should be uninstalled and the environment considered tainted. The official Docker image (ghcr.io/berriai/litellm) was NOT compromised — the incident was PyPI-only. ←PreviousNext→ 2Check for the persistence file⌄ Grep site-packages for litellm_init.pth. If it exists, treat the machine as compromised: rotate every credential that was present in env vars or on disk (Anthropic, OpenAI, cloud, DB, SSH, K8s tokens) and forensic-scan for the systemd backdoor. ←PreviousNext→ 3Verify Docker image signatures with cosign⌄ From v1.83.0-nightly onward, LiteLLM signs its images. Verifying with cosign before rollout catches a repeat of this incident at the container layer. ←PreviousNext→ 4Prefer the container image over pip install in production⌄ The Docker image escaped the attack; the PyPI wheel did not. That's a durable signal: for a networked service that holds API keys, running the pinned container is safer than a pip-installed venv on a shared host. ←PreviousNext→ 5Add outbound egress alerting⌄ The malware phoned home to models.litellm[.]cloud and checkmarx[.]zone — neither is legitimate. Egress allowlists on production LLM proxies catch this class of attack early. ←PreviousNext→ The wider lesson isn't "don't use LiteLLM" — it's "assume every dependency in your AI stack, including security scanners, can be a delivery vector." Pin versions, sign images, and put your gateway on a network segment that only reaches the model providers. Последняя проверка: 2026-07-27. Safe-version guidance verified on the date above against LiteLLM's official incident post and the PyPI incident report. Before installing or upgrading LiteLLM in production, re-check the current safe versions and any follow-up CVEs from the vendor's security page. Сверьтесь с официальным источником.
documents.s: The March 2026 LiteLLM supply-chain incident: what to actually do

documents.t: Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1How many providers, and who runs the infra?⌄ One or two providers with a small team → skip the gateway; direct SDKs are fine. Three+ providers OR a team where 'who has the key' matters → gateway. If you have DevOps and privacy requirements, self-host LiteLLM or Portkey OSS. If you'd rather pay someone else to run it, OpenRouter (hosted-only) or Vercel AI Gateway (great if you already deploy there). ←PreviousNext→ 2Do you need virtual keys, budgets, and per-team spend?⌄ Yes → LiteLLM (native, mature) or Portkey (native, plus semantic caching). No → OpenRouter or Vercel AI Gateway are lighter. ←PreviousNext→ 3Do you need to route between providers in ONE request?⌄ OpenRouter's models[] and Vercel AI Gateway's provider-options fallbacks are the shortest path. LiteLLM does it too via fallbacks: in the config, but writes closer to a rules engine than a one-line array. ←PreviousNext→ 4Is Claude Code the primary consumer?⌄ Then LiteLLM wins by a mile — it's the only gateway with first-class docs for the ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL + virtual-key pattern, so a team of ten Claude Code users behind one proxy just works. ←PreviousNext→ 5Are you regulated / air-gapped?⌄ Self-hosted only: LiteLLM proxy container or Portkey OSS via npx @portkey-ai/gateway. Egress-allowlist the proxy to the providers it's authorised to reach. ←PreviousNext→ Common combinations that ship in production: Solo dev / prototype: OpenRouter direct. One key, 300+ models, done. Small team, Claude-first: LiteLLM proxy with Anthropic + one fallback provider, virtual keys per engineer, Redis prompt caching. Vercel-native product: Vercel AI Gateway with the AI SDK; add OpenRouter as a provider-options fallback for exotic models. Regulated / EU: Self-hosted LiteLLM or Portkey OSS in-VPC with Presidio PII masking in front (see Claude + Local Models for the redaction pattern). AI-product with heavy repeat traffic: Portkey (semantic caching commonly drives 30–50% cost reduction on chat-style workloads, per Portkey's own case studies — verify on your traffic before believing headline numbers).
documents.s: Choose the right gateway for your situation

documents.t: Gateways are middleware — they change how you reach models, not which model is right. Two things still need real work: Prompt portability. Claude, GPT, and Gemini answer the same prompt differently, and system-prompt conventions vary. A gateway doesn't rewrite your prompt for the fallback provider — that's what Porting prompts across models and Cross-AI translation are for. Evals. The gateway makes it easy to A/B two models on the same request. It cannot tell you which one was actually better on YOUR task. Run a real eval (see Evals) before switching defaults. A common mistake is to install a gateway and consider "multi-model" done. The gateway is the transport layer; portability and evals are the product layer. Check yourself 0/5 Key takeaways An AI gateway is the missing router between your app and every model — it exists to make virtual keys, budgets, fallback, logging, and caching a single implementation instead of N per provider Pick on TWO axes first: self-hosted vs. hosted (LiteLLM/Portkey OSS vs. OpenRouter/Vercel), and minimalist vs. control-panel (OpenRouter/Vercel vs. LiteLLM/Portkey) The Claude Code killer workflow: point ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL at your own LiteLLM proxy and issue per-developer virtual keys — team gets shared limits, logs, and one-click revoke without touching the root Anthropic key OpenRouter's models[] array is the shortest path to silent Claude → GPT → Gemini fallback, but note that moderation refusals are a fallback trigger too — review the list like an ACL After the March 2026 LiteLLM supply-chain attack, pin to v1.82.6 or earlier, or v1.83.0+; prefer the signed Docker image over pip; egress-allowlist the proxy A gateway is transport, not product — prompt portability and evals still need real work, no matter how many models you can now reach

Скопировать как Markdown Средний At WWDC 2026 (announced 8 June 2026) Apple shipped the third generation of its Foundation Models — AFM 3 — and expanded the Foundation Models framework in a way that matters even if you never write Swift: the framework now takes third-party LLM providers (Anthropic Claude and Google Gemini are shipping as Swift packages), and the on-device path stops being a toy 3B model and adds a 20-billion-parameter sparse MoE that runs on Apple Silicon by keeping most experts in NAND and swapping only what a prompt needs into RAM. If you build Claude apps and have been treating "on-device" as a separate universe from your API workflows, that gap is closing this year. This page unpacks what actually shipped, the non-obvious mechanisms, and the concrete migration and compatibility choices you now have. What you'll learn Name the four AFM 3 models — Core (3B), Core Advanced (20B sparse), Cloud, Cloud Pro — and which one runs where Understand the flash-plus-DRAM expert-routing trick that lets a 20B model fit on an iPhone at all Use the Foundation Models framework's @Generable / @Guide macros for constrained decoding — the model literally cannot emit invalid JSON Know what changed at WWDC26: the LanguageModel / LanguageModelExecutor protocols that let you plug Claude or any other LLM into the same Swift session API Decide when to reach for the on-device 3B, when to jump to Private Cloud Compute, and when to keep the workload on the Claude API Последняя проверка: 2026-08-09. На этой странице приводятся факты, которые меняются со временем — считайте дату выше показателем её актуальности. Источники: Apple ML Research 'Introducing the third generation of Apple's foundation models' (8 June 2026) + Apple Developer WWDC26 session 339 'Bring an LLM provider to the Foundation Models framework'.
documents.s: Apple Foundation Models 3 & the On-Device LLM Stack for Claude Users

documents.t: AFM 3 is Apple's second serious swing at on-device LLMs: a rebuilt 3B dense model (Core), a new 20B sparse MoE (Core Advanced) that runs on iPhone by keeping most experts in flash storage, a Cloud and Cloud Pro pair on Apple Silicon plus NVIDIA GPUs in Google Cloud, and a framework that now treats Anthropic Claude and Google Gemini as first-class swappable providers behind the same LanguageModel protocol. Free for developers to call on-device; free on Private Cloud Compute for App Store Small Business Program members under 2M first-time downloads.
Everyone is writing the "Apple has a 3B on-device model" headline. Here are the mechanisms most write-ups skip.

The naive read of "20-billion-parameter model on iPhone" is impossible: even at 4-bit, 20B weights is ~10 GB, well past what an iPhone can hold in RAM. Apple's trick, per the WWDC 2026 announcement, is to store the full AFM 3 Core Advanced model in flash memory (NAND) and swap only the input-dependent routed experts into DRAM at inference time. The architecture has shared experts that stay resident and routed experts that a router picks per prompt (activating 1–4B parameters at a time, not the full 20B). Combined with Quantization Aware Training, this is what lets Apple ship a 20B-class model on a device that has ~8 GB of usable RAM. The consequence for you: iPhone-side latency is now dominated less by matrix multiply and more by NAND read bandwidth and the router's choices — a very different performance envelope than a 3B dense model.
documents.s: 1. The 20B model fits on iPhone because most of it lives in NAND, not RAM

documents.t: The framework's @Generable macro is often described as "structured output," which understates what it does. @Generable runs at compile time: it generates a JSON schema and a parser for your Swift type, and the framework then uses that schema for constrained decoding — the on-device model is forced, at the token level, to produce output that parses back into your Swift struct. There is no "hope it's valid JSON, then retry." A @Guide annotation lets you add constraints (.anyOf(["PG", "PG-13", "R", "G"]), ranges, descriptions) that are also enforced at decode time. If you have spent time writing JSON-repair fallbacks around a Claude tool-use loop, the on-device 3B model side of your app can drop that entire retry layer.
documents.s: 2. Constrained decoding is baked into the Swift compiler, not the runtime

documents.t: The WWDC 2026 session "Bring an LLM provider to the Foundation Models framework" shipped two new protocols: LanguageModel (declares capabilities and executor configuration) and LanguageModelExecutor (handles the actual generation, KV cache, and streaming). Anyone can ship a Swift package that conforms to them — Apple explicitly named Anthropic Claude and Google Gemini as launch-time providers. The consequence: from the app's point of view, the same LanguageModelSession, the same @Generable types, the same tool-calling contract, and the same transcript model apply whether the underlying model is the on-device 3B, Private Cloud Compute, Claude on Anthropic's API, Gemini on Google Cloud, or an MLX weights file from Hugging Face. Model choice becomes a Swift package dependency rather than an SDK rewrite.
documents.s: 3. The framework now takes any LLM — including Claude and Gemini — behind one Swift API

documents.t: Guided walkthrough1 of 4 1AFM 3 Core (3B) — always on-device⌄ Runs on any Apple Intelligence device. Free to call from Swift via the Foundation Models framework — no API key, no network, no per-token bill. This is where you put classification, extraction, summarization, on-device rewrites, and anything that must work in airplane mode. ←PreviousNext→ 2AFM 3 Core Advanced (20B) — newer iPhones only⌄ Runs on Apple's most powerful silicon; older Apple Intelligence devices transparently fall back to Core. Use this when the 3B refuses or hallucinates on a task and the request can wait for expert-swap latency but must stay on-device (e.g. private health/finance reasoning). ←PreviousNext→ 3AFM 3 Cloud / Cloud Pro — Private Cloud Compute⌄ The framework routes to PCC when the device model isn't enough. You do not choose the specific server SKU — you request a reasoning level and Apple picks. Same privacy contract as on-device: PCC's node attestation prevents Apple staff from reading your requests. ←PreviousNext→ 4Third-party providers — via Swift package⌄ Add a package that conforms to LanguageModel + LanguageModelExecutor (Anthropic Claude and Google Gemini are the launch-time examples). From the session API the code is identical — model choice is a package dependency. ←PreviousNext→

The framework's headline feature is that you can get typed, schema-validated output from the on-device 3B with almost no ceremony. On-device 3B call with @Generable structured output (Swift) CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ import FoundationModels @Generable struct TripIdea { @Guide(description: "Short, evocative title") let title: String @Guide(description: "One-paragraph pitch, 40–80 words") let summary: String @Guide(.range(1...14)) let estimatedDays: Int @Guide(.anyOf(["easy", "moderate", "hard"])) let difficulty: String } let session = LanguageModelSession() // defaults to on-device Core let idea = try await session.respond( to: "Suggest a shoulder-season trip in Puglia for a family with a 6-year-old.", generating: TripIdea.self // constrained decoding ) print(idea.title, idea.difficulty, idea.estimatedDays) At runtime the model is forced, at the token level, to emit tokens that keep the running text parseable as a TripIdea. You never see a JSON string; you receive a TripIdea value. This is the same contract whether the session is talking to the on-device 3B, PCC, or a third-party provider you plumbed in as a Swift package.

The WWDC 2026 "Bring an LLM provider" session made this concrete: implement LanguageModel and LanguageModelExecutor, publish it as a git-tagged Swift package, and app code that already used the on-device 3B can call your provider by changing one initializer. Sketch of a third-party provider conforming to LanguageModel CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ import FoundationModels public struct ClaudeSonnet5: LanguageModel { public let capabilities = LanguageModelCapabilities(capabilities: [ .toolCalling, .guidedGeneration, .reasoning ]) public var executorConfiguration: ClaudeExecutor.Configuration } public final class ClaudeExecutor: LanguageModelExecutor { public struct Configuration: Hashable { // hashable = KV-cache key public var modelID: String public var tokenProvider: TokenProvider // NOT a plain API key string } public required init(configuration: Configuration) throws { /* … */ } public func respond( to request: LanguageModelExecutorGenerationRequest, model: Model, streamingInto channel: LanguageModelExecutorGenerationChannel ) async throws { // 1. Map Foundation Models transcript → Anthropic /messages payload // 2. Stream deltas back via channel.send(.response(action: .appendText(...))) // 3. Surface tool calls / reasoning via the same transcript entry types } } Two subtleties the API deliberately pushes you toward. First, Configuration is Hashable on purpose: the framework caches executors by configuration, so same config = same executor = preserved KV cache across turns. Second, the guidance explicitly discourages plain API-key strings in initializers — prefer a TokenProvider or a sign-in flow, keychain-persist tokens, and use App Attest for cloud calls to verify the device isn't a tampered build hitting your endpoint from the outside.

documents.t: Pro tip Reach for on-device AFM 3 Core (3B): summarization, classification, entity extraction, on-device rewrites, keyboard suggestions — anything where a bounded prompt and typed output beats a network round-trip. Free. Reach for AFM 3 Core Advanced (20B): private reasoning that cannot leave the device (health, finance, unreleased documents) and that the 3B fumbles. Expect variable latency because of NAND expert-swap. Reach for Private Cloud Compute (Cloud / Cloud Pro): larger context, longer reasoning, or multimodal where the 20B on-device can't keep up but privacy still rules out third-party APIs. Stay on Claude via the Anthropic API (or the new Swift-package provider): long agent runs, extended thinking, big-context codebase work, and cross-platform apps that need the same model on Android and web. See the Claude vs others foundations page. Do NOT wrap the on-device 3B in a JSON-repair loop: it has constrained decoding. If your output isn't parsing, the schema is wrong or you skipped @Generable.

Скопировать как Markdown Продвинутый On September 22, 2026, Unreal Labs released Unreal Agent — an MIT-licensed agent harness written in Go — and published benchmark runs showing it matching Codex's pass rate on Terminal-Bench 4.0 for $1,428 against $2,350. Same model, same tasks, same score, 39% less money. The interesting part is not the number. It is where the money went. Unreal Agent's central claim is that a large slice of what you pay a coding agent is not reasoning at all — it is the model sitting in the loop managing its own waiting. This page is about that mechanism, because it transfers to any harness you build or buy, including ones that have nothing to do with Unreal Labs. What you'll learn Understand the async tool-call event flow: what gets appended to the session log, when, and what the model actually sees Learn why turn count — not output length — is the unit that drives agent cost, and how to measure it in your own loop Read the published cost table honestly: what the dollar figures cover and what they do not Know the three designs Unreal Labs deliberately refused to build (sub-agents, workflows, harness-level security hooks) and the argument for each Apply the transferable rules to your own agent, whichever harness you already use Последняя проверка: 2026-09-23. Benchmark figures, architecture and design rationale are from Unreal Labs' launch post and repository, published September 22, 2026. All benchmark runs are the vendor's own, executed with GPT-6 Astra at xhigh reasoning; no independent replication existed at the time of writing. The repository showed roughly 1.4k stars the day after launch. Сверьтесь с официальным источником.
documents.s: Async-First Agent Harnesses: What Unreal Agent Changes

documents.t: Unreal Agent is an MIT-licensed Go harness that appends every tool call to an append-only session log as an in-progress event and lets execution continue in the background, so the model never blocks and never polls — which cuts turns, and turns are what you actually pay for.

Here is a normal synchronous agent turn: Model emits a tool call. Harness runs the tool. The loop is suspended. Tool returns. Harness appends the result. Harness calls the model again with the full transcript. Now the same turn in Unreal Agent: Model emits a tool call. Harness immediately appends an event to the session log saying the call is in progress, and starts execution in the background. Execution continues. The model is free to issue more calls. When the tool completes, its result is appended to the log — and that append is what triggers the next model call. The model sees the running state and then the final result, in order, in its own transcript. It never has to encode "wait for this", never issues a poll, never carries heartbeat bookkeeping in its reasoning. Unreal Labs' framing: the harness lets the model "issue more heavy tool calls per model turn without wasting tokens on polling or waiting for them." That is the whole idea. It is small. It is also the part most harnesses get wrong, because a synchronous loop is the obvious thing to write.

Every model turn re-sends the accumulated transcript. A 30-turn agent run does not cost 30× a single call — it costs roughly the sum of a growing context across 30 calls. Turn count is therefore closer to a quadratic cost driver than a linear one, and it dominates anything you save by trimming the system prompt. Look at what the published runs report alongside the dollars: Benchmark Pass rate Unreal Agent Turns Codex Pi Pi turns Terminal-Bench 4.0 57.9% $1,428 28 $2,350 $1,827 44 SWE-Atlas Codebase QnA 65.8% $936 16 $1,303 $1,033 — DeepSWE 1.1 72.4% $1,367 26 $1,633 $1,584 — ALE-CLI 30.0% full pass $217 — — — — On Terminal-Bench 4.0 the comparison is 28 turns versus Pi's 44 — a 36% reduction in turns for a 22% reduction in cost against Pi, and 39% against Codex. The turn column is the causal one; the dollar column is the consequence. This is the same lesson AILmanac covers from the other direction in why agents burn tokens: the expensive thing in an agent is not the answer, it is the re-reading. Pro tip Instrument turn count before you instrument anything else. If you only log tokens, you will optimise prompts and miss the loop. A useful diagnostic: count how many of your agent's turns produced no tool call and no user-visible output. Those are pure loop overhead — waiting, checking, re-planning — and they are what an async harness removes. Parallel-capable tools amplify the effect. If your three slowest tools can run concurrently, a synchronous loop pays for all three serially in wall-clock AND in turns.
documents.s: Why this shows up as money

documents.t: The rationale matters more than the code, because these are arguments you can apply to whatever harness you already run.
documents.s: Three things they deliberately did not build

documents.t: Unreal Labs chose "a straightforward asynchronous tool-calling model" over sub-agent delegation and predefined workflows. The reasoning is that once tool calls are genuinely async, most of what sub-agents were for — running things in parallel without stalling the parent — is already handled by the loop. Sub-agents then add context-splitting, result-merging and their own turn overhead for a problem you no longer have. This is a real position, not the only one. Multi-agent designs still win where you genuinely want isolated context, not just parallelism. But "we need sub-agents to do two things at once" is a claim worth re-testing against an async loop first.

This is the sharpest argument in the launch post, and it is worth quoting the shape of it: security and approvals that rely on harness hooks "tend to require more maintenance and be less robust than deterministic environment or sandbox constraints, outside the harness." What they recommend instead: allowed and disallowed hosts, granular access tokens, and proxies with approval gates. In other words, put the control where the agent physically cannot reach it. The logic is straightforward once stated. A harness hook is code running in the same process as the agent loop, gating a tool the agent can already invoke. A sandbox boundary is enforced by the kernel or the network, below the agent entirely. If your agent has a bash tool — and Unreal Agent's does — an in-process allowlist is a speed bump, not a wall. AILmanac's securing local and hybrid agents covers how to build the outer boundary.

Unreal Labs moved away from vendor SDKs (Anthropic's Agent SDK is named) because those assume "local sessions, subprocesses, and resource limits that don't translate neatly into production use." That is a deployment-shape argument, not a quality one. An SDK modelled on a local CLI session assumes one process, one machine, one lifetime. A production agent fleet wants sessions that outlive a process and can be resumed on a different box — which is exactly what Unreal Agent's append-only, versioned session store provides, including forking a session to branch a run. If you are building a product on top of an agent loop, this is the question to ask of any SDK: can a session survive the process that created it?

The harness is deliberately small and explicitly composable — eight replaceable components behind documented interfaces: Session inbox — deduplicates inputs. Every input carries a globally unique, stable caller ID, so retries do not double-apply. Coordinator — owns LLM turns and dispatches operations. Session store — append-only persisted history, supports forking, versioned. Context builder — assembles the model input. Performs no I/O. LLM adapter — talks to the provider. Tool registry and translators — validate calls synchronously and must "perform no I/O or suspend the loop". Operation manager — runs the durable background work. Two constraints in that list do the heavy lifting and are easy to miss: the context builder and tool translators are forbidden from doing I/O. That is what keeps the coordinator's hot path deterministic and non-blocking — all latency is pushed into operations, which are the things designed to be async. If you build your own harness, this is the rule to steal. Storage formats and operations are versioned, and an unsupported session version errors explicitly on resume rather than half-loading. That is the correct failure mode for durable state, and it is rarer than it should be. The built-in tool surface is three tools: Bash, ViewImage, and Skill-use — the last of which hooks into the portable skill format AILmanac covers in SKILL.md as an open standard. Three tools is the point: a small, token-cheap tool surface is part of the cost story.

Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Install⌄ Go 1.27+ toolchain, then go install the runner from the cmd/ path, or clone and use the bundled Makefile (make build, make test). ←PreviousNext→ 2Pick a provider⌄ Selected by environment variable. OpenAI, OpenAI Codex, OpenRouter, Fireworks and Ollama are supported, so you can point the same harness at a hosted frontier model or a local one. ←PreviousNext→ 3Run a single prompt⌄ The runner takes -p for a prompt and -workspace for the directory the agent works in, in the same shape as claude -p. Output is a JSONL transcript you can redirect to a file. ←PreviousNext→ 4Read the transcript, not the summary⌄ The JSONL run log is where the async event flow is visible: in-progress events, then results. Counting the model-call events in it gives you the turn count that drives your bill. ←PreviousNext→ 5Put the boundary outside⌄ Before you point it at anything real, set the sandbox: restricted filesystem, allowlisted hosts, scoped tokens. The harness deliberately does not do this for you. ←PreviousNext→ Install and run (from Unreal Labs' documented usage) CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ go install github.com/unreallabsai/unreal-agent/cmd/unreal-agent-runner@latest export OPENAI_API_KEY="..." unreal-agent-runner -p 'Inspect this project and explain how to run its tests.' Point it at a different provider and keep the transcript CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ export UNREAL_HARNESS_LLM_PROVIDER=openrouter export UNREAL_HARNESS_LLM_MODEL=<model-id> unreal-agent-runner \ -workspace ./my-project \ -p 'Summarize this project.' > run.jsonl

Four caveats, because the numbers are good enough that they deserve scrutiny: Every run is the vendor's own. No third party had replicated them at the time of writing. One model. All published runs used GPT-6 Astra at xhigh reasoning. The async advantage should generalise — it is a loop property, not a model property — but "should" is not "was measured". The dollars are whole-suite totals, not per-task costs. They are comparable to each other and not to your workload. Pass rates are matched, not improved. The claim is explicitly same score, less money. On DeepSWE 1.1 Unreal Agent reports 72.4% at $1,367 against Codex's $1,633 — a 19% saving, notably smaller than the 39% on Terminal-Bench. The advantage scales with how tool-heavy and how long-running your tasks are. On short tasks with few tool calls, expect close to nothing. That last point is the practical one. If your agent does three tool calls and finishes, async buys you almost nothing. If it does sixty over half an hour, it buys you the difference between the two columns.

You do not have to adopt Unreal Agent to use any of this: Measure turns. It is the cost variable most teams do not log. Make slow tools non-blocking, even if your harness is otherwise synchronous. Returning a handle immediately and delivering the result as a later event is a change you can make inside most loops. Keep the hot path I/O-free. Context assembly and tool-call validation should never wait on the network. Move approvals out of the process. Network policy, scoped credentials and a gating proxy beat an in-process allowlist that lives next to a bash tool. Shrink the tool surface. Three good tools cost fewer tokens per turn than fifteen mediocre ones, on every single turn. Check yourself 0/5 Key takeaways Turn count, not token count, is the cost variable in an agent loop. Instrument it first. Making tool calls non-blocking removes polling and waiting turns — 28 turns vs 44 for the same Terminal-Bench 4.0 pass rate is the whole argument. The advantage is proportional to tool-heaviness: 39% on Terminal-Bench, 19% on DeepSWE, ~0 on a three-call task. Security belongs outside the harness. An in-process approval hook next to a bash tool is a speed bump; a sandbox and a gating proxy are a boundary. Keep context assembly and tool validation I/O-free. Push every wait into a durable operation. All published numbers are vendor runs on one model. Treat them as a well-argued hypothesis about your workload, not a measurement of it.
