documents.t: For most teams the honest answer is no. Do the breakeven math per your workload: Path Cost When it wins Moonshot API $3.00/M in, $0.30/M cache-hit, $15/M out Prototyping, low volume, non-sensitive data Runpod hosted K3 $0.95/M in, $4/M out Steady mid-volume, need OpenAI-compatible endpoint, don't care where compute runs Runpod 8× B300 by the hour $59.12/hr Bursty runs, need control over serving config, still don't want capex Own the hardware $80k–$500k+ capex Strict data-residency, 24/7 saturation, or you're building a competing inference product At the 16× GB10 cluster's decode of ~21 tok/s, one node produces ~76k output tok/hr. At Runpod-K3 hosted pricing that's $0.30 of output tokens per hour. To beat a $59/hr hosted rate you'd need throughput closer to ~15M output tokens/hr at high batch and near-100% utilization — achievable with concurrency, but only if you actually have that much demand. Below that, hosted wins by an order of magnitude. The correct reasons to self-host K3 in 2026: Data residency / regulatory — the prompts and completions cannot leave your VPC. Continuous saturation — you have a fleet of agents running 24/7 and cache-hit pricing still hurts. Model modification — you're training a custom DSpark speculator, doing LoRA finetunes on the MoE experts, or experimenting with routing changes. Learning value — a lab or a team that specifically wants to understand frontier-MoE serving at the metal. If none of those apply, call the API and route the saved engineering time toward better prompts, better evals, and better context engineering.
documents.s: Step 6 — Should you self-host at all?

documents.t: vLLM exposes an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, so the same client works against your own rack, Runpod's hosted K3, or Moonshot's API. Call your K3 endpoint with the OpenAI Python SDK CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ from openai import OpenAI client = OpenAI( base_url="http://localhost:8000/v1", # or Runpod / Moonshot base URL api_key="EMPTY", # self-hosted vLLM ignores keys ) resp = client.chat.completions.create( model="moonshotai/Kimi-K3", messages=[ {"role": "system", "content": "You are a terse coding assistant."}, {"role": "user", "content": "Explain DSpark speculative decoding in three bullets."}, ], max_tokens=8192, temperature=0.2, ) print(resp.choices[0].message.content)

Скопировать как Markdown Средний On July 16, 2026, Moonshot AI shipped Kimi K3 — a 2.8-trillion-parameter Mixture-of-Experts model and currently the world's largest open-weight release at that class. Headlines called it the Chinese lab's moonshot. The actual number to watch is quieter: K3 scored fourth on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, behind Claude Fable 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol, but squarely ahead of Claude Opus 4.8. For a model whose full weights land on Hugging Face on July 27, 2026, that's an unusual sentence to write. This page covers what's genuinely non-obvious about K3 — the architectural changes, the pricing trap that makes it look expensive until you check the cache hit rate, and the specific tasks where it outranks every other model, open or closed. What you'll learn Understand why 2.8T parameters doesn't mean 2.8T compute: the MoE arithmetic and how sparse activation works Learn the three architectural innovations in K3 (KDA, AttnRes, LatentMoE) that give it 2.5× better scaling efficiency than K2 Know the cache-hit pricing math: why K3 costs closer to $0.30/M than $3.00/M in real coding workloads Place K3 in the benchmark landscape: where it leads all models, where it trails, and what the hallucination rate caveat means Get started with the API in three lines using an OpenAI-compatible client
documents.s: Kimi K3: World's Largest Open-Weight Model

documents.t: Kimi K3 is an open-weight (full weights dropping July 27, 2026), 2.8-trillion-parameter sparse MoE from Moonshot AI, tuned for long-horizon agentic coding and knowledge work, with native vision and a 1-million-token context window — priced like a frontier API but often cheaper in practice because coding workloads hit the prompt cache more than 90% of the time.

The headline number is dramatic, but K3 is a Mixture-of-Experts model. It has 896 expert sub-networks, and only 16 experts fire per token — that's the "Stable LatentMoE" component. The model is enormous in storage but compact in compute per forward pass. At inference, the active parameter footprint is far smaller than 2.8T. This is the same architectural trade-off as DeepSeek V4 Pro (which also uses MoE), and it's why a model this large can run efficiently on manageable hardware once the weights are self-hosted. The practical implication: don't compare parameter counts directly between dense and MoE models. A 2.8T MoE with 16/896 experts active has a different compute profile than a 70B dense model — and a very different hardware requirement for self-hosting. Последняя проверка: 2026-07-23. MoE configuration (896 experts, 16 active) is from Moonshot's official technical blog. Hardware requirements for self-hosting the full 2.8T model will depend on quantization; MXFP4 weights bring down the memory footprint significantly, but exact figures are not yet confirmed for the full open-weight release. Сверьтесь с официальным источником.
documents.s: 1. "2.8 trillion parameters" does not mean 2.8 trillion activations per token

documents.t: K3 API pricing is $3.00/M input tokens and $15.00/M output tokens — expensive at first glance. But Moonshot offers a cache-hit price of $0.30/M input (a 10× discount), and in coding workloads the company reports cache hit rates above 90%. That means the effective per-million-token input price for an ongoing coding session is closer to $0.30–$0.45, not $3.00. Here's the practical comparison at task-level cost (sourced from third-party evaluations): Model Cost per agentic task Kimi K3 $0.94 GPT-5.6 Sol $1.04 Claude Opus 4.8 $1.80 K3 also uses 21% fewer output tokens than K2.6 — it learned to be terser — which further reduces the bill. At headline prices K3 looks premium; at realistic task prices it undercuts frontier competition.
documents.s: 2. The cache-hit rate flips the cost math completely

documents.t: K3 ships three new components that are baked into the model from training: Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) — a hybrid linear-attention mechanism that handles the 1M-token context window efficiently without the quadratic cost of standard attention at long range. Attention Residuals (AttnRes) — instead of uniform accumulation across depth, AttnRes selectively retrieves representations from earlier layers, letting the model "look back" at its own earlier thinking during a long agentic run. Per-Head Muon and Sigmoid Tanh Unit (SiTU) — optimizer and activation improvements that contributed to what Moonshot claims is a 2.5× improvement in overall scaling efficiency versus K2. The MXFP4 weight quantization (with MXFP8 activations) is also training-aware, not applied after the fact. This matters for quality: post-hoc quantization typically costs benchmark points; quantization-aware training largely eliminates that tax.
documents.s: 3. The architectural innovations are training-time, not post-hoc

documents.t: K3 ranked 4th overall on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index (as of July 2026): Rank Model Score 1 Claude Fable 5 ~60 2 GPT-5.6 Sol ~59 3 (closed tie area) — 4 Kimi K3 ~57 5 Claude Opus 4.8 ~56 Where K3 leads all models (open and closed): Frontend Code Arena (ranked #1 at 1,679 points), a real-world evaluation of UI component generation and iterative visual coding. The model's 1M-token context and native vision capability contribute here. Where to apply caution: K3's hallucination rate is approximately 51% in independent evaluations — higher than frontier closed models. The benchmark accuracy jumped from K2.6's 33% to K3's 46%, but factual grounding didn't improve at the same rate. Verify K3 outputs for factual claims; it's strongest in code and structured task completion, less reliable on open-ended knowledge questions without retrieval. Последняя проверка: 2026-07-23. Hallucination rate, benchmark scores, and per-task cost figures are from third-party benchmark aggregators, not Moonshot's self-reporting. The Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index scores are approximate as of launch week and may shift as the index updates with more evaluations. Сверьтесь с официальным источником. DeepSWE (long-horizon software engineering): K3 scored 67.3, the highest published score on an open-weight model as of this writing, matching frontier territory. BrowseComp (long-context navigation, no context management): 90.4 with the 1M-token window enabled — notably achieved without any chunking or retrieval strategy, which most models require at this scale.
documents.s: Where K3 sits in the benchmark landscape

documents.t: Moonshot K3's training leaned into long-horizon, minimal-supervision tasks — the kind where a model has to plan, tool-call, debug, iterate, and stay coherent across a large repo or a multi-hour workflow. Specific capabilities the official blog demonstrates: GPU kernel optimization (CUDA/Triton-level work, not just Python wrappers) GPU compiler development (built a MiniTriton compiler from scratch as a benchmark task) Chip design and RTL verification (hardware engineering) Multi-agent subagent orchestration — K3 can coordinate 20+ concurrent subagents in its own Kimi Work environment Interactive research visualizations and dashboard generation (where the vision-first design and Frontend Code Arena #1 ranking make sense) The "thinking mode" is always enabled at launch (maximum effort). The API does not yet support tunable effort levels — at launch, every call uses max thinking, which adds tokens. Additional reasoning effort levels are on the roadmap but not available yet.

K3 uses an OpenAI-compatible API shape, so if your codebase already calls GPT or Claude via an OpenAI client shim, pointing it at Kimi is a small change: Guided walkthrough1 of 3 1Get an API key from platform.kimi.ai⌄ Sign in at platform.kimi.ai, create an API key. K3 is available under the model ID `kimi-k3`. ←PreviousNext→ 2Use the OpenAI-compatible endpoint⌄ Set the base URL to `https://api.moonshot.cn/v1` and the model to `kimi-k3`. The client can be the standard `openai` Python or JS SDK — or OpenRouter if you prefer a single aggregator. ←PreviousNext→ 3Enable long context and vision as needed⌄ Pass images in the messages array using the standard `image_url` content type. For 1M-token tasks, no special parameter is needed — the context window is always 1M. ←PreviousNext→ Kimi K3 via OpenAI SDK (Python) CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ import openai client = openai.OpenAI( api_key="YOUR_MOONSHOT_KEY", base_url="https://api.moonshot.cn/v1", ) response = client.chat.completions.create( model="kimi-k3", messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Refactor this 5,000-line Python codebase..."}], ) print(response.choices[0].message.content) Via OpenRouter (single API key, lets you A/B K3 against Claude or GPT easily): Kimi K3 via OpenRouter CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ import openai client = openai.OpenAI( api_key="YOUR_OPENROUTER_KEY", base_url="https://openrouter.ai/api/v1", ) response = client.chat.completions.create( model="moonshotai/kimi-k3", messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Review this TypeScript and suggest optimizations."}], ) print(response.choices[0].message.content) Open weights (self-hosting, from July 27, 2026): Weights will be released on Hugging Face under Moonshot AI's organization page. The model ships in MXFP4 quantization natively; broad hardware compatibility was an explicit design goal. Full hardware requirements will be confirmed at release.

documents.t: You might already have K2 tooling from the Kimi K2 for Claude users page. Here's how to decide: Kimi K2 (1T param) Kimi K3 (2.8T param) Total params 1 trillion 2.8 trillion Active params / token ~32B ~16/896 experts Native vision No Yes Context window 128K 1M Open weights available Now July 27, 2026 Benchmark rank ~7th (Artificial Analysis) 4th Output cost Lower $15/M (offset by cache) Best for Cost-conscious agentic tool use, self-hosting now Long-horizon visual coding, large repos, multimodal tasks Reach for K3 when: you need the frontier-tier quality (top-5 models), the task is long and likely to hit the prompt cache repeatedly, or vision is required. Especially useful if you want open weights for compliance/privacy but can wait until July 27. Stick with K2 when: you need to self-host right now, cost is the primary constraint and the task doesn't benefit from K3's extra depth, or you're already running K2 in production with working tooling.

Скопировать как Markdown Средний Последняя проверка: 2026-09-14. Ollama's context defaults and truncation behaviour are read from the main branch docs and source on the date shown. Older builds defaulted to a flat 2,048 or 4,096 tokens regardless of hardware; the VRAM-tiered default described below is current as of this verification. Check ollama --version and the linked docs before trusting a number. Сверьтесь с официальным источником. What you'll learn Do the context-budget arithmetic before you move a prompt, and see why a 35 KB prompt that is invisible on Claude is a quarter of a small local window Know exactly what Ollama does when the prompt is too long — it drops the middle, keeps a few prefix tokens, and only tells the server log Recognise the five behavioural signals of context exhaustion in a local agent before it wastes an hour Restructure a monolithic prompt into single-objective units that fit, and hand state between them on disk Tune the runtime knobs that matter: OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH, KV-cache quantisation, flash attention, and the parallel-request multiplier A post that hit the Hacker News front page on September 13–14, 2026 described an experience many people are about to have: a 35 KB system prompt that had been running fine on Claude Opus was pointed at a self-hosted 27B model through Ollama, and within about three minutes the agent was re-reading files it had already read, repeating identical tool calls, and rewriting finished work. Nothing was "wrong" with the model. The prompt plus the session history had simply exceeded a 65K-token window, and the runtime had started throwing parts of the conversation away. This page is the guide the author wished existed. It is about prompt size versus context budget, which is a different problem from prompt wording across models, covered in Porting Prompts Across Models, and from which local model to pick, covered in Run Models Locally with Ollama.
documents.s: Why a 35 KB System Prompt Breaks on a Local Model

documents.t: On Claude a 35 KB system prompt is roughly 9,000 tokens, sitting inside a 1,000,000-token window: under 1 %. You never think about it. On a local runtime the same prompt is the same 9,000 tokens, but the window is whatever you configured, and the default is small: Ollama default context (current main docs) Machine 4K tokens under 24 GiB VRAM 32K tokens 24–48 GiB VRAM 256K tokens 48 GiB VRAM or more At 4K, a 9,000-token system prompt does not fit at all. At 32K it is 28 % of the window before the user says a word. At the 65K the HN author configured it is 14 %, which sounds fine until you add what an agent session actually carries: tool definitions (a few hundred to a few thousand tokens), every file the agent reads, every tool result, and the model's own output. A coding agent that reads three medium files and runs two commands is routinely 20–30K tokens into the conversation. With a 9K fixed cost, the usable working memory is gone in a handful of turns. The two cloud habits that make this invisible on Claude are absent locally: the window is two orders of magnitude smaller, and there is no built-in compaction. Claude Code summarises the conversation when it approaches the limit (Context Management); a raw Ollama endpoint does not. Some local agent harnesses do their own compaction, but the runtime underneath them does not. Measure the prompt before you migrate (any OpenAI-compatible local endpoint) CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ # Count what the model will actually see, from Ollama's own tokenizer. # prompt_eval_count in the response is the tokenised prompt length. curl -s http://localhost:11434/api/chat -d '{ "model": "qwen3:32b", "messages": [{"role":"system","content":"'"$(cat system-prompt.md | sed 's/"/\\"/g')"'"}, {"role":"user","content":"ping"}], "stream": false, "options": {"num_predict": 1} }' | jq '{prompt_tokens: .prompt_eval_count, cached: .prompt_eval_cached_count}' Compare that number against the num_ctx you run with, then subtract the tool schema and a realistic transcript. If the remainder is under about half the window, the prompt is too big for the setup, and no amount of wording will fix it.
documents.s: The arithmetic that nobody does first

documents.t: This is the mechanism that turns "slightly too long" into "mysteriously stupid", and it is documented nowhere in prose; it is in the source. When a request's prompt is longer than the context and truncation is enabled (it is, by default, for /api/chat and /api/generate), the llama.cpp-backed runner in Ollama does the following, in llm/llama_server.go: Keeps the first num_keep tokens of the prompt. The default num_keep is 4, set "to avoid issues on context shifts". Computes a target length that leaves roughly half of the remaining context free for generation. Discards tokens from the middle: the kept prefix stays, the tail stays, the block between them is removed. Logs truncating input prompt with the before/after sizes on the server. The API response carries no flag, and a client library sees a normal completion. The project's own test table makes the scale concrete: with a 4,096-token context and the default num_keep, an over-long prompt is cut to 2,050 tokens. Half of the window is deliberately reserved for the reply. So a 9,000-token system prompt on a 4K window arrives at the model as four tokens of its opening, then a hole, then whatever fits at the end of the conversation. The instructions are gone; the last user message survives. That is exactly the "restating objectives, repeating tool calls" behaviour the HN post describes: the model is being asked to act on a conversation whose rules were silently deleted. Two ways out of the silent version: Send "truncate": false in the request. Ollama then returns HTTP 400 with a message that the prompt is longer than the context currently available, instead of guessing. For an agent harness this is the correct behaviour: fail loudly, then compact or restart. Raise num_keep to the length of your system prompt so the prefix survives a shift. This preserves the rules but still deletes conversation from the middle; it is a band-aid, not a fix. The chat endpoint has a second, gentler layer above this: when the message list is too long for the limit, Ollama's prompt builder drops older messages first while keeping the system message and the latest turn (see server/prompt.go). You can lose intermediate tool results this way too, which is why an agent may "forget" it already read a file. Watch the server log; with OLLAMA_DEBUG=1 the trimming is visible. Not just Ollama llama.cpp's server has the same context-shift behaviour under a different flag, vLLM refuses over-long prompts by default, and LM Studio exposes the context length as a per-model setting that is easy to leave at its small default. The pattern to internalise is: know whether your runtime truncates or errors, and prefer the error.
documents.s: What Ollama does when the prompt does not fit

documents.t: The author of the HN post kept a list of what context exhaustion looked like from the outside, and it matches what people report about every small-window agent. Treat any of these as "the window is full", not as "the model is bad": Identical consecutive tool calls. The model no longer has the previous result in view, so it asks again. Re-reading a file it already read. Same cause; the read result was trimmed. Restating the objective in its own words mid-task, sometimes with drift. The system prompt has been cut, and the model is reconstructing the task from the tail of the conversation. Tool-call parsing failures that appear after a run of clean calls. Once the examples and schema in the prompt are gone, small models fall back to their default formatting. High turn count relative to files actually changed. The ratio is the cheapest metric to track in a harness; when it spikes, stop and restart with fresh context. If you run through an OpenAI-compatible client, log prompt_eval_count every turn. When it stops growing while the conversation keeps growing, truncation has started.

A 35 KB prompt is usually a whole product's worth of rules: personas, coding standards, tool etiquette, output formats, edge cases, and a long list of "never do X". On a 1M-token model that works by brute force. On a 32K model it does not, and the fix the HN author landed on is the same one that the strongest commenters argued for independently: split the prompt into single-objective units and run each in its own short session. Guided walkthrough1 of 6 1Inventory the prompt by objective⌄ Go through the 35 KB and tag every paragraph with the job it serves: planning, editing, testing, reviewing, writing the commit. Most monoliths contain five to eight distinct jobs plus a shared core (persona, repo facts, safety rules) that is under 2 KB. ←PreviousNext→ 2Cut one prompt per job⌄ Each job gets the shared core plus only its own rules and examples. Aim for 2–4K tokens each. On Ollama, ship them as separate Modelfiles (`PARAMETER num_ctx` set explicitly, `SYSTEM` block per job) or as per-agent prompt files in your harness. ←PreviousNext→ 3Hand state between jobs on disk, not in context⌄ Each unit writes a short structured summary (what it did, what remains, which files) to a file when it finishes; the next unit reads only that file plus the slice of the repo it needs. The session ends. This is the local-model equivalent of Claude Code's compaction, done by hand. ←PreviousNext→ 4Replace negatives with positives⌄ Small models follow 'only do X' far better than 'don't do Y', and negative lists are where monolith prompts bloat. Convert `never touch tests` into `edit only files under src/`. ←PreviousNext→ 5Reduce tool calls per step⌄ Every tool result is context you pay for until it is trimmed. Prefer tools that return a slice (one function, one hunk) over tools that return a whole file; one HN commenter's `inspect_function` / `replace_function` pair is the canonical example. ←PreviousNext→ 6Restart on completion, not on failure⌄ Finish the unit, write the hand-off, kill the session. Do not wait for the failure signals; by then the prompt has already been truncated and the output is untrustworthy. ←PreviousNext→ A hand-off file the next single-objective unit reads first CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ # HANDOFF — written by unit 2 (implement), read by unit 3 (test) Objective completed: renamed getUser -> fetchUser across src/ Files changed: src/api/user.ts, src/pages/profile.tsx, src/hooks/useUser.ts Not done: tests still reference getUser (tests/user.test.ts) Constraints carried forward: no new dependencies; keep TypeScript strict Next unit should: update tests, run `npm test`, write result to HANDOFF.md This is also the honest answer to the commenter who said a 35 KB prompt is "confusing and unfocused on any LLM". Frontier models paper over the bloat; local models expose it. Splitting by objective usually improves results on Claude too, and it is the design Claude plus local models assumes when it routes cheap steps locally.
documents.s: Restructure: single-objective prompts and state on disk

documents.t: Once the prompt is right-sized, four knobs decide how much window you can actually afford. All are from the Ollama FAQ and docs. Knob What it does Gotcha OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH=65536 ollama serve (or num_ctx per request, or PARAMETER num_ctx in a Modelfile) Sets the window Larger context costs memory. The docs say so bluntly; the KV cache grows linearly with it OLLAMA_KV_CACHE_TYPE=q8_0 Quantises the KV cache; about half the memory of the default f16. q4_0 is about a quarter Requires flash attention; small quality cost, larger with q4_0 OLLAMA_FLASH_ATTENTION=1 Enables flash attention; prerequisite for KV quantisation and reduces memory for long contexts Not every backend/model supports it; set it and check the server log OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL (default 1) Concurrent requests per model Required memory scales by OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL × OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH. Two parallel slots at 64K cost the KV memory of one at 128K A useful order of operations on a fixed memory budget: pick the largest model you can hold with a small window, then enable flash attention and q8_0 KV cache, then raise the context until the server log shows it spilling to CPU. Split context across GPU and CPU is where tokens per second collapse; several HN commenters reported dense 27B–32B models at FP8 with very long windows on dual-GPU setups, but on a single 128 GB unified-memory box the practical ceiling was the 65K the author used. Prefix caching helps, but only for the prefix Ollama reports prompt_eval_cached_count in every response. A stable system prompt at the very start of the conversation is re-used from the KV cache across requests, so its cost is paid once per session, not per turn. Anything after the first change in the conversation is recomputed. Put the fixed material first and the volatile material last, the same rule as Claude's prompt caching (Prompt Caching Economics).

Tokenise the system prompt with the local tokenizer and write the number down. Set num_ctx explicitly. Never rely on the default; it depends on the machine's VRAM. Decide truncate-or-error. For agents, send "truncate": false and handle the 400. Split the prompt by objective; shared core under 2K tokens; each unit 2–4K. Hand off between units through a file; end the session after each unit. Log prompt_eval_count per turn and alert when it plateaus. Enable flash attention and q8_0 KV cache before raising the window. Watch the server log for truncating input prompt during the first week. Check yourself 0/5

Скопировать как Markdown Продвинутый Every reasoning model you have ever used thinks by writing. Extended thinking, <thinking> blocks, scratchpads, ReAct traces — the model's deliberation is a stream of tokens, which means you can read it, and it means you pay for every word of it. Latent reasoning asks what happens if you cut out the words. Instead of sampling a token from the final hidden state and feeding the token's embedding back in, you feed the hidden state itself back in. No vocabulary projection, no sampling, no text. The model keeps thinking; the thought is now a vector. This has been a research curiosity since Meta's Coconut in late 2024. On 13 October 2026 it became something you can download: Together AI's HybridAgent is the first latent-reasoning agent — it thinks in hidden states, calls a Python interpreter and a search engine through text, and ships as MIT-licensed 8B and 14B checkpoints. It hit the Hacker News front page with 396 points and 192 comments, and the comments split almost exactly down the middle between "this is the way" and "you just deleted the only thing we could audit." Both camps are right about something. This page covers the mechanism, the numbers, the reason several testers got an infinite loop instead of an answer, and the one claim in the paper you should not take at face value. What you'll learn Explain latent reasoning in one sentence: feed the hidden state back as the next input embedding instead of projecting it to a token Read the HybridLink formula and understand why a ~10M-parameter adapter is all that stands between a text model and a latent one Cite the real split: 170-183 latent steps per instance against ~302 text tokens, where a text-only agent spends ~596 Know why loading these weights in llama.cpp or plain Transformers gives you a looping text model, not a latent agent Argue both sides of the inspectability claim — including the paper's own causal test showing latent thoughts carry 44.9-51.3% of the accuracy Place HybridAgent against Coconut and Soft Thinking, and know which of the three needs no training at all Последняя проверка: 2026-10-19. HybridAgent was submitted on 13 October 2026 and the repository is days old (216 stars, 28 forks at the time of writing). Benchmark numbers, checkpoint names, download counts and the serving story will all move. The mechanism — hidden states as the reasoning medium, a small adapter as the bridge, and the monitorability trade it forces — is the durable part. Re-check the repo before you build on any specific command. Сверьтесь с официальным источником.
documents.s: Latent Reasoning: Agents That Think Without Words

documents.t: Take a standard decoder. At step t it produces a last-layer hidden state h_t, projects it through the unembedding matrix to logits over the vocabulary, samples a token, looks that token up in the embedding table, and feeds the embedding in as input t+1. That round trip through the vocabulary is a bottleneck in the literal information-theoretic sense. A hidden state in a modern 8B model is a few thousand floating-point numbers. A token is a choice from ~150,000 options — roughly 17 bits. Sampling a token throws away almost everything the hidden state contained and keeps the one discrete symbol a human can read. Latent reasoning skips the round trip. Feed h_t back in directly. The model's next forward pass conditions on the full continuous state rather than on the 17-bit summary of it. The problem is that h_t lives in the output space and the model expects something from the input embedding space. The distributions do not match, and feeding one into the other naively produces garbage. HybridLink is the fix, and it is almost embarrassingly small: e_{t+1} = h_t + W_2 · σ(W_1 · h_t) A two-layer MLP with a residual connection. The residual is the load-bearing part: it carries h_t through unchanged so semantics survive, while the MLP branch nudges it into the input distribution. The paper puts it at roughly 2 · d_h² parameters — about 10M for a 4B backbone. Three orders of magnitude smaller than the model it steers. What you'll learn A token is ~17 bits. A hidden state is thousands of floats. Sampling is lossy compression of the model's own thought, performed once per step. HybridLink is e_{t+1} = h_t + W_2·σ(W_1·h_t) — a residual two-layer MLP, ~10M params for a 4B model. That adapter is the whole bridge. The residual connection is not decoration. The authors' ablation shows the residual design gives consistent gains across all three downstream benchmarks.

Coconut and Soft Thinking both do latent reasoning. Neither can call a tool, because tools are a text interface: you emit a function call, something runs, text comes back. A model mid-latent-thought has no tokens to emit and nowhere to put the result. HybridAgent solves this with two pieces. Guided walkthrough1 of 4 1Anchor tokens mark the mode boundary⌄ The tokenizer gains <latent> and </latent>. The model emits <latent> in text mode to enter latent mode; HybridLink then loops hidden states back in. Latent mode closes when the nearest-neighbour token to the current (projected) state is </latent> — the model's own geometry decides when it has thought enough. There is no fixed latent budget. Coconut, by contrast, settled on a constant number of latent thoughts because letting a classifier decide performed no better. ←PreviousNext→ 2A continuous working memory carries everything across turns⌄ Instead of serialising the turn to text and re-encoding it, HybridAgent appends KV entries — M⁽¹⁾ = M⁽⁰⁾ ⊕ [K≤t, V≤t] — so text spans, latent spans and tool outputs accumulate in one cache. Latent thoughts have no text form, so there would be nothing to re-encode: the KV cache IS the transcript. This is why the paper calls the hybrid context 'lossless' across turns. ←PreviousNext→ 3Two training stages teach the mode switch⌄ HybridSFT teaches the backbone to coordinate with HybridLink on tool-integrated hybrid sequences. Then HybridRL scales it with reward r(τ) = r_correct + r_format + r_tool. Note what is absent: there is NO reward term for using latent mode. The text/latent balance is emergent, not incentivised. ←PreviousNext→ 4Tools stay ordinary⌄ A sandboxed Python interpreter and a live search engine (Tavily in the paper's setup), capped at 10 calls per trajectory with top-10 snippets per query. Nothing about the tool layer is exotic — the agent drops back to text to call them, exactly as ReAct would. ←PreviousNext→ The training detail worth stealing is self-conditioned supervision. Naive teacher forcing feeds ground-truth latent embeddings during training, so at inference the model meets its own HybridLink outputs for the first time and drifts. The fix is a two-pass scheme: pass one teacher-forces the ground-truth hybrid sequence, pass two replays the identical sequence with the model's own generated latent embeddings substituted in. Table 3 reports this worth 30.5% on average across AIME25/26 and MATH500 over activating HybridLink without it. It is the same exposure-bias problem that scheduled sampling addresses in sequence models, and the same shape of fix.
documents.s: What makes it an agent, not just a reasoner

documents.t: Watch out These are the authors' own numbers on their own harness, days old, with no independent replication. Read them as a claim, not a measurement you can bank. The headline '10.4% improvement' is an average across 3 model scales and 11 benchmarks against a mix of baselines. Per-benchmark it ranges from +1.8 points to +42.5. Claim Figure Average performance gain +10.4% across 3 scales, 11 benchmarks Token reduction 35.5-54.7% Inference speed 1.8x-2.6x faster Cost 2.7x-3.7x cheaper Text tokens per instance (8B) ~302, against a text agent's ~596 Latent steps per instance 170-183 The last two rows are the ones that actually explain the architecture. HybridAgent emits roughly half the text of a text-only agent — and performs 170-183 additional forward passes that produce no text at all. It is not thinking less. It is thinking in a medium that does not bill by the word. That also tells you where the cost saving comes from, and where it does not. A latent step is still a full forward pass: same FLOPs, same latency, same memory traffic as generating a token. The saving is not free computation. It comes from (a) not paying the decode-and-re-embed overhead, (b) a far shorter KV sequence because latent spans are dense rather than spelled out, and (c) fewer total steps to reach an answer. If your bill is dominated by prefill of a large static context, latent reasoning does nothing for you. Against latent baselines the gaps are large — on GAIA Level 1 the paper reports +39.8% over Coconut and +28.2% over Soft Thinking, and around +41-42% on WebWalker for both. That is less a vindication of HybridAgent's reasoning than a reminder that Coconut and Soft Thinking were never built to hold a multi-turn tool loop together. Against the text baselines the margins are modest and honest: AIME25 39.2% vs ARPO's 37.1%, MATH500 84.6% vs 82.8%, MuSiQue 32.0% vs 28.5%.

Several people on the launch thread reported the same failure: ask the 8B "who is the pope?" and it loops forever. One tester saw identical looping with the 14B in llama.cpp at both 8-bit and 16-bit, and concluded the problem was llama.cpp rather than the model. That diagnosis is almost certainly right, and the model card says why in one line: standard Transformers loading yields a text-only variant, because the hybrid behaviour lives in adapter.pt / adapter_config.json — the HybridLink weights — plus the custom generation engine in the repo. Think through what a generic runtime does with these weights. The tokenizer has <latent> and </latent>. The fine-tuned backbone has learned to emit <latent> and then expect HybridLink to take over. In llama.cpp or plain AutoModelForCausalLM, nothing takes over. There is no component that loops hidden states back, and no component that evaluates the nearest-neighbour closing condition. The model enters a mode that does not exist and never finds its way out. Watch out This is an inference-stack-shaped model, not a weights-shaped model. GGUF conversion, vLLM, Ollama and plain Transformers will not reproduce the paper's behaviour — they cannot, because HybridLink is not in the graph. Infinite generation on a trivial question is the signature of a missing HybridLink, not a broken checkpoint. The README documents no serving path other than the repo's own batch inference engine. Treat 'can I serve this?' as unanswered, not as yes. The only path that runs the actual architecture CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ git clone https://github.com/togethercomputer/HybridAgent.git && cd HybridAgent conda create -n hybridagent python=3.11 -y && conda activate hybridagent pip install torch==2.11.0 --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu128 pip install -r requirements.txt && pip install -e . cp .env.example .env # set TAVILY_API_KEY — the search tool needs it python -m hybrid_inference.run_batch \ --model togethercomputer/HybridAgent-8B-Agentic \ --input examples/questions.jsonl \ --output outputs/results.jsonl --num_samples 4 If you want to see latent thoughts rather than benchmark them, the repo ships a dedicated viewer that renders a run as an HTML report with pseudo-text thoughts interleaved with tool calls and observations: Render one trajectory's latent thoughts as readable pseudo-text CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ python -m interpretable_latent_mode \ --model togethercomputer/HybridAgent-14B-Agentic \ --question "Which of these two papers reports a larger token reduction, and by how much?" \ --output report.html Training is a different scale of commitment. HybridSFT wants 8-16 GPUs; HybridRL wants 32 GPUs across 4 nodes. This is not a fine-tune you run on a workstation.
documents.s: The gotcha that bit everyone on day one

documents.t: The paper's strongest rhetorical move is that latent reasoning does not cost you transparency. Every latent step can be read out as pseudo-text, by taking the state HybridLink produced and finding its nearest neighbour in the embedding table by cosine similarity. Figure 2 shows the result is readable and context-specific, and stays semantically aligned with the surrounding text reasoning. It is a real capability, and it is more than Coconut offered. It is also the weakest link in the argument, for a reason a commenter put precisely: nearest-neighbour decoding "loses meaning where the model is expressing combinations of tokens in a vector." The entire premise of latent reasoning is that a hidden state carries more than any single token can. Reading it out as a single token necessarily discards the surplus — the exact surplus that made the technique worth doing. The paper's own experiment makes this concrete and is the most interesting result in it. Table 5 runs causal interventions: corrupt the latent thoughts and accuracy drops 44.9-51.3%. The latent stream is not a decorative side channel. It is carrying roughly half the model's problem-solving. So the two claims — latent thoughts are load-bearing and latent thoughts are faithfully readable as single tokens — are in tension. A readout that compressed a load-bearing vector down to its nearest word and lost nothing would mean the vector never needed to be a vector. This matters beyond interpretability aesthetics, because reading the chain of thought is currently a live safety control. The 2025 cross-lab position paper Chain of Thought Monitorability — 41 authors including Yoshua Bengio, Anca Dragan and Dan Hendrycks, from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google DeepMind and others — argues exactly that reasoning models externalise their deliberation in a readable form, that monitoring it is a genuine oversight opportunity, and that the opportunity is fragile: architecture changes can remove the monitorable substrate as a side effect of an efficiency decision. Latent reasoning is the textbook instance of that side effect. The informal name for the endpoint is neuralese — reasoning with no human-readable trace at all. The launch thread also surfaced the subtler training-time version, which commenters tagged with Zvi Mowshowitz's phrase "the Most Forbidden Technique": if you optimise against a chain-of-thought monitor during RL, you do not remove the bad behaviour, you remove its visibility. Latent reasoning arrives at a similar destination from a different road — not by teaching the model to hide its thinking, but by moving the thinking somewhere there is nothing to hide.
documents.s: The contested claim: are latent thoughts really inspectable?

documents.t: The paper's own framing of this, in its Discussion section, is the detail most coverage skipped. Latent thoughts exist only as hidden states, readable through HybridLink — and the argument offered is that this is a feature: a deployed provider can run safety assessment on the full reasoning trace while the trace never leaves their infrastructure, so reasoning cannot leak to users the way text thinking can. Read that twice. It is a coherent position — reasoning traces genuinely are a competitive asset and an exfiltration surface, which is why so many providers summarise rather than expose extended thinking. But the structure it describes is asymmetric transparency by construction: the lab holding the adapter can read the thoughts, and nobody else can. For an MIT-licensed checkpoint that ships its own adapter, the asymmetry is moot — you hold the key. For a hosted frontier model built the same way, it would not be.
documents.s: The part that deserves more attention than it got

documents.t: Honest answer for three different readers. If you are… Then Shipping an agent on an API Nothing to do today. There is no hosted latent-reasoning endpoint. The transferable lesson is the diagnosis, not the cure: measure how much of your bill is deliberation tokens versus input and action tokens. If deliberation dominates, this line of work is aimed at you. Running open weights Worth an afternoon, on a GPU box, through the repo's own engine — and only the repo's engine. Expect a research artifact: 8B/14B on Qwen3-Base is not frontier-competitive on general chat, and the benchmarks that matter here are agentic search and math. Doing interpretability or safety work This is the most useful thing on the list. A released, MIT-licensed, tool-using latent agent with a shipped readout tool and a published causal-intervention result is a far better object of study than a lab's internal claim about its hidden reasoning. The skeptics on the launch thread had one more point worth keeping: continuous chain-of-thought is not new, looped-transformer architectures reach for something similar, and frontier labs may well already run variants of this privately. Nothing about HybridAgent's existence tells you whether any shipping product thinks in latent space. What it does tell you is that the engineering is no longer hard — a ~10M-parameter adapter plus two training stages — which is precisely why the monitorability question stops being hypothetical. Check yourself 0/6

Hybrid Reasoning Agents (arXiv 2610.18861) — Zou, Qi, Chen, Bianchi, Zhu, Lu, He, Zou; submitted 13 October 2026. Inference engine, SFT and RL pipelines, the interpretable_latent_mode viewer, and the GPU requirements (8-16 for SFT, 32 across 4 nodes for RL). togethercomputer/HybridAgent-8B-Agentic and -14B-Agentic — the checkpoints, on Qwen3-8B-Base and Qwen3-14B-Base. The model card is where the "standard Transformers loading yields a text-only variant" warning lives. The origin of chain-of-continuous-thought, the emergent-BFS result, and the finding that a learned mode-switch classifier performed no better than a fixed latent budget.
