Скопировать как Markdown Средний У вопроса «Сколько стоит ИИ?» нет единого ответа — всё зависит от того, какой архетип ценообразования вы покупаете и сколько вы им реально пользуетесь. Долларовые цифры меняются каждые несколько месяцев; сама структура стоимости почти не двигается. Эта страница учит устойчивой форме: три способа, которыми оценивается ИИ, как оценить нагрузку до того, как вы её построите, рычаги, снижающие счёт, и настоящую развилку между арендой API и самостоятельным хостингом. What you'll learn Различать три архетипа стоимости: API с оплатой за токены, фиксированная подписка и open/самостоятельный хостинг Оценивать стоимость любой нагрузки по формуле токены × ставка × объём — до того, как вы её выпустите Использовать главные рычаги, снижающие расходы без ущерба для качества Знать, когда open/самостоятельный хостинг выигрывает у API по стоимости, а когда выигрывает API Знать, какие числа быстро устаревают — и где проверить сегодняшнюю правду Последняя проверка: 2026-06-28. Ставки за токен, уровни подписок, скидки за кэш и пакетную обработку, а также то, какая модель дешевле всего, меняются почти ежемесячно — считайте любую конкретную долларовую цифру скоропортящейся. Эта страница учит устойчивой модели (архетипы + как оценивать + рычаги); за сегодняшними цифрами обращайтесь к странице цен каждого провайдера (ссылки в разделе «Источники»), к независимому трекеру вроде Artificial Analysis, и посчитайте сами в нашем Калькуляторе стоимости. Сверьтесь с официальным источником.
documents.s: Сколько на самом деле стоит ИИ (у разных провайдеров)

documents.t: Почти любой способ платить за ИИ сводится к одной из трёх форм. Учите формы, а не цены. API с оплатой за токены (usage-based). Вы обращаетесь к размещённой модели через API и платите за токен — причём вход и выход оцениваются раздельно, и выход почти всегда дороже. Более крупные/умные модели стоят больше за токен; меньшие модели стоят гораздо меньше. Большинство провайдеров также предлагают скидки: сниженную ставку за кэшированный вход, который вы пересылаете повторно, и фиксированную пакетную скидку для несрочных асинхронных задач. Так вы платите, когда строите продукт на Claude, GPT или Gemini. Стоимость растёт прямо пропорционально использованию — копейки на малом масштабе, доминирующая статья расходов на большом. Фиксированная потребительская/пользовательская подписка. Фиксированная ежемесячная плата за чат-приложение или ассистента в IDE (потребительские планы Claude / ChatGPT / Gemini, места в стиле Copilot). Вы не видите токенов; вы получаете лимит использования и ограничения по скорости. Предсказуемо и дёшево для человека за клавиатурой — но это не масштабируется на программную/высоконагруженную работу, и стоимость за место складывается по всей команде. Open / локальный (самостоятельный хостинг). Вы запускаете модель с открытыми весами (Llama, Mistral, Qwen, DeepSeek) на своём железе или арендованном GPU. Здесь нет цены за вызов — вы платите за железо (или почасовую аренду GPU) + электричество + эксплуатацию, занята модель или простаивает. Предельная стоимость ещё одного вызова фактически близка к нулю на масштабе, но вы несёте фиксированные расходы и операционную нагрузку. См. Запуск моделей локально с Ollama. Pro tip Ключевое разделение: API и подписки — это ПРЕДЕЛЬНАЯ стоимость (платишь за использование); самостоятельный хостинг — в основном ФИКСИРОВАННАЯ стоимость (платишь за поддержание мощностей, используешь ты их или нет). На API самый большой сюрприз в том, что ВЫХОДНЫЕ токены обычно стоят в несколько раз дороже входных — многословные ответы стоят реальных денег. Фиксированная подписка — правильный инструмент для человека, который общается в чате; API с оплатой за токены — правильный инструмент для приложения, вызывающего модель в цикле.

Вы можете прикинуть счёт за API ещё до написания строки продакшн-кода. Вся модель — это одна формула: стоимость ≈ (входные токены × ставка за вход) + (выходные токены × ставка за выход), за вызов × число вызовов Ставки указываются за миллион токенов, и у входа и выхода разные ставки — поэтому оценивайте две половины отдельно и складывайте. Грубое правило для токенов: ~1 токен ≈ 4 символа английского текста, или ~0,75 слова. Для точного подсчёта используйте область Оценщика токенов и читайте Токены и цены. Полная механика того, где прячутся токены, — в Экономике токенов. Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Оцените токены ОДНОГО вызова⌄ Сложите вход: системный промпт + инструменты + извлечённый контекст + история + ход пользователя. Затем оцените выход, который вы запрашиваете. Считайте вход и выход отдельно — они оцениваются по-разному. ←PreviousNext→ 2Умножьте каждую сторону на её собственную ставку⌄ входные токены × ставка за вход, плюс выходные токены × ставка за выход. Используйте сегодняшние числа за миллион со страницы цен провайдера (не доверяйте цифре, которую запомнили — см. VerifyNote). ←PreviousNext→ 3Масштабируйте по реальному объёму⌄ Умножьте стоимость за вызов на число вызовов в день × число дней. Стоимость, ничтожная за один вызов (доли цента), становится вашей главной статьёй расходов при миллионах вызовов — моделируйте ВАШ реальный трафик, а не один запрос. ←PreviousNext→ 4Примените скидки, которыми реально воспользуетесь⌄ Если большой кусок входа повторяется каждый вызов, считайте его по КЭШИРОВАННОЙ ставке, а не по полной входной. Если задача офлайн — примените ПАКЕТНУЮ скидку. На масштабе это резко меняет ответ. ←PreviousNext→ 5Сверьтесь с трекером, затем режьте⌄ Сравните ваши допущения по токенам с независимым трекером и нашим Калькулятором стоимости, затем атакуйте счёт рычагами ниже. ←PreviousNext→ Прикидка на салфетке (подставьте сегодняшние ставки) CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ Per call: input_tokens = system + tools + context + history + user_turn output_tokens = the answer you ask for call_cost = (input_tokens * input_rate_per_million / 1e6) + (output_tokens * output_rate_per_million / 1e6) Per month: monthly_cost = call_cost * calls_per_day * 30 Then adjust: - cached repeated input -> use the (lower) cache-read rate for that slice - offline / non-urgent -> apply the batch discount to the whole job Rates change monthly — pull today's numbers from the provider's pricing page.

Большинство реальных нагрузок несут мёртвый груз. Эти рычаги, примерно в порядке отдачи, снижают расходы, не трогая качество — сначала используйте дешёвые структурные. Подберите модель по размеру. Не платите по ставке флагмана за задачу, с которой прекрасно справляется маленькая/дешёвая модель. Классификация, извлечение, маршрутизация и простое форматирование обычно отлично работают на самом младшем уровне за долю цены за токен. Приберегите большую модель для по-настоящему сложных рассуждений и рассмотрите маршрутизацию: дешёвая модель обрабатывает лёгкое большинство, эскалация только сложных случаев. См. Выбор модели. Урезайте контекст, который отправляете. Самый дешёвый токен — тот, который вы никогда не отправляете. Обрезайте раздутые системные промпты, сжимайте длинные истории в текущее резюме и открывайте только те инструменты, что нужны задаче — каждый из них это вход, за который вы платите заново на каждом вызове. RAG вместо запихивания огромного контекста. Вставлять 50-страничный документ, чтобы ответить на один вопрос, — значит платить за 50 страниц на каждом вызове. Извлечение (retrieval) достаёт только несколько релевантных фрагментов — гораздо меньше входных токенов при том же (часто лучшем) ответе. Тянитесь к гигантскому окну контекста только тогда, когда вам действительно нужен весь корпус целиком. Кэширование промптов. Если многие вызовы разделяют большой неизменный префикс (системный промпт, каталог инструментов, справочный документ), кэширование обрабатывает его один раз и переотдаёт с крутой скидкой на каждом последующем вызове. Самое высокоотдачное структурное изменение для чат- и агентных нагрузок, потому что оно окупается на каждом ходу. Отправляйте несрочное в пакетную обработку. Оценки (evals), массовая разметка, суммирование архива — всё, где ответ не нужен за секунды, — проходит через асинхронный пакетный путь с фиксированной скидкой у большинства провайдеров. Обменяйте мгновенность на ощутимо меньший счёт. Сокращайте выход. Выход — более дорогая сторона. Просите JSON или строгую схему вместо болтливого абзаца: меньше выходных токенов и никаких догадок при парсинге вниз по потоку. Меньшие / open модели для лёгкой доли. Для высокообъёмного, низкосложного большинства вызовов open или маленькая модель может быть драматически дешевле за вызов — иногда почти бесплатно, если вы уже держите самостоятельный хостинг. Оставьте фронтир-модель для случаев, которым она действительно нужна. Pro tip Они складываются мультипликативно: кэшированный вход × правильно подобранная модель × более краткий выход × пакетная скидка компонуются в большое суммарное сокращение на лёгкой задаче — при неизменном качестве. Используйте структурные рычаги (подбор размера, кэш, RAG, пакет) прежде чем микрооптимизировать формулировки — они двигают счёт куда сильнее. Всегда ИЗМЕРЯЙТЕ изменение по реальному счёту, а не по догадке. Глубокий сборник приёмов — это Экономика токенов.

Это решение, которое реально двигает ваш бюджет на ИИ. Это переход между фиксированной и предельной стоимостью, и объём — переменная, которая его решает. Open / самостоятельный хостинг выигрывает при ВЫСОКОМ, устойчивом объёме. Как только вы гоняете достаточно вызовов, чтобы держать GPU занятым большую часть времени, близкая к нулю предельная стоимость за вызов бьёт вечную оплату за токены. Вы амортизируете фиксированную стоимость железа/аренды по огромному числу вызовов, получаете приватность данных и полную кастомизацию — и принимаете операционную нагрузку (провижининг, масштабирование, аптайм, MLOps) как плату за вход. API выигрывает при НИЗКОМ или РВАНОМ объёме, либо без инфраструктуры. Если трафик мал, всплесковый или непредсказуемый, оплата за токены означает, что вы платите только за то, что используете, и ничего в простое — никакого GPU, греющегося в 3 часа ночи. Вы также избегаете всей эксплуатации. Для большинства команд, выпускающих продукт, прототипирующих или с трафиком всплесками, API одновременно и дешевле, и гораздо меньше работы. Watch out Самостоятельный хостинг редко бывает «бесплатным». Веса модели могут быть бесплатны, но GPU, электричество и часы инженеров на поддержание работы — нет; честно посчитайте их, прежде чем заявлять об экономии. Простаивающие GPU — чистый убыток: инфраструктура с фиксированной стоимостью бьёт оплату за токены только при ВЫСОКОЙ утилизации. Низкий или всплесковый трафик каждый раз в пользу API. Точка перехода сдвигается всякий раз, когда падают цены на API или дешевеет железо — периодически пересчитывайте, не решайте один раз и не забывайте. Проверь себя 0/3 Key takeaways Три архетипа: API за токены (usage-based, вход и выход оцениваются раздельно), фиксированная подписка (предсказуемо, не масштабируется на большой объём) и open/самостоятельный хостинг (фиксированная стоимость, почти ноль за вызов). Оценивайте до того, как строить: (вход × ставка за вход) + (выход × ставка за выход), за вызов × объём — затем примените скидки за кэш и пакет. Крупнейшие рычаги: подобрать модель по размеру, урезать контекст, RAG вместо огромного контекста, кэширование промптов, пакетировать несрочное, сокращать выход. Самостоятельный хостинг выигрывает при ВЫСОКОМ устойчивом объёме (амортизация фиксированной стоимости); API выигрывает при НИЗКОМ/всплесковом объёме или без инфраструктуры (платишь только за использование). Любая долларовая цифра быстро устаревает — проверяйте на странице цен провайдера и на трекере, и считайте свои числа в Калькуляторе стоимости.
documents.s: Когда open/самостоятельный хостинг выигрывает у API — и когда выигрывает API

documents.t: Anthropic — Pricing — актуальные ставки Claude за токен, скидки за кэш и пакет. OpenAI — API Pricing · OpenAI — Pricing overview — актуальные ставки GPT за токен и уровни. Google — Gemini API Pricing — актуальные ставки Gemini, бесплатный уровень и платные уровни. Mistral — Pricing — цены open-weight + API, ориентир с упором на эффективность. Artificial Analysis — независимые, часто обновляемые кросс-провайдерные сравнения цены/скорости/качества (трекер для сверки любой заявленной цифры). Ollama — запускайте open-weight модели локально, чтобы свести цену за вызов к нулю на масштабе.

Выберите правильную (и правильно оценённую) модель → Выбор модели Найдите, где реально утекают токены → Экономика токенов Механика оплаты за токены в глубину → Токены и цены Посчитайте свои числа → Калькулятор стоимости Поделиться страницей X LinkedIn Reddit Hacker News Скопировать ссылку

Скопировать как Markdown Средний What you'll learn Understand what is actually inside 16.9 MB — and which part of the 9x size headline is architecture versus a quantization choice the comparison does not hold constant Read the vendor's own WER chart including the competitor bars it never labels: Whistle wins 5 of 8 head-to-heads and loses the three that look most like real life Know why 30 seconds is a wall in the encoder rather than a setting, and build the VAD segmentation it forces on you Find the streaming API the launch discussion concluded did not exist, and understand why its real latency is not the 11.1 ms time-to-first-token Use keyword biasing as the primary accuracy lever, not a nicety — it is the difference between 41% and 96% on a closed vocabulary Decide between Whistle, Whisper, Parakeet and a cloud API for your specific audio On 8 October 2026 a blog post titled "Whistle: Speech to Text in 16.9 MB" reached 768 points on Hacker News. The number in the title is the whole pitch, and it is true: the entire multilingual speech recognition model is a single 16.9 MB file that runs on a CPU with no GPU and no dependencies. The discussion that followed split cleanly in two. People who read the benchmark chart were impressed. People who pointed a microphone at it were not — one tester reported 70 correct out of 170 utterances. Both groups were right, and the reason they were both right is printed in the vendor's own chart. It is just in the bars that carry no number.
documents.s: Whistle: Speech-to-Text in 16.9 MB — and the Benchmark Bars Nobody Labelled

documents.t: Whistle buys its size by quantizing a small encoder–decoder ASR model to 2–4 bits and band-limiting its front end to 250–3500 Hz, which costs it almost nothing on close-microphone single-speaker speech — where it genuinely beats Whisper base — and costs it a great deal on far-field, overlapping or accented speech, where it is the worst of the three models in its own comparison.

Component Detail Front end 25 ms window, 10 ms hop, 80 log-mel bins, band-limited 250–3500 Hz Stem 128-channel convolutional, downsamples to one frame per 80 ms Encoder 8 Simple Attention blocks, Monarch Hadamard MLP Decoder 8 laddered Simple Attention blocks, width 512, 8 query heads to 2 KV heads Vocabulary 8,192 text pieces plus 7 language tokens Output ceiling 320 tokens per clip Input ceiling 480,000 samples — 30 s at 16 kHz mono Container .cact, Cactus Quants, 2–4 bit Licence Apache-2.0 Three of those rows do more work than the rest, and two of them are the ones people skip.
documents.s: What is actually in the 16.9 MB

documents.t: The comparison everyone quotes is 16.9 MB against Whisper base's 145.3 MB. That is one ninth the size — but the vendor's own footnote says Whistle is measured at 2 to 4 bit while Whisper is fp32 in memory on the CPU. Those are 8–16x apart in bits per weight before a single architectural decision is made. The honest apples-to-apples row in the same chart is Moonshine tiny v2 at 41.9 MB in int8. Whistle is 2.5x smaller than that, not 9x. The remaining 2.5x is real and is where the architecture earns its keep — but if you repeat the 9x number you are mostly repeating a quantization choice. This is the same trap covered in how to read an AI benchmark without getting fooled: the number is not wrong, the comparison is not held constant.
documents.s: The 9x size headline does not hold precision constant

documents.t: The front end keeps 250–3500 Hz and throws away everything else. That is roughly telephone band, and it is a sensible choice for a model meant to run on a wearable — most speech energy lives below it. Most, not all. The acoustic-phonetics literature is specific here: 3–4 kHz is enough bandwidth for intelligible vowels but not for most voiceless fricatives, whose spectra are concentrated above 4 kHz. English s has its greatest energy concentration in roughly the 5–10 kHz range, peaking near 8 kHz — more than twice Whistle's cutoff — and sh centres near 4 kHz with energy extending to 8. Cutting at 3500 Hz does not make those sounds inaudible. It removes the band that separates them from each other most cleanly. So before you run a single test you can predict the error class: confusions and dropped word-endings on fricatives, worst on speakers whose rhythm or accent gives those consonants less duration to compensate with. The field reports in the launch thread — Spanish output with "non-existent words and terrible typos", Mexican and Venezuelan accents not detected, heavy accents degrading sharply — are that prediction arriving on schedule.
documents.s: Band-limiting to 3500 Hz is a design decision with a predictable error class

documents.t: Here is the part worth the page. Whistle's chart plots word error rate across nine test sets for three models. It prints a number on every Whistle bar and on none of the others. The bars are still there, drawn to a linear scale. Whistle's printed labels calibrate that scale exactly — 6.867 pixels per WER point, consistent to ±0.01 across all nine — so the competitor values are recoverable from bar height. Doing that produces the table the chart stops just short of giving you. Test set What it is Whistle Whisper base ≈ Moonshine tiny v2 ≈ LibriSpeech test-clean Read audiobooks, clean 4.31 4.89 4.51 LibriSpeech test-other Read audiobooks, harder 10.49 11.00 11.71 SPGISpeech Financial calls 7.65 — 7.70 Earnings-22 Earnings calls, accented 19.01 — 21.25 AMI Meetings, far-field, overlapping 26.07 21.50 22.78 AMI cleaned Same, cleaned refs 22.87 — — TED-LIUM Conference talks 7.61 4.99 5.64 FLEURS Multilingual read speech 21.39 24.50 — MLS Multilingual audiobooks 24.90 23.10 — Lower is better; bold marks the winner of each row. Whistle's column is the vendor's printed figures. The other two columns are read off the chart's bars — the vendor states they are Whisper's and Moonshine's own published numbers, and declines to print them. Whistle wins five of the eight rows where a comparison exists. For a model 2.5x smaller than its nearest-precision rival that is a genuine result, and the FLEURS row — 3.1 points better than Whisper base on multilingual read speech — is the most impressive thing in the chart. Now look at what it loses: AMI, by 4.57 points to Whisper base. Far-field microphones, multiple speakers, overlap, interruption. Whistle is not merely behind here, it is the worst of the three, losing to a model 8.6x its size. TED-LIUM, by 2.62 points. Single speaker, but a large room, a stage mic and unscripted delivery. MLS, by 1.80 points. Multilingual long-form, averaged over six non-English languages. The pattern is not subtle once the numbers are side by side. Every row Whistle wins is close-microphone and effectively single-speaker. Every row it loses has either distance between the mouth and the microphone or more than one person in the room. Read-audiobook and dictation audio is exactly the profile a 16 kHz band-limited front end with a tiny encoder handles well. Reverberation and overlapping talkers are exactly what it cannot afford the capacity to disentangle. That single sentence reconciles the two halves of the launch thread. Everyone who tested dictation into a phone held near their face liked it. Everyone who pointed it at a film clip, a meeting or a room disliked it. Nobody was measuring wrong. The number to carry away 4.31 and 26.07 are the same model on the same weights. If you only remember one WER figure for Whistle, remember the spread, not the headline.

The most-quoted field result in the thread — 70 correct out of 170, against 168/170 for a much larger Qwen ASR model — is a real measurement, but it is a measurement of stock settings on a closed vocabulary. The same tester reported 164/170 after tuning. What changed is the subject of the next section, and it is the most under-sold feature on the model card.

Whistle decodes with five beams scored by length-normalised log probability, and it will accept a list of words you expect to hear and favour them during that search, matched with an Aho-Corasick automaton. In a general-purpose ASR model this is a convenience. In a 16.9 MB model with an 8,192-piece vocabulary it is closer to load-bearing. The model has very little capacity to spend on an implicit language model, so proper nouns, product names, place names and domain jargon are precisely what it gets wrong — and precisely what a keyword list fixes. Going from 70/170 to 164/170 is 41% to 96% on the same weights. Transcribe with the two arguments that matter CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ import needle r = needle.transcribe( "clip.wav", keywords=["Kubernetes", "Grafana", "Prometheus", "Aoife", "Nguyen"], word_timestamps=True, language="en", # skip detection when you already know ) print(r["text"]) for w in r["words"]: print(w["word"], w["start"], w["end"], w["probability"]) Three things in that snippet are worth stating plainly: keywords is not a post-processing filter. It changes the beam search, so it can recover a word the decoder would otherwise never have placed. language="en" removes a failure mode, not just latency. Automatic detection across seven languages on a short or noisy clip is one more thing that can go wrong. If your app knows the language, say so. Every word carries its own probability. That is your confidence gate — see the handoff pattern below. Watch out A keyword list that is too long dilutes the bias and starts pulling the decoder toward words nobody said. Keep it to the vocabulary your users actually produce in this context — the current screen, the current contact list, the current document — not your entire product glossary.
documents.s: Keyword biasing is the primary accuracy lever

documents.t: 30 seconds at 16 kHz is 480,000 samples. After the convolutional stem that is one frame per 80 ms, so 375 encoder frames, and the decoder tops out at 320 output tokens. Those are fixed shapes in a 16.9 MB tensor file. There is no flag that raises them, and a launch-thread tester who recorded past the limit got a runtime error rather than a truncated transcript. So any clip longer than 30 seconds means you own the segmentation — and segmentation is where long-form ASR accuracy actually lives, because a cut through the middle of a word or a clause is an error the model cannot recover from. Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Resample and downmix first⌄ 16 kHz mono is not a recommendation, it is the input contract. A 44.1 kHz stereo file needs converting before it reaches the model; the base install handles 16 kHz WAV and raw samples, and the [mic] extra adds resampling and microphone capture. ←PreviousNext→ 2Segment on silence, not on a timer⌄ Run a voice-activity detector and cut in the gaps. Fixed 30-second slices will eventually cut mid-word, and that error lands in your transcript permanently. Target 10–25 second segments so you keep headroom for a long final clause. ←PreviousNext→ 3Overlap the segments by about a second⌄ Give consecutive passes a shared region so you can stitch on agreement instead of trusting a hard boundary. The cost is re-decoding a second of audio; at 1,319 tokens/s decode that is not your bottleneck. ←PreviousNext→ 4Stitch with the word timestamps, not the text⌄ Every word comes back with a start and an end, so dedupe the overlap region by time rather than by string matching. This is the only reliable way to drop a doubled word without dropping a legitimately repeated one. ←PreviousNext→ 5Gate on probability and hand off⌄ Average the per-word probabilities over each segment. Low-confidence segments are your queue for a bigger model — on-device for free, off-device when it matters. Do not re-run everything. ←PreviousNext→
documents.s: The 30-second wall is in the encoder, not in a config file

documents.t: The model card makes a specific and welcome claim: silence and steady noise return an empty transcript rather than an invented sentence, because silence detection runs before the beam search. That is a direct fix for Whisper's most notorious failure — confidently hallucinating subtitles over nothing. Read the claim precisely. It covers silence and steady noise. It does not cover quiet, distant or overlapping speech, and the thread contains exactly that failure: a tester reported the model emitting "Thank you." repeatedly for over a minute while real dialogue was playing, and another found a negation flipped — "can handle" for "can't handle" — plus a word invented outright. Those are the classic artefacts of training on web video captions, where "Thanks for watching" occupies an enormous share of the text, and they survive the silence gate because the gate was never aimed at them. If a dropped n't would change what your application does, a per-word probability check is not optional.
documents.s: Silence is handled; low-SNR speech is not

documents.t: A recurring complaint in the discussion was that Whistle cannot do live transcription, because the demo showed no partial text while speaking. The demo did not; the library does. needle.stream(chunks) takes live microphone input and commits words that consecutive overlapping passes agree on. That policy — decode an overlapping window repeatedly, emit only the prefix two passes agree on — is the LocalAgreement family of streaming ASR, and knowing that tells you the thing the spec sheet will not: Your perceived latency is not the 11.1 ms time-to-first-token. It is the agreement delay: how long a word has to wait before a second pass confirms it. TTFT is a decode-speed measurement on a complete 10-second clip. In a streaming loop the user-visible number is set by your window stride and how long you are willing to wait for stability, and it will be hundreds of milliseconds, not eleven. Fast is still fast — 11.1 ms against Whisper base's 73.2 ms and Moonshine's 22.8 ms, and 1,319 tokens/s decode against 266 and 262, measured on 10 s of audio on an Apple M4 Pro CPU. Just do not promise a product manager 11 ms of live captioning.
documents.s: Streaming exists — the launch thread concluded it did not

documents.t: Every depth from two layers up is a deployable model, selected at load time with --audio-depth. You download one 16.9 MB blob and choose your accuracy/latency point on the device, which is the right place to choose it — a watch and a phone can run the same artifact at different depths. For scale, the sibling Needle text model decodes at roughly 4,000 tokens/s at two layers and 400 at twenty on a Raspberry Pi 5.
documents.s: The decoder is laddered, so one file is a family

documents.t: The encoder output is available directly: one row per 80 ms frame, via needle.Whistle().embed(audio). That is wake-word spotting, command matching, audio deduplication and "find where in this recording someone said this" — without decoding text, without a language model, and without the error classes discussed above, because you never ask it to spell anything. For a lot of embedded jobs ("did the user say one of these eleven things?") this is the correct tool and transcription is the detour. Run it from the CLI, including the built-in three-way comparison CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ pip install cactus-needle # microphone playground needle whistle playground # put Whistle next to Whisper and Moonshine on YOUR audio needle whistle compare my-clip.wav # air-gapped / embedded: fetch a platform engine and the weights needle download macos-arm64 needle download whistle ./macos-arm64/needle --model whistle.cact --audio clip.wav --audio-word-timestamps The compare subcommand deserves a mention: the vendor ships the tool that checks its own claims against your audio. Given how sharply the WER spread above depends on recording conditions, running it on a representative clip of your audio is worth more than any table on this page.
documents.s: embed() gives you speech matching with no transcript at all

documents.t: The engine reads no environment variables. Every behaviour is a compiled default or an explicit flag. That means the same blob plus the same flags scores the same on any machine, which is a property most inference stacks cannot claim and which matters enormously when you are trying to work out whether last week's eval regressed or last week's shell did.

Your situation Pick Why Dictation on a phone or wearable, close mic, offline, 7 supported languages Whistle This is the design centre. 16.9 MB, no GPU, word timestamps, and it beats Whisper base on exactly this audio profile Wake words or fixed command sets on a microcontroller Whistle embed() Skip transcription entirely; match encoder frames Meeting recordings, multiple speakers, room mics Not Whistle Its own chart puts it last on AMI. Use a full-size Whisper, Parakeet, or a cloud ASR with diarization Any language outside the seven Not Whistle English, German, French, Spanish, Italian, Dutch, Polish only. No Chinese, despite being the most-requested addition in the launch thread Best open-weight accuracy-per-second on a GPU, English Parakeet NVIDIA's parakeet-tdt-0.6b-v2 was the practitioner favourite in the thread; CC-BY-4.0 Audio you cannot send anywhere, and accuracy matters more than size Whisper large, local Still the accuracy reference. You are trading ~100x the footprint for it Medical, legal or financial transcripts of record Cloud ASR with a human in the loop The negation-flip failure mode above is disqualifying on its own A hybrid is usually the right answer, and it is the same shape as every other local/remote split on this site: run the small model on everything, use the per-word probabilities as the gate, escalate the uncertain fraction. See Claude plus local models for the general pattern and a private local AI stack for where a transcription step belongs in it.
documents.s: Choosing: Whistle, Whisper, Parakeet, or a cloud API

documents.t: Whistle is a good instance of a pattern now showing up across small models: the capability is real and the operating envelope is narrow, and only the first half fits in a headline. The 2-bit quantization is not a cheat — the model genuinely works — but it buys its size by spending the capacity that would have handled hard audio, and the vendor's chart shows exactly where that bill lands while labelling only the rows where it does not. The practical rule generalises past ASR: when a small model publishes a wide benchmark spread, the spread is the specification. Find the row where it does worst, work out what that test set has that the others do not, and check whether your real input looks like that row. For Whistle the answer is distance and overlap. For a quantized language model it is usually long context — see what "98.2% retention" hides. Check yourself 0/6 Последняя проверка: 2026-10-09. На этой странице приводятся факты, которые меняются со временем — считайте дату выше показателем её актуальности. Whistle's WER figures are its own printed labels. The Whisper base and Moonshine tiny v2 columns are derived from the chart's bar heights against the scale Whistle's labels establish (6.867 px per WER point, self-consistent to ±0.01 — the derived AMI-cleaned value reproduces the printed 22.87 as 22.86); the vendor states these are the respective authors' published figures. Star counts, download counts and the model's API surface will drift — re-read the model card before relying on a flag or argument name.

Скопировать как Markdown Средний A chat turn costs a fraction of a cent. The same question handed to an agent — one that reads files, calls tools, and loops until done — can cost dollars. Teams are discovering this the hard way: a coding agent left running racks up a bill that a human at a keyboard never would. The scary part isn't the average; it's that you can't predict it in advance, and the cost of the same task can swing wildly. This page explains why agents burn tokens (the mechanism is not what most people guess), shows the numbers that surprise even experienced builders, and gives you the four levers that actually cut the bill — the same levers whether you're on Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, or a home-grown loop over any model. What you'll learn Explain the context snowball — why agent cost grows roughly QUADRATICALLY with steps, not linearly Cite the real multipliers: agentic tasks ~1000x a chat's tokens, and the SAME task varying up to 30x Know when a second agent is worth it — and the benchmark showing it usually isn't Pull the four cost levers that work: budget caps, prompt caching, model-tier routing, context pruning Diagnose a runaway agent bill and put a hard ceiling on it Последняя проверка: 2026-07-15. Per-token prices, per-developer monthly spend, and which model is cheapest change almost monthly — treat every dollar figure here as perishable and illustrative. The mechanism (context snowball, re-read tax) and the levers are durable; the exact ratios come from 2026 benchmarks and research linked in Sources. Confirm today's rates on each provider's pricing page before quoting a bill to anyone. Сверьтесь с официальным источником.
documents.s: Why AI Agents Burn Tokens (and How to Cap the Bill)

documents.t: Here's the trap. A chat is one turn — one input, one output, done. An agent is a loop: it reads a task, takes an action, reads the result, takes the next action, and so on until the job is finished. The catch is that on every step, the model re-reads the entire accumulated conversation so far — the original prompt, every prior action, and every tool result — before deciding what to do next. So the input grows on every step, and you pay for the whole snowball again each time it rolls forward: Step 1 processes the prompt. Step 2 re-reads the prompt + step 1's action + result. Step 3 re-reads all of that + step 2's action + result. …and so on. Add up the input across a run and the total scales roughly with the square of the number of steps, not linearly. The Stanford Digital Economy Lab found agentic tasks to be "uniquely expensive, consuming 1000x more tokens than code reasoning and code chat" — and crucially, it's the input tokens that dominate, not the output. The agent isn't writing more; it's re-reading more. What you'll learn The cost driver is re-reading, not thinking. Each loop step re-processes the full transcript, so a 20-step run pays for early context ~20 times over. This is why 'just let the agent figure it out' is expensive: every extra step it takes multiplies against everything before it. Output-heavy tasks (write me an essay) are cheap by comparison; input-heavy loops (explore this repo, then fix the bug) are where the money goes.
documents.s: The context snowball: why cost grows quadratically

documents.t: Three figures reset most people's intuition: ~1000x. Agentic tasks can consume roughly a thousand times the tokens of an equivalent chat or code-completion, per the Stanford analysis — driven by the snowball above, not by a bigger model. Up to 30x variance on the same task. The same agent, run on the same task, can cost up to 30x more one time than another — because the path it takes (how many tools it calls, how far it wanders) is non-deterministic. You genuinely cannot know the bill until it's done. This is why "result-based pricing" for agents is so hard: you only see the cost after everything runs. More agents rarely pay for themselves. 2026 production benchmarks found that a multi-agent setup added only ~2.1% accuracy at 2x the cost versus a well-configured single agent on 64% of tasks. A hierarchical-supervisor pattern pushed a document task from 85% → 95% accuracy — but at roughly $0.15/task vs $0.003 for the single agent (~50x). More agents buys a little accuracy for a lot of money. Watch out Because the same task varies up to 30x, an average-based budget WILL be blown by the tail. Cap the ceiling, don't budget the mean. Adding agents to 'be safe' usually multiplies cost far faster than it adds accuracy. Reach for a second agent only when the task genuinely decomposes into parallel, independent subtasks.

Before the loop even starts, how the agent reaches its tools sets a floor on cost. Connecting a set of MCP servers can inject tens of thousands of tokens of tool definitions into every step of the snowball. A rough comparison many builders hit: a plain CLI command averages ~200 tokens, while the equivalent MCP operation can cost 32k–82k tokens once tool schemas and wrapping are counted. That gap rides along on every loop step. That doesn't make MCP wrong — it's the right choice for auth, multi-tenancy, and governed access. It means the tool surface is a cost lever you chose at design time. AILmanac has a dedicated deep-dive: The MCP Token Tax covers Tool Search, deferred loading, and code execution as the three fixes.
documents.s: Your tool surface is part of the bill

documents.t: Optimization advice is endless; only four levers move the number materially. In rough order of leverage: Guided walkthrough1 of 4 1Cap the budget — a hard ceiling, not a hope⌄ Set a per-run or per-user token/dollar cap that HARD-STOPS the agent. Because the same task can cost 30x more on a bad run, a ceiling is the only thing that bounds the tail. Most agent harnesses expose a max-tokens or max-steps limit — use it. This is the single most important control. ←PreviousNext→ 2Cache the stable prefix⌄ The system prompt, tool definitions, and house rules are re-sent on every loop step (the snowball). Prompt caching charges those repeated tokens at a fraction of the input rate. On a long agentic run this is often the biggest single saving, because the cached part is exactly what gets re-read the most. ←PreviousNext→ 3Route by model tier⌄ Don't run one frontier model for the whole loop. Use a cheap, fast model (Haiku-class, or a small open model) for the grunt work — reading files, formatting, routine tool calls — and reserve the expensive frontier model for the hard reasoning or the orchestrator role. Orchestrator-worker splits with cheaper workers cut cost 40–60% in production benchmarks at near-parity accuracy. ←PreviousNext→ 4Prune the context aggressively⌄ The snowball is the problem, so shrink it. Compact old turns, drop tool outputs the agent no longer needs, summarize instead of carrying raw transcripts, and start fresh sub-tasks with a clean context instead of one ever-growing thread. Every token you remove is a token you stop paying for on EVERY remaining step. ←PreviousNext→ Audit a runaway agent (paste your run's token breakdown) CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ You are a cost engineer. Here is a token-usage breakdown of one agentic run (input vs output tokens per step, tool calls, model used). Diagnose where the money went, in priority order: 1. Is input or output driving cost? (Agents are almost always input-heavy.) 2. Which repeated content should be prompt-CACHED (system prompt, tools, rules)? 3. Which steps could run on a CHEAPER model without losing correctness? 4. Where is context snowballing — what can be pruned, compacted, or summarized? 5. What is a safe per-run token CAP that stops the worst tail without hurting the median run? Give me the estimated % saving per fix and the ONE change to make first.
documents.s: The four levers that actually cut the bill

documents.t: The cheapest agentic run is the one you don't make. If a task is a single, well-specified transformation — summarize this, classify that, rewrite this — a plain chat/completion call does it at a fraction of the cost, with no snowball at all. Reach for an agent when the work genuinely requires reading, deciding, acting, and re-checking in a loop against a changing environment (explore a repo, debug across files, drive a browser). If you can write the exact steps yourself, script them — don't pay a model to re-derive them every run. Check yourself 0/3
documents.s: When an agent is the wrong tool

Скопировать как Markdown Средний On September 28, 2026 AMD announced it is acquiring World Labs for about $8.2 billion in stock — its second-largest deal ever, behind only Xilinx — and Fei-Fei Li will join as executive vice president and chief scientist reporting to Lisa Su. A day later OpenAI's DevDay took the front page. Between them, "world model" became the phrase of the week. Here is the problem with the phrase. Two products that share it are architecturally opposite. One keeps the world inside the model and streams you frames as you move; it is interactive, it cannot be exported, and a session is capped in seconds. The other generates a 3D scene you download, own and render yourself for free; it is persistent, engine-ready, and completely inert. Picking the wrong one is not a preference mistake, it is a re-architecture. This page is the practical split: what each family really produces, the verified API and export details, the one benchmark that settles a common assumption, the open weights you can run on your own GPU, and the five things neither family will do for you. What you'll learn Tell the two families of world model apart, and pick by what you need to persist Know the real limits: the 60-second wall, the physics disclaimer, the export tier that gates commercial rights Read the World API correctly — async operations, the WLT-Api-Key header, and which splat formats come out Use the WorldScore evidence instead of vibes when choosing between a video model and a 3D model Run an open world model yourself, and understand why inverse dynamics is the part worth $8.2 billion Последняя проверка: 2026-09-30. Deal terms from AMD's own newsroom release: approximately $8.2 billion, all stock, announced September 28, 2026, expected to close by the end of 2026 subject to regulatory approval — so it is not closed, and product roadmaps may move once it is. Project Genie access, Marble plan tiers and World API pricing are all live commercial surfaces that change without notice; the resolution and frame-rate figures for Genie 3 come from third-party reporting, not from Google's Project Genie post, which states only the 60-second generation limit. WorldScore leaderboard positions move as teams submit. Read the linked primary sources before you quote any number here. Сверьтесь с официальным источником.
documents.s: World Models: What You Can Actually Build Today

documents.t: Frame generators 3D generators Examples Genie 3 / Project Genie, driving world models Marble (World Labs) What it outputs A video stream, frame by frame, conditioned on your actions A scene: Gaussian splats, panoramas, optionally a mesh Where the world lives Inside the model's rolling context In a file you download Interactive? Yes — that is the whole point No. You navigate it, but it does not react Exportable? No geometry to export Yes — SPZ, PLY, GLB, collider meshes Cost shape Per second of interaction, per viewer, forever Once at generation. Rendering is then yours Fails by Drifting, forgetting, running out of session Being static and not simulating anything If you need a world that responds — a player pressing a key, a robot policy taking an action and seeing what happens — you need a frame generator. If you need a world that persists — an asset in your game, a set in your render pipeline, a scene five users load next month and see identically — you need a 3D generator. Almost every confused "why can't it just…" question on this topic is someone holding one and asking for the other.

Google's Project Genie went from research preview to a public-ish product on January 29, 2026. The access shape is narrow and worth knowing before you plan around it: Google AI Ultra subscribers, United States only, 18+, and explicitly not available on Google AI Ultra for Business. Google calls it an "experimental research prototype". The limit that teaches you the most is Google's own: generations are limited to 60 seconds. That is not a billing decision, it is a state problem. In a frame generator the world is not stored anywhere — it is implied by the model's context. Every frame is predicted from the prompt, the accumulated frames and your actions. Consistency is therefore bounded by the same thing that bounds a long chat: how much history the model can hold and keep coherent. Walk away from a wall and back, and whether the wall is still there is a memory question, not a rendering one. Google's stated caveats are the rest of the honest spec sheet: generated worlds "might not look completely true-to-life or always adhere closely to prompts or images, or real-world physics", and characters "can sometimes be less controllable, or experience higher latency in control". Read that physics line carefully if you were planning to use a frame generator as a simulator. It is a plausibility engine, not a solver. Nothing guarantees momentum is conserved between frame 300 and frame 301.
documents.s: The frame generators, and the 60-second wall

documents.t: Interactive generation at the commonly reported 24 fps gives you about 41.7 ms per frame, end to end, including your input reaching the server. That single number explains most of the product decisions in this family: why sessions are short, why access is gated to a paid tier, why there is no public API yet, and why the cost curve is per viewer-second rather than per asset. You are not buying a file. You are renting a GPU that must beat a 42-millisecond deadline for as long as someone is looking.

World Labs' Marble turns text, an image, a panorama, multiple views or a video clip into a navigable 3D scene. The important engineering fact is the representation: the output is 3D Gaussian splats, not a mesh. Splats are millions of small, oriented, semi-transparent blobs with colour and view-dependent shading. They photo-reconstruct beautifully and render fast on commodity GPUs. They also have no surfaces, no edges and no faces — which is why the next section matters more than it looks. What Marble's own export docs say you get: Export Availability Gaussian splats — SPZ and PLY Standard plan 360 panoramas Standard plan Collider meshes Standard plan Textured mesh (GLB) + commercial rights Pro plan only Anything at all Not on Free — generate only Two gotchas live in that table. First, collider meshes are a separate export — you need them because you cannot raycast, collide or do physics against splats directly. The splats are what the player sees; the collider mesh is what the engine tests against. Ship only the splats and your beautiful world has no floor. Second, commercial rights are tied to the Pro tier, not to the act of exporting. Check the plan before you put a generated world in a product. Marble's docs also note that lower-resolution exports are "optimized to be as perceptually similar as possible to the higher-resolution files" — a hint that you should test the small tier before paying to ship the big one.
documents.s: The 3D generators, and what you actually receive

documents.t: A detail several write-ups get wrong: SPZ is Niantic's format, open-sourced by Niantic Spatial, not a World Labs invention — Marble simply exports to it. It is worth using anyway. SPZ stores each spherical-harmonics coefficient as an 8-bit signed integer with optional further quantisation, landing at roughly 10× smaller than the equivalent PLY with no perceptible quality loss. Niantic's own testing puts around 5 bits as the sweet spot for most scenes, with essentially-zero MSE at 8 bits and about 18× compression at 3. SPZ 4, released in 2026, splits compression into six parallel ZSTD streams — one per attribute class — for roughly 3–5× faster compression and 1.5–2× faster end-to-end loading at the same ~10× size advantage. If you are shipping splats over the web, that is the difference between a scene that loads and one that does not.
documents.s: SPZ: the 10× that is not World Labs'

documents.t: The World API exposes Marble's generation to your own code. The verified shape, from World Labs' docs index and its official Python client: Inputs: text, images, panoramas, multi-view inputs, video. Outputs: splats in SPZ, PLY, SOGS, KSPLAT and SPLAT. Auth: an API key passed in the WLT-Api-Key header; the Python client reads WORLDLABS_API_KEY from the environment. Execution model: asynchronous. You submit a generation, get an operation back, and poll until it is done. There is also a credit-balance endpoint, media upload/retrieve, and world create/retrieve/list/export/delete. Client: worldlabsai/worldlabs-api-python, Python 3.12+. A CUDA GPU is only needed for local rendering, not for API use. Pricing: usage-based. Generate a world from text and poll for it CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ # github.com/worldlabsai/worldlabs-api-python (Python 3.12+) # export WORLDLABS_API_KEY=... from worldlabs_api.client import WorldLabsClient from worldlabs_api.models import WorldTextPrompt, WorldsGenerateRequest client = WorldLabsClient(api_key="your-key-here") request = WorldsGenerateRequest( display_name="Mystical Forest", world_prompt=WorldTextPrompt(text_prompt="A mystical forest"), ) op = client.generate_world(request) # returns an operation, not a world done = client.poll_operation(op.operation_id) # poll until done is true world = done.response Design your integration around that async boundary from day one. World generation is a job, not a request — the same lesson as batch inference or video generation. If your handler waits inline for a world, you will rewrite it.

World Labs also maintains Spark, an MIT-licensed 3D Gaussian splatting renderer for THREE.js / WebGL2, so a generated world can ship as a web page. It loads .PLY, .SPZ, .SPLAT, .KSPLAT and .SOG, fuses splats with ordinary meshes in the THREE.js pipeline, and targets the ~98% of devices with WebGL2. Spark 2.0 (April 15, 2026) is the release that makes big scenes viable in a browser: a level-of-detail splat tree that renders a fixed number of splats per frame regardless of scene size, a streaming .RAD format that supports HTTP Range requests so a coarse proxy appears almost instantly and refines progressively, and virtual splat paging against a fixed GPU memory pool so scenes larger than GPU memory still render — including on phones and Quest 3. Put a generated world on the web CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ npm install @sparkjsdev/spark three # docs and live examples: https://sparkjs.dev # repo: https://github.com/sparkjsdev/spark # # Export from Marble as .spz (≈10x smaller than .ply), serve it as a # static file, and load it into a THREE.js scene with Spark. # For scenes over a few hundred MB, convert to .RAD so the viewer can # range-request a coarse proxy first. Note what just happened to your cost curve. After generation, you are serving a static file from a CDN and rendering on the user's GPU. Serving the world is free. That is the inverse of the frame-generator model, where every viewer-second is inference.
documents.s: Rendering it without a game engine

documents.t: "Just use a video model" is the most common shortcut here, and there is now a benchmark that answers it. WorldScore (Stanford, arXiv:2504.00983) is a unified benchmark for world generation across 3D, 4D, text-to-video and image-to-video models — about 3,000 examples, with metrics for controllability, consistency, perceptual quality and motion, and explicit 3D consistency and camera-control measures. The result that should change a decision: on WorldScore-Static, dedicated 3D scene generators lead — WonderWorld at 72.69 and LucidDreamer at 70.40 — clearly above the video models. If your requirement is a geometrically consistent world you can move a camera through, a video model is the wrong tool even when its individual frames look better. Two caveats. The leaderboard is live and moves as teams submit. And WorldScore-Static measures exactly what its name says — a static world; strong static consistency tells you nothing about dynamics.

You do not need a vendor's API to have a world model. NVIDIA published Cosmos 3 — an open omnimodel for physical AI — with weights on Hugging Face: Model Size Runs on nvidia/Cosmos3-Edge 4B Edge devices, robots, vision agents nvidia/Cosmos3-Nano 16B = 8B reasoner + 8B generator Workstation class, e.g. RTX PRO 6000 nvidia/Cosmos3-Super 64B = 32B reasoner + 32B generator Hopper / Blackwell, large-scale synthetic data Architecturally it is a Mixture-of-Transformers handling text, image, video, audio and action in one model, pairing an autoregressive subsequence for reasoning with a diffusion subsequence for generation. It is wired into Hugging Face Diffusers, so the entry point is ordinary Python. Run an open world model locally CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ pip install --upgrade diffusers transformers accelerate # Cosmos3-Nano is 16B (8B reasoner + 8B generator); check the model # card on Hugging Face for the licence and the exact torch version # before you build on it. import torch from diffusers import Cosmos3OmniPipeline pipe = Cosmos3OmniPipeline.from_pretrained( "nvidia/Cosmos3-Nano", torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16 ) Now the part that explains the price tag. Cosmos 3's task table is not a list of video tricks: Input Output What it is Text / image / video Video Video generation Text / video Text Vision-language reasoning Action + image + text Video Forward dynamics — "if I do this, what happens?" Text + video Action Inverse dynamics — "what actions produced this?" Image + text Video and action Policy generation Inverse dynamics is the quiet one. It turns footage into labelled actions — which means ordinary video becomes robot training data, and a generated world becomes a place to train and evaluate a policy without hardware. AMD's own release describes World Labs as building models that "generate, reconstruct and simulate interactive 3D environments" plus technology for "robotic learning and simulation", and frames the deal around reasoning, robotics, simulation and physical AI informing its future silicon roadmap. Read as a compute story rather than a graphics story, $8.2 billion for a training-environment flywheel is a different kind of bet than $8.2 billion for a text-to-3D tool.
documents.s: Open weights: Cosmos 3, and what AMD actually bought

documents.t: Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1It is not a reasoning model, and your prompting does not transfer⌄ None of your chain-of-thought, XML-tag or tool-use technique carries over. Conditioning a world model is closer to directing a camera than to instructing an assistant: what matters is the input image, the viewpoint, the described lighting and the action sequence. The one habit that does transfer is source discipline — a clean, well-framed conditioning image beats an elaborate paragraph. ←PreviousNext→ 2It will not give you physics you can trust⌄ Google states plainly that generated worlds may not adhere to real-world physics. Cosmos-style forward dynamics predicts a plausible next observation, which is not the same as solving for one. Use a world model to generate scenarios and a real physics engine to adjudicate them. If a wrong answer costs money or safety, a solver has to be in the loop. ←PreviousNext→ 3Splats will not collide, and a mesh export is a separate thing⌄ Gaussian splats have no surfaces. Raycasts, character controllers, navmeshes and physics all need geometry, which is why Marble exports collider meshes separately and gates high-quality textured GLB to the Pro tier. Plan for two assets per world — the one you see and the one you hit — and budget the mesh export in the tier you actually pay for. ←PreviousNext→ 4A frame-generated world cannot be saved, diffed or versioned⌄ There is no file. The world exists for the length of the session and then it is gone, and a re-run of the same prompt is a different world. That rules out the whole class of workflows built on persistent state: reviewing a level, shipping a fix to it, having two users load the same scene, or asserting in a test that the scene has not changed. If you need any of those, you need exportable geometry. ←PreviousNext→ 5It will not tell you which plan you are allowed to ship on⌄ The export matrix is the licence. Free generates but cannot export at all; splats, panoramas and colliders sit on Standard; textured mesh and commercial rights sit on Pro. For open weights the equivalent step is reading the Hugging Face model card's licence before shipping, not after. This is the cheapest failure on the list to avoid and the most expensive to discover late. ←PreviousNext→
documents.s: Five jobs a world model will not do for you

documents.t: Game or product asset, multiple users, must look the same tomorrow → 3D generator. Export SPZ for the web or GLB for an engine, and remember the collider. Interactive exploration, one user, novelty is the point → frame generator, and design inside a 60-second session. Training or evaluating a policy → open weights with forward and inverse dynamics, on your own GPU, with a real simulator for anything safety-relevant. A camera moving through a consistent scene → not a video model. WorldScore says so.
Check yourself 0/5

Скопировать как Markdown Начальный Одно из самых значимых применений ИИ получает меньше всего внимания: использование его как вспомогательного инструмента. Claude может адаптировать информацию под вас — под ваш темп, ваш формат, ваш язык, — и это способно по-настоящему уравнивать возможности.

Дислексия / нагрузка при чтении — «перепиши это короткими, простыми предложениями», «выдели ключевые мысли», «объясни это простым языком». Слабое зрение — сочетайте с голосовым режимом, чтобы слушать и диктовать; просите чистый, хорошо структурированный текст, который легко считывают программы экранного доступа. Нейроотличия / концентрация (СДВГ и т. п.) — «разбей это на чек-лист», «какой один следующий шаг?», превратите стену текста в понятный план, набросайте письмо, на котором вы застряли. Изучающие языки — переводите, упрощайте, объясняйте идиомы, отрабатывайте разговор или получайте одну и ту же мысль на разных уровнях сложности. Тревога перед письмом — получите безоценочный первый черновик, на который можно отреагировать, что снижает порог для начала работы.

Rewrite this so it's easy to read: short sentences, simple words, one idea per line. Keep all the meaning. Text: {paste} Turn this into a step-by-step checklist with the single most important step marked. {paste} Explain this in {your language}, then give me 3 phrases to practice.

Это помощник, а не врач. Для решений, связанных со здоровьем, медициной или юридическими вопросами, обращайтесь к специалисту — проверяйте всё важное (Ответственное использование). Голос и мобильные устройства делают его доступным где угодно (Голосовой режим, Мобильные устройства). Ваши данные принадлежат вам — делитесь только тем, чем готовы поделиться (Конфиденциальность). Скопировать как Markdown Все уровни Для основателей и небольших команд ИИ — это рычаг: он одновременно выполняет работу младшего маркетолога, аналитика и ассистента. Направляйте его правильно и оставляйте за собой суждения по вопросам, которые действительно важны.

Позиционирование и месседжинг — точно сформулируйте ценностное предложение, а затем выводите из него тексты. Маркетинговый контент — лендинги, письма, реклама, соцсети, FAQ (см. Письмо). Коммуникация с клиентами — черновики ответов, работа с жалобами, написание анонсов. Исследования — анализ рынка и конкурентов (проверяйте!), наборы вопросов для интервью с клиентами. Планирование — превращение целей в приоритизированные планы с временными рамками. Документы и операции — регламенты (SOP), вакансии, резюме встреч.

Прежде чем писать любые тексты, сформулируйте точную однострочную суть: Write 3 versions of a value proposition using: for {audience} who {need}, {product} is a {category} that {key benefit}, unlike {alternative}. Then critique each in one line. Всё последующее (реклама, письма, лендинги) даётся легче, как только это станет чётким.

Не выдумывайте доказательства и следите за утверждениями Никогда не придумывайте отзывы, метрики, кейсы или награды — используйте заглушки [insert real number] и заполняйте их реальными данными. Следите за регулируемыми или необоснованными утверждениями (здоровье, финансы, «№1», гарантии). Проверяйте рыночные факты и цифры, прежде чем действовать (Галлюцинации). Защищайте данные — не вставляйте персональные данные клиентов или конфиденциальные цифры в непроверенные инструменты (Конфиденциальность).
Превратите свои лучшие промпты в многоразовые активы — Проект с вашим голосом бренда и документами или набор навыков для бизнеса и маркетинга, чтобы стандарты применялись автоматически.

Скопировать как Markdown Продвинутый Последняя проверка: 2026-09-23. Runner concurrency caps, queue timeouts and merge-queue settings are platform limits that GitHub changes without much noise. The mechanisms below are stable; re-check the exact numbers against the limits page before you size a pipeline on them. Сверьтесь с официальным источником. What you'll learn Know why the merge queue — not the runner budget — is the first thing that breaks under agent PR volume Do the batching arithmetic: how a few points of failure rate collapse speculative merging Rank the four levers correctly, because 'add more runners' is the weakest one Ship a gate that proves an agent's test actually fails without the agent's fix Quarantine flakes on evidence instead of vibes, and know the caching gotcha that silently poisons CI Your coding agents work. That is the problem. A team that merged 5 pull requests a day and now merges 40 has not changed its test suite, its runner budget, or its branch protection rules. It has changed the arrival rate into a queueing system that was tuned for the old one. Everything downstream — merge queue, flaky-test noise, runner concurrency, review attention — was sized for human throughput, and queueing systems do not degrade gracefully. They hold, hold, hold, then fall over inside a week. This page is the pipeline side of the verification bottleneck. That page asks who checks the code. This one asks whether your CI can physically absorb the volume, and what to do when it can't.

−7.2%. DORA's 2024 Accelerate State of DevOps report modelled a 25% increase in AI adoption and estimated a 7.2% decrease in delivery stability alongside a 1.5% decrease in throughput. Individual productivity and job satisfaction went up. Delivery-level outcomes went down — the report ties this to larger changesets and weaker batching discipline. The 2025 follow-up reframes it: AI is an amplifier, magnifying whatever your delivery system already is. A pipeline that was fragile at 5 PRs/day becomes unusable at 40. 19%. METR's randomised trial (July 2025) took 16 experienced open-source maintainers and 246 real issues from their own repositories, randomising whether AI tools were allowed. With AI, tasks took 19% longer. The gap that matters for CI planning is the perceptual one: developers predicted a 24% speed-up, and after the slowdown still believed they had been sped up by 20%. Nobody on your team will tell you the pipeline is the constraint, because nobody experiences it as one — they experience it as "waiting", which feels like weather. 1.5% / 16% / 84%. Google's published flakiness data: roughly 1.5% of test runs report a flaky result; about 16% of their 4.2M tests have shown flakiness at some point; and around 84% of observed pass→fail transitions involve a flaky test rather than a real regression. Hold onto that 1.5% — it is small enough to ignore at 5 PRs/day and load-bearing at 40.
documents.s: Three numbers that frame the whole problem

documents.t: Most teams assume the ceiling is compute. It isn't. It's the merge queue, and the reason is a mechanism most people have never read the docs for. GitHub's merge queue does speculative checking. Queue PRs #1, #2, #3 and it builds temporary branches: main + #1, main + #1 + #2, main + #1 + #2 + #3 — and tests all of them in parallel. If every check passes, all three land in one round. That is the whole value proposition: batching turns N serial validations into one. Now read the failure path. When a check fails for the group containing PR #1, GitHub removes #1 from the queue — and every group behind it contained #1's changes, so those groups are invalid and get rebuilt without it. One bad PR does not cost you one slot. It costs you the rest of the batch's CI round. That makes queue throughput a function of your pass rate, and it's steeper than intuition suggests. Model it: batch size N, each PR independently failing with probability p, and you merge the run of PRs up to the first failure. Expected merges per round is a geometric expectation: E[merges] = (1 − p) · (1 − (1 − p)^N) / p With N = 10: Per-PR failure rate p Expected merges per round Rounds to clear 10 PRs 2% 8.9 ~1.1 5% 7.6 ~1.3 10% 5.9 ~1.7 20% 3.6 ~2.8 30% 2.3 ~4.4 Two consequences most teams get backwards: A flaky suite is a throughput tax, not a nuisance tax. Flakiness adds directly to p. Going from 5% real failures to 5% real + 5% flake takes you from 7.6 merges per round to 5.9 — roughly 23% of your merge capacity, lost to tests that were never testing anything. Raising the batch size is the wrong lever when p is high. Bigger N only helps when (1 − p)^N stays near 1. At p = 0.2, a batch of 10 delivers 3.6 merges; the fix is lowering p, not queueing more optimism. And agent volume pushes p the wrong way — DORA's stability finding is exactly a statement about p rising.
documents.s: Why the merge queue breaks first

documents.t: Do this on a napkin before you buy runners. Assumptions stated, because they're what make it wrong for your team: Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Count job-minutes, not wall-clock⌄ A 45-minute suite fanned out into 15 parallel jobs still costs ~45 job-minutes. Parallelism buys latency, never cost. Take your suite's total job-minutes from a recent run, not from the slowest job. ←PreviousNext→ 2Multiply by validations per PR, not by PRs⌄ With a merge queue every PR is validated at least twice: once on the PR branch, once inside a merge group. Reruns and rebuilds from the p-math above add more. Budget 2.5x as a floor, not 1x. ←PreviousNext→ 3Divide by the burst window, not the day⌄ 40 PRs x 2.5 validations x 45 job-min = 4,500 job-minutes. Spread over 24 hours that is trivial. It does not arrive over 24 hours — it arrives in two or three hours around review time. 4,500 job-min into a 2-hour window needs ~37 sustained concurrent jobs. ←PreviousNext→ 4Compare against your plan's hard ceiling⌄ GitHub-hosted standard runners cap total concurrent jobs at 20 (Free), 40 (Pro), 60 (Team) and 500 (Enterprise). The napkin above quietly exceeds Free and sits on top of Pro — during the burst, which is the only window that matters. ←PreviousNext→ 5Find the silent failure⌄ A queued job is cancelled after 24 hours. On a saturated queue this shows up as jobs that never ran rather than jobs that failed, which is far harder to notice and does not page anyone. ←PreviousNext→ The takeaway is not "buy Enterprise". It's that the constraint is burst concurrency, and the daily-average number that makes your pipeline look fine is the number hiding the problem.

Teams reach for these in almost exactly the reverse of the useful order. 1. Lower p (highest leverage, lowest cost). Every point of failure rate removed pays off nonlinearly in the batching math. Concretely: make agents run the fast suite locally before opening a PR, require a green pre-merge check before a PR is allowed into the queue, and quarantine flakes aggressively (below). This costs no compute. 2. Cut the work per validation — test selection. This is the only lever that changes the exponent rather than the constant. Instead of running everything, run what the change can plausibly break: Develocity Predictive Test Selection builds a model from your own Build Scan history plus cross-project patterns, and ships a simulator so you can measure the savings and the missed-failure rate before enabling it. Two safety details worth stealing even if you never buy it: you can pin must-run tests by class pattern or annotation, and it always selects recently flaky tests, because a flaky test is by definition unpredictable from the change. Pair it with a "remaining tests" run post-merge or nightly so nothing is skipped forever. Bazel / Buck2 get this structurally: the build graph knows which targets depend on the changed files, so bazel test on affected targets is target determination for free. No build graph? Python has pytest-testmon, which records which tests cover which code and re-runs only the affected ones. Jest ships --changedSince out of the box. Test selection, three ecosystems CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ # Bazel — test only what the diff can reach bazel test $(bazel query "rdeps(//..., set($(git diff --name-only origin/main)))" --output=label 2>/dev/null) # Python — coverage-based impact analysis pip install pytest-testmon pytest --testmon # first run builds the DB, later runs select # Jest — built in, no plugin npx jest --changedSince=origin/main 3. Cache aggressively — and know the gotcha. Remote caching stores action results keyed by a hash of inputs, command line and whitelisted environment. Bazel's own docs flag the trap: tools outside the workspace are not tracked, so two machines with different compiler versions can get a cache hit on work that would have produced different outputs. Whitelist what matters with --action_env, and keep write access to CI only — developer machines should read: Remote cache, CI-writes-only CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ # CI: read and write bazel test //... --remote_cache=grpcs://cache.internal:443 # Developer machines: read only, never poison the shared cache bazel test //... --remote_cache=grpcs://cache.internal:443 \ --remote_upload_local_results=false 4. Add runners (last). Linear cost, linear benefit, and it does nothing about p. Do it after the first three, when you actually know your burst concurrency number.

Everything above applies to any high-volume pipeline. This one is specific to agent-written code, and it is the gap most CI setups have. When the same agent writes the fix and the test for the fix, "tests pass" carries much less information than you think. Two failure shapes show up constantly: The test asserts the behaviour of the implementation rather than the requirement — it passes because it was written by reading the code it is testing. The agent, when a pre-existing test fails, edits the test to match the new behaviour instead of fixing the code. The diff is green and the regression shipped. That behaviour has a name and a literature — see reward hacking in coding agents for why models do it and which defenses have measured effect sizes. What follows is the pipeline-side control, not the model-side one. The cheap structural gate: a new test must fail against the pre-change code. That's the red-green discipline of TDD turned into a machine check, and it's what mutation testing formalises at scale. You do not need a mutation-testing framework to get most of the value — you need one CI job: CI gate: new tests must fail without the change CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ #!/usr/bin/env bash # must-fail-first.sh — run in CI on PRs that add tests set -euo pipefail NEW_TESTS=$(git diff --name-only origin/main...HEAD -- 'tests/**' 'test/**') [ -z "$NEW_TESTS" ] && { echo "no new tests, skipping"; exit 0; } # Keep the new tests, revert everything else to the base commit git stash push --keep-index -- $NEW_TESTS git checkout origin/main -- src/ git stash pop # The new tests MUST fail now. If they pass, they prove nothing. if pytest $NEW_TESTS -q; then echo "FAIL: new tests pass against unmodified source — they do not test the change." exit 1 fi echo "OK: new tests fail without the fix." Two honest caveats. It only works when source and tests live in separate trees, and a test that fails for the wrong reason (import error, missing fixture) passes this gate. It is a floor, not a proof — but it catches the single most common way an agent-authored PR is green and worthless. The complementary review-side control is a reviewer that doesn't share the author's context: see the hybrid AI code reviewer and the PR-review GitHub Action.
documents.s: The AI-specific failure mode: the agent grades its own homework

documents.t: Given 84% of pass→fail transitions are flakes, "rerun it" is the default human response and it is the most expensive one available — it burns a full validation on a test that was never going to tell you anything. Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Measure before you judge⌄ A flaky test is one that produces different results on the same commit. Run the suite N times on an unchanged main and record per-test failure counts. That is your evidence; developer memory is not. ←PreviousNext→ 2Quarantine on a threshold, not an argument⌄ Anything above your threshold moves to a non-blocking job that still runs and still reports. It stops gating merges immediately — that is the throughput win — and it stays visible so it does not become dead code. ←PreviousNext→ 3Cap the quarantine and give it an owner⌄ An uncapped quarantine is a graveyard. Fixed budget (say 1% of tests), a name attached, an expiry date. Over budget means the next flake evicts the oldest one back into blocking. ←PreviousNext→ 4Never let test selection skip a flake⌄ This is the counter-intuitive rule Develocity encodes: recently-flaky tests are always selected, because the model cannot predict them from the diff. Selecting away your flakes hides the signal you need to fix them. ←PreviousNext→ 5Re-derive p after each round⌄ Recompute your per-PR failure rate monthly and put it on the dashboard next to merge-queue throughput. It is the one number that tells you whether the pipeline is getting better or the agents are just getting louder. ←PreviousNext→
documents.s: Flake quarantine that survives contact with agents

documents.t: merge_group is not automatic. GitHub's docs are explicit: you must add the merge_group event to your workflow triggers, or your checks never fire inside the queue and merges fail on missing required checks. This is the single most common merge-queue misconfiguration. The 24-hour queue cancellation is silent. Saturated queue → jobs vanish rather than fail. Alert on queue depth, not just on red builds. Matrix jobs cap at 256 per workflow run. Generated matrices (a common agent-scaffolding pattern) hit this without a useful error. Cross-machine cache hits can be wrong. Untracked external toolchains produce false hits. Pin toolchains, whitelist environment with --action_env. Branch protection with wildcard patterns is incompatible with merge queues. If your protection rules use wildcards, the queue will not engage. Agent PRs touching CI are a security boundary, not a style question. A PR that can edit workflow files can exfiltrate CI secrets — see GitHub issue → CI secrets and hardening autonomous runs.
documents.s: Gotchas that cost a day each

documents.t: There is no configuration that makes a pipeline absorb unbounded agent output. What the levers above buy you is a system whose cost grows with the size of the change rather than the number of pull requests — test selection and caching are sublinear, runners are linear, and merge-queue batching is only sublinear while your pass rate stays high. Which puts the real constraint back where DORA's 2025 framing puts it: AI amplifies the delivery system you already have. If small batches, fast suites and low flakiness were already your practice, agents make you much faster. If they weren't, agents find out. Check yourself 0/6 Key takeaways The merge queue breaks before the runner budget does. Speculative batching is a bet on your pass rate, and one failing PR invalidates every group behind it. Compute E[merges] = (1 − p)(1 − (1 − p)^N)/p once for your real numbers. It turns 'CI feels slow' into a decision about which lever to pull. Flakiness is throughput, not hygiene. At Google's published rates the noise is bigger than the signal — 84% of pass→fail transitions are flakes. Size for burst concurrency, never daily average. The daily number is the one hiding the problem, and a saturated queue cancels jobs silently at 24 hours. Test selection is the only sublinear lever: Bazel/Buck2 target determination, Develocity PTS with its simulator, pytest-testmon, or jest --changedSince. When the agent writes both the fix and the test, green means less than you think. Gate on the test failing against pre-change source. DORA's framing holds: AI amplifies the delivery system you already have. Small batches, fast suites and low flake were always the advice — agents just made ignoring it expensive.

Скопировать как Markdown Все уровни Учитесь ли вы программировать или выпускаете промышленное ПО, ИИ меняет рабочий цикл. Выигрывают те, кто относится к нему как к быстрому, знающему напарнику — и проверяет всё, что он создаёт.

Объясняет незнакомый код или ошибки простым языком. Генерирует шаблонный код, тесты и первые черновики функций. Рефакторит ради ясности и отлаживает, рассуждая по стек-трейсу. Переводит между языками и фреймворками. Проверяет дифф на наличие багов и «душков». Для реальных кодовых баз делайте это внутри вашего репозитория с помощью Claude Code, который умеет читать файлы, запускать тесты и редактировать с вашего одобрения.

Дайте контекст — нужный код, ошибку, что вы ожидали против того, что получили. Расплывчато на входе — расплывчато на выходе. Попросите план для нетривиальных изменений до правок (Режим планирования). Сгенерируйте изменение. Прочитайте его — поймите, прежде чем принять. Код — ваш. Запустите его — тесты/линт/сборка. Никогда не верьте «это работает» без запуска. Шаг, который отделяет хорошие результаты от плохих, — это стрелка обратно наверх: когда тест проваливается, не правьте вслепую — снова подайте сбой как свежий контекст.

Explain what this function does and any edge cases it mishandles: {code} Write tests for {function}. Cover the happy path and the edge cases. {code} This throws {error}. Here's the code and stack trace. Find the root cause and propose a minimal fix. {context}

Проверяйте и защищайте свои секреты Запускайте и проверяйте сгенерированный код — он может быть незаметно ошибочным или выдумывать несуществующие API. Скопировать как Markdown Все уровни Чтобы получать ответы из данных с помощью ИИ, не обязательно быть дата-сайентистом, — но держать его в честных рамках придётся. ИИ пишет запрос и объясняет результат; вы подтверждаете, что цифры настоящие.

Пишет SQL / формулы для таблиц / pandas по вопросу на естественном языке. Объясняет, что означает запрос или результат в бизнес-терминах.
