Опишите свои данные — столбцы, типы и гранулярность (одна строка = ?). Не предполагайте названий. Сформулируйте вопрос, на который должен ответить анализ. Получите запрос + однострочное объяснение того, что он делает, и его допущений. Запустите его сами на реальных данных. Принесите результаты обратно для интерпретации простым языком и оговорок. My table `orders` has columns: order_id, customer_id, created_at, total_eur, status. One row per order. Write SQL for monthly revenue from completed orders in 2025, and explain any assumptions.

Никогда не доверяйте цифрам, которые он не вычислял Если ИИ заявляет результат, не запустив запрос на ваших данных, эта цифра может быть выдуманной. Запускайте запросы сами; считайте любую цифру, которую вы не вычисляли, непроверенной. И помните: корреляция ≠ причинно-следственная связь — попросите его помечать утверждения о связях. См. Галлюцинации. Проверяйте порядки величин на здравый смысл — неправдоподобный результат? разбирайтесь, а не публикуйте. Указывайте допущения (пропуски, дедупликация, часовые пояса, валюта). Скопировать как Markdown Продвинутый Последняя проверка: 2026-07-24. Anthropic's evaluation guide is the source of truth for methodology (SMART criteria, exact-match, LLM-graded Likert/binary). Agent-trajectory eval is an emerging discipline — treat framework names as illustrative and confirm APIs at each vendor's docs. Сверьтесь с официальным источником. What you'll learn Understand why agent evals differ from prompt evals — trajectory matters, not just the final answer Build a golden set of 20–100 real cases with clear pass criteria Score four layers: tool-call correctness, trajectory quality, task success, production drift Use LLM-as-judge safely: rubric first, calibrate against humans, spot-check verdicts Ship an eval that runs in CI and fails a bad change before it reaches users An agent eval answers a harder question than "did the prompt return the right words?" It asks: did a model running in a loop pick the right tools, in the right order, with the right arguments, arrive at the right outcome — and stay within budget and safety bounds? Skip this step and you'll ship a "helpful" agent that quietly regresses every time you tweak the system prompt.

A single-prompt eval scores one input → one output. An agent produces a trajectory: a chain of reasoning, tool calls, intermediate observations, and revisions across many turns. Two failure modes make this hard: Right answer, wrong path. The agent stumbles onto the correct output after wasteful loops, unsafe actions, or lucky guesses. Final-answer-only evals mark this a pass; production won't. Wrong answer, plausible path. Every step looks reasonable in isolation, but the agent misused a tool, ignored a constraint, or hallucinated an intermediate fact. You need to look at the trace, not just the reply.
documents.s: Why agents need their own evals

documents.t: Layer them cheapest-first so a bad change fails fast without waiting for expensive graders. Guided walkthrough1 of 4 1Layer 1 — Tool-call correctness (deterministic)⌄ For each expected step, check tool name matches, required parameters are present, and types validate. Pure code, milliseconds, no model needed. Catches 'called search when it should have called write_file' before anything else runs. ←PreviousNext→ 2Layer 2 — Trajectory quality (rubric + LLM-judge)⌄ Score the full trace: did the agent take a sensible path, or wander, loop, or backtrack? Number of steps vs. minimum needed, redundant calls, retries after tool errors, whether it stopped when done. Use an LLM judge with an explicit rubric here. ←PreviousNext→ 3Layer 3 — Task success (end-to-end)⌄ Did the goal get met? Deterministic where possible (schema valid, file written, test passes), LLM-judged where fuzzy (summary faithful, answer helpful). This is your headline number. ←PreviousNext→ 4Layer 4 — Production drift & safety⌄ In prod, sample real traces and re-grade a slice. Watch intervention rate (how often a human had to step in), refusal rate, and cost per successful task. When these shift, your model, tools, or inputs changed underneath you. ←PreviousNext→

Not every metric belongs on the dashboard. These five drive shipping decisions in 2026: Metric What it measures Why it matters Task success rate % of golden-set cases the agent finishes correctly The headline. Everything else is diagnostic. Cost per successful task $ / passing case (tokens in + out, tool costs) Success at 10× the cost is a regression. Latency (p50 / p95) Wall-clock per task, tail included p95 is what real users feel — averages lie. Tool-call accuracy % of expected tool calls with correct name + args Predicts trajectory quality; cheap to compute. Intervention rate % of tasks needing human takeover in prod The autonomy number. Rising = trust falling. Track them together — one moving without the others is usually a leading signal, not noise.

Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Mine real inputs⌄ Pull 20–100 tasks from actual usage (logs, support tickets, user requests). Cover the frequent easy path, the tricky middle, and the edge cases that already bit you. ←PreviousNext→ 2Write pass criteria per case⌄ For each: what does 'done' look like? Exact expected output, required facts, valid JSON schema, files that must exist, or a rubric for fuzzy cases. If you can't write the criterion, the case is unusable — cut or clarify it. ←PreviousNext→ 3Annotate the ideal trajectory⌄ For a subset, sketch the tool sequence a good agent would take. This is what Layer 1 checks against. ←PreviousNext→ 4Freeze it, version it⌄ Commit the set to your repo. Never edit a case in place — add v2 alongside v1 so score history stays comparable. ←PreviousNext→ 5Grow it from failures⌄ Every prod bug becomes a new eval case before you fix it. That's how the set stays predictive instead of decaying. ←PreviousNext→

Grading fuzzy outputs by hand doesn't scale. A capable model reading against an explicit rubric does — Anthropic's own eval methodology guide recommends this pattern for tone, faithfulness, helpfulness, and safety. Judges have well-documented biases: they prefer longer answers, the first option shown, and outputs that echo their own phrasing. Three habits keep them honest: Rubric, not vibes. "Rate helpfulness 1–5" is useless. Anchor every point on the scale to observable behavior. Calibrate on a human-labeled sample. Have humans grade 30–50 cases; measure judge-vs-human agreement (aim for Cohen's κ ≥ 0.6). If it disagrees, tighten the rubric. Use a different model as judge. Grading with the same model that produced the output leaks bias in both directions. Spot-check verdicts weekly. Read 10 random judge scores and their reasoning. It's the cheapest way to catch drift. LLM-as-judge rubric template CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ You are grading an AI assistant's response against a rubric. Be strict. Cite exact evidence from the response. <task>{task}</task> <response>{response}</response> Rubric (rate 1–5 per dimension): - Task completion: 1 = ignored task; 3 = partial; 5 = fully done, no gaps. - Faithfulness: 1 = contains false claims; 3 = mostly grounded, one soft claim; 5 = every claim traceable to input/tools. - Efficiency: 1 = wandered/looped; 3 = extra steps; 5 = minimum viable path. Output JSON only: {"task_completion": N, "faithfulness": N, "efficiency": N, "evidence": "<quote>", "verdict": "pass"|"fail"} Trajectory review prompt (Layer 2) CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ You are auditing an AI agent's tool-call trajectory. The goal was: {goal} Expected minimum steps: {n_min} <trajectory> {list of tool_name(args) -> result, in order} </trajectory> Answer in JSON: {"steps_taken": N, "wasted_steps": N, "wrong_tool_calls": [<indices>], "unsafe_actions": [<indices>], "verdict": "pass"|"fail", "reason": "<one sentence>"} Adversarial case generator (grow the set) CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ Generate 5 new eval cases that are likely to break an agent whose current failures cluster around: {failure_pattern}. For each case give: input, expected output OR pass criterion, ideal tool sequence, and why this case is hard. Return YAML.
documents.s: LLM-as-judge — cheap, fast, but calibrate it

documents.t: The eval only pays off when it blocks regressions automatically. Wire it into CI as a check on every prompt / model / tool change: # tests/eval_gate.py — runs on every PR import json, sys from anthropic import Anthropic from my_agent import run_agent client = Anthropic() golden = json.load(open("evals/golden.v3.json")) results = [] for case in golden: trace = run_agent(case["input"]) layer1 = tool_calls_match(trace, case["expected_tools"]) # deterministic layer3 = judge(client, case, trace.final_output) # LLM rubric results.append({"id": case["id"], "layer1": layer1, "layer3": layer3["verdict"]}) pass_rate = sum(r["layer3"] == "pass" for r in results) / len(results) tool_acc = sum(r["layer1"] for r in results) / len(results) # Gates — tighten over time assert pass_rate >= 0.85, f"Task success dropped to {pass_rate:.0%}" assert tool_acc >= 0.90, f"Tool-call accuracy dropped to {tool_acc:.0%}" print(f"PASS: task={pass_rate:.0%} tools={tool_acc:.0%}") Store per-run scores so you can chart the trend. A drop of 3+ points between merges is a real regression, not noise. Anti-patterns that make evals under-deliver Judging the final answer only — misses every trajectory bug. Score Layers 1 and 2 too. Static golden set — if it doesn't grow with every prod failure it stops predicting prod. Budget time monthly. Same model as agent and judge — bias in both directions. Rotate to a different model for grading. No cost or latency in the gate — a prompt tweak that adds 8 tool calls can 'pass' the eval while 10×-ing the bill. Vibes-only scoring — 'feels better' is not a metric. If you can't diff two numbers, you can't ship confidently. Key takeaways Agents produce trajectories, not answers — evaluate the path, not only the outcome Layer cheapest-first: tool-call correctness → trajectory quality → task success → production drift The five metrics that ship decisions: task success rate, cost per success, p50/p95 latency, tool-call accuracy, intervention rate LLM-as-judge scales, but only with an explicit rubric, a different model, and calibration against human labels A golden set that doesn't grow from prod failures stops predicting prod — grow it monthly Wire the eval into CI as a hard gate — the check that catches a regression before users do
documents.s: CI gate: fail the bad change before it ships

Скопировать как Markdown Средний Последняя проверка: 2026-11-02. All framework numbers below come from one experimental benchmark published 28 October 2026, run on a single app with Claude Opus 5.5. The author is explicit that it is not definitive. Model prices change, agents change, and a re-run next quarter will move the ordering. The mechanisms in this page are the durable part; treat the specific dollar figures as a dated snapshot and re-measure before you spend a stack decision on them. Сверьтесь с официальным источником. What you'll learn Read the one benchmark that put real numbers on 'which framework is cheaper for an agent to work in' Spot the three things the headline gets wrong — including a per-token rate that runs backwards Understand why the token bill tracks the agent's LOOP, not the size of the code it writes Know which single number actually compounds across your project's life (it is not cost-per-build) See the uncontrolled confound that may explain several rows, and why it is a lever you own Run the same measurement on your own stack, with a protocol that survives LLM variance For twenty years, picking a frontend framework meant trading developer experience against bundle size. Agents added a third axis that nobody had numbers for: how expensive is it for a model to work in this codebase? On 28 October 2026, Nolan Lawson published the first serious attempt to measure it. The result went to the front page of Hacker News and spawned a week of "Angular costs 86% more" posts. The headline is real. It is also the least interesting thing in the dataset. This page is the careful read. Three findings in the data contradict the way it is being quoted, and the most actionable lever in the whole experiment is one the benchmark did not even intend to test.
documents.s: Your Stack Choice Is an Agent Cost Lever

documents.t: Twelve stacks, one app, five runs each. Guided walkthrough1 of 4 1The task⌄ Build a Pokémon app on PokéAPI — search, filtering, type display, and move data across multiple game versions. The author characterises it as content-heavy with minimal interactivity. Hold onto that; it decides what the results generalise to. ←PreviousNext→ 2The agent⌄ Claude Opus 5.5 at high effort, given the framework spec, the official MCP server or skill where one existed, and a conformance test suite to code against. ←PreviousNext→ 3The runs⌄ Five independent runs per framework — three for Angular, which failed outright in 2 of 5 attempts. Medians and full ranges reported, which is the detail that makes the honest read possible. ←PreviousNext→ 4The measurements⌄ API cost in USD, wall-clock minutes, tokens consumed, non-blank lines of code, Lighthouse scores, and JavaScript kilobytes transferred to the browser. ←PreviousNext→ Here is the core result — cost, tokens and code size, sorted by median cost: Stack Cost (median) Cost range Tokens Lines of code JS shipped Hono+htmx $2.67 $2.23–$3.19 4.26 M 1,370 18 KiB Astro $2.76 $2.16–$3.63 4.13 M 1,461 0 KiB Nuxt $2.82 $2.39–$4.25 3.85 M 1,415 84 KiB Vanilla (Vite) $2.98 $2.24–$3.37 5.00 M 1,492 7 KiB Next.js $3.14 $2.58–$4.13 4.99 M 1,539 142 KiB Qwik $3.27 $2.35–$3.80 5.64 M 1,744 40 KiB TanStack Start $3.54 $3.11–$3.96 7.07 M 1,697 118 KiB SolidStart $3.79 $2.84–$4.81 7.13 M 1,630 40 KiB React Router $3.81 $2.82–$3.97 7.58 M 1,564 115 KiB SvelteKit $4.28 $3.59–$4.65 8.53 M 1,611 36 KiB Gracile+Lit $4.65 $3.92–$5.07 9.04 M 1,717 8 KiB Angular $4.97 $3.19–$6.82 9.76 M 2,009 93 KiB Wall-clock tracked cost closely: Astro 8.2 min and Hono+htmx 8.6 min at the fast end, Angular 17.2 min at the slow end.

Compare the spreads: Tokens: 3.85 M (Nuxt) → 9.76 M (Angular) = 2.54x Lines of code: 1,370 (Hono+htmx) → 2,009 (Angular) = 1.47x If tokens were mostly the agent writing code, those two ratios would be close. They are not — the token spread is more than 70% wider than the code spread. The extra 5.9 million tokens Angular consumed did not go into the 639 extra lines it produced. They went into the loop: reading files, re-reading them after each edit, running the conformance suite, interpreting failures, and trying again. An agent's token bill is dominated by how many times it has to go around, and how much context it drags along each time. The final artifact is a rounding error. That reframes the whole question. "Which framework produces less code" is a weak proxy. The real question is which framework lets an agent converge in fewer turns — a function of how predictable the file layout is, how legible the error messages are, how much ceremony a change requires, and how well-represented the framework's current idioms are in training data. What you'll learn Angular's two outright failures are a loop failure, not a code-quality failure. In both runs the agent built an SSR app that rejected non-localhost connections, despite instructions specifying reverse-proxy deployment. That is the agent misreading a deployment constraint — the kind of thing a sharper CLAUDE.md fixes, and a reason to classify failures rather than just count them.
documents.s: Finding 1: the token bill tracks the loop, not the artifact

documents.t: This is the finding that is absent from every summary I have read, and it falls out of dividing two columns that nobody divided. Take median cost ÷ median tokens for each row: Stack Tokens Cost Effective $/Mtok Nuxt 3.85 M $2.82 $0.73 Astro 4.13 M $2.76 $0.67 Hono+htmx 4.26 M $2.67 $0.63 Next.js 4.99 M $3.14 $0.63 Vanilla 5.00 M $2.98 $0.60 Qwik 5.64 M $3.27 $0.58 SolidStart 7.13 M $3.79 $0.53 Gracile+Lit 9.04 M $4.65 $0.51 Angular 9.76 M $4.97 $0.51 The rate falls as the token count rises, almost monotonically. The frameworks that burn the most tokens pay the least per token. Why? Opus 5.5 lists at $4 per MTok fresh input, $20 output, and $0.20 for cache reads — a 5% cache-read multiplier where the platform standard is 10%. A blended rate between $0.51 and $0.73 sits just above the $0.20 cache-read floor and roughly six times below the fresh-input rate. There is only one mix that produces those numbers: the overwhelming majority of counted tokens are cache reads. Pair pure cache reads with about 11% fresh-and-output traffic and you land at $0.62; shift that to 8% and you land at $0.50 — Angular's number. So the mechanism is this. Every extra step in a long agentic session replays the same growing context. That replay is cache reads at $0.20. The marginal token in a heavy framework costs a twentieth of the first token, which is why Angular's 2.54x token count turns into only a 1.86x bill. Two consequences that matter more than the ranking: Prompt caching is doing the heavy lifting in every row. This benchmark is substantially a measurement of cache-read volume. Any agent setup without effective caching would see these same token spreads hit a bill at up to 20x the rate — and the gap between frameworks would widen rather than compress. If you want to know your real exposure to a verbose stack, check your cache hit rate first. See prompt caching across providers and prompt caching economics. Cost-per-build systematically understates the penalty of a heavy stack, because caching absorbs exactly the thing heavy stacks generate. Which leads to the number that actually compounds. Watch out This arithmetic is mine, not the author's. Median cost ÷ median tokens is not the median of the per-run ratios, and medians of two columns can come from different runs — so treat these as approximate, directional figures rather than per-run truth. The direction is consistent across all twelve rows, which is what makes it worth reporting.
documents.s: Finding 2: the effective rate per token runs backwards

documents.t: Angular's cheapest run cost $3.19. Hono+htmx's most expensive run cost $3.19. Identical. Nuxt ranged $2.39–$4.25; Astro $2.16–$3.63; SolidStart $2.84–$4.81. Across five stochastic runs, within-framework variance is comparable to — and often larger than — between-framework differences. The defensible claims from this dataset are coarse: Defensible: the lean MPA cluster (Hono+htmx, Astro, Nuxt) is cheaper than the heavy cluster (SvelteKit, Gracile+Lit, Angular), by roughly 1.5–1.9x. Not defensible: "Astro beats Nuxt," "SolidStart beats React Router," or any other neighbouring pair. Those gaps are inside the noise. The author says as much — the goal was "not to write the end-all-be-all benchmark" but to show evidence-based selection is possible at all. The blog posts converting his medians into league tables dropped the ranges, and the ranges are where the honesty lives. This is the same discipline our reading AI benchmarks page applies to model leaderboards: a median without a spread is a vibe wearing a number.
documents.s: Finding 3: the ranges overlap, so most adjacent pairs prove nothing

documents.t: Buried in the methodology is the most actionable thing in the experiment. Each agent was offered the framework's official MCP server or skill. Whether it used them varied wildly: Stack Runs that used the official MCP / skill SvelteKit 5 of 5 Next.js 1–2 of 5 (read guidance files) TanStack Start 2 of 5 (discovered skills) Nuxt 0 of 5 (MCP never used) Sit with that. Across 60 runs, a significant fraction of the variance may not be "how expensive is this framework" but "did the agent notice the documentation that was sitting right there." SvelteKit used its MCP every time and still landed near the expensive end; Nuxt never touched its MCP and came third cheapest. Those two facts alone should stop anyone from reading this table as a clean framework ranking. The practical inversion: documentation discovery is a variable you control completely, and framework choice is one you mostly cannot. Before you migrate a codebase to save $2 a build, make the docs un-missable: Put the framework's conventions directly in CLAUDE.md rather than hoping a skill gets discovered — see our CLAUDE.md template and generator. State deployment constraints explicitly. Angular's two failures were exactly this gap. If you ship an MCP server or skill for your own framework or internal library, measure whether agents actually invoke it. A tool that is used in 0 of 5 runs is, economically, a tool that does not exist.
documents.s: The uncontrolled confound — and the lever you actually own

documents.t: A build happens once. Every subsequent task pays a tax proportional to how much code the agent must pull into context to understand the thing it is changing. That makes lines of code the durable quantity, and the spread is narrower than the token spread but permanent: 1,370 for Hono+htmx against 2,009 for Angular — roughly a 32% smaller standing context tax on every future task, forever. Combine that with Finding 2 and you get the right mental model. At build time, caching compresses the difference between stacks. Over a maintenance lifetime you pay the LOC difference again on every task, and much of the baseline repo read is fresh input on the first turn of each new session rather than a cache hit. The one-off $2.30 gap is noise; a third more code to carry for three years is not. Watch out Do not read this as 'always pick the leanest stack.' Lines of code is one term in the cost function. A framework that prevents a class of state-synchronisation bug may save far more agent loops than it costs in context — and a top HN comment made exactly this case, arguing htmx needs extensive testing to catch state bugs under AI codegen while React's heavy training-data representation helps agents on genuinely interactive apps. That is a real effect this benchmark's content-heavy app cannot see.
documents.s: The number that compounds: cost to edit, not cost to build

documents.t: The limits are load-bearing. The author lists most of them; I have added the ones the coverage dropped. Limit Why it matters One app type Content-heavy, minimal interactivity. Dashboards, editors, games and real-time apps invert the trade-offs that favour MPAs here. Lighthouse favours MPAs LCP in particular punishes client-side routing. The lean stacks winning both cost and Lighthouse is partly a measurement artifact, not two independent wins. Five runs, high variance Not enough to separate adjacent rows. Lighthouse itself was inconsistent across runs, picking different LCP elements. One model, one effort level Opus 5.5 at high effort. A cheaper model, or a lower effort setting, changes both the absolute bill and plausibly the ordering. Chromium + mobile throttling only 4x CPU, Slow 4G, one browser, one laptop. No maintenance tasks measured The compounding cost argued above is an inference from the LOC column, not a measured result. Nobody has run the maintenance benchmark yet. Human time unpriced Angular's 17.2-minute median against Astro's 8.2 is a ~9-minute gap. If an engineer supervises the run, those nine minutes of attention plausibly cost more than the entire $2.30 token delta. Optimising the API bill while ignoring wall-clock is the wrong objective function.

The strongest thing about this benchmark is that it is reproducible — the harness and the raw results are both public. Your codebase is not a Pokémon app, so the numbers that should drive your decisions are yours. Guided walkthrough1 of 6 1Pick a task that represents your real work⌄ Not a greenfield build — that is the one case you will do least often. Pick three recent closed tickets of typical size and use them as the task set. Greenfield benchmarks measure the thing you do once. ←PreviousNext→ 2Fix everything except the variable⌄ Same model, same effort level, same harness, same prompt, same acceptance tests. If you are comparing two stacks, the conformance suite must be behaviour-level so it can run against both. ←PreviousNext→ 3Run at least five iterations per arm⌄ Five is the floor, not the target — the published ranges show why. Record every run, not just the median, and report the spread. If the ranges overlap, your result is 'no detectable difference' and that is a real answer. ←PreviousNext→ 4Log the right four numbers⌄ Cost, tokens split by type (fresh input / output / cache read — the split is the whole story from Finding 2), wall-clock, and resulting diff size. Cost alone hides the mechanism. ←PreviousNext→ 5Check whether the agent used your tooling⌄ Grep the transcripts for your MCP calls and skill loads. If discovery is inconsistent, fix that first and re-run — it is cheaper than a migration and may erase the gap you were trying to close. ←PreviousNext→ 6Decide on the compounding term⌄ Weight resulting diff size and standing context tax above one-off build cost. You pay the former on every future task. ←PreviousNext→ Measure the agent cost of a task on your own stack CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ I want to measure how expensive a task is for you to complete in this codebase, so I can compare stacks and tooling with evidence instead of vibes. Task: <paste a real, closed ticket of typical size> Rules: 1. Work only inside this repo. Do not install new dependencies. 2. Stop when the existing test suite passes for the changed behaviour. 3. Do not optimise for token use — work the way you normally would. I am measuring the honest cost, not a best case. When you are done, report exactly: - Files read, and how many times each was re-read - Number of test/build invocations - Lines added and removed - Anything in the repo that made you go around an extra time: missing docs, surprising file layout, an unclear error message, a convention you had to infer. Be specific and name the file. That last list is what I am really after. Rank it by how many turns each item cost you. The last question is the one that pays. The agent is the only entity that knows which of your conventions cost it three extra loops, and it will tell you if you ask. Those answers convert into CLAUDE.md lines, and a good CLAUDE.md line is worth more than a framework migration. Check yourself 0/5 Key takeaways Agent token cost tracks the number of loops, not the lines produced: a 2.54x token spread over a 1.47x code spread. The effective rate per token runs backwards ($0.73 → $0.51/Mtok) because extra agent steps bill as $0.20 cache reads. Caching is absorbing most of the penalty — check your hit rate before trusting any cost-per-build figure. Report ranges or report nothing. Angular's best run equalled Hono+htmx's worst, so only the coarse lean-vs-heavy cluster claim survives. Documentation discovery was uncontrolled and may explain several rows. It is also free to fix and entirely yours to control — do that before a migration. Optimise the quantity that compounds: resulting code size, paid on every future task, not the one-off build bill. A ~9-minute wall-clock gap under human supervision plausibly costs more than the entire $2.30 token delta. Do not optimise the API bill in isolation.

Скопировать как Markdown Все уровни ИИ может стать терпеливым, всегда доступным наставником, какого у большинства из нас никогда не было, — если использовать его, чтобы понимать, а не чтобы перепоручать мышление. Разница между обучением и списыванием — в рабочем процессе.

Объясни как новичку. «Объясни [понятие] просто, с одной аналогией и одним примером.» Затем углубляйтесь слоями. Сократическое наставничество. «Не давай мне ответ — задавай вопросы, которые приведут меня к нему.» Пересказ. Он объясняет, затем вы пересказываете; ИИ исправляет ваши пробелы. Именно здесь настоящее обучение закрепляется. Проверь меня. «Сгенерируй 5 вопросов по [теме], затем оцени мои ответы и объясни промахи.» План занятий. «У меня 2 недели на [экзамен]. Составь план и проработай мои слабые места.»

Tutor me on {topic}. Start by asking what I already know, then teach one step at a time and check my understanding before moving on. Don't just give answers. I'll explain {concept} back to you. Point out anything wrong or missing, kindly and specifically. Here's my explanation: {your attempt}

Для оцениваемых работ просите подсказки, а не ключ к ответам Если вы вставите домашнее задание и скопируете вывод, вы ничему не научились (и, возможно, нарушите правила своего учебного заведения). Просите подсказки, проверки и объяснения, которые приведут вас к ответу. Отвечайте за результат сами. Проверяйте факты — наставники могут уверенно ошибаться; перепроверяйте ключевые утверждения (Галлюцинации). По одному понятию за раз — глубина важнее широты. Интервальная практика — возвращайтесь и проходите проверку заново; именно это закрепляет знания.

Скопировать как Markdown Начальный Пять вещей, которыми почти кто угодно может воспользоваться уже сегодня. К каждой прилагается стартовый промпт — вставьте его, замените содержимое в скобках, уточняйте простым языком.

"Here's an email I received. Draft a polite, concise reply that [accepts the meeting but proposes Thursday instead]. Keep it under 80 words. Email: [paste]" Полезные уточнения: «more formal», «add a line thanking them», «give me two versions».

"Summarise this in 5 bullet points a busy manager could read in 30 seconds, then list any decisions or action items separately. Text: [paste]" Работает со статьями, заметками со встреч, тредами и отчётами. Для очень длинных входных данных просите сначала резюме, а затем углубляйтесь.

"I need to [organise a 30-person team offsite] by [October]. Give me a step-by-step plan with rough timing, and flag the 3 things most likely to go wrong." Отлично подходит для планов проектов, чек-листов и превращения расплывчатой цели в следующие действия.

"I'm deciding between [option A] and [option B] for [situation]. Lay out the trade-offs in a table, then tell me what else I should consider before deciding." Используйте его как спарринг-партнёра — попросите его отстаивать противоположную позицию, чтобы проверить ваши рассуждения на прочность.

"Write a first draft of [a LinkedIn post announcing our new feature]. Match this voice: [paste a paragraph you wrote]. Then suggest a punchier opening line." Дать образец вашего письма — вот секрет результатов, которые не звучат шаблонно.

documents.t: Дайте контекст, затем итерируйте Каждый промпт выше называет цель, формат и ограничения — это Основы промптинга. И ни один из них не обязан быть верным с первого раза; уточняйте простым языком. Проверяйте всё фактическое Даты, числа, имена, цитаты и «факты» могут быть уверенно неверными. Для всего, что важно, проверяйте это — см. Галлюцинации.

Скопировать как Markdown Все уровни ИИ — превосходный ускоритель исследований, и опасный, если довериться ему слепо. При правильном использовании он сжимает часы чтения в минуты; при небрежном — уверенно выдумывает источники. Вот дисциплинированная версия.

Резюмируйте длинный документ/статью в ключевые мысли + выводы. Сравнивайте несколько источников в таблице (в чём они согласны/расходятся). Стройте обзор предметной области — карту игроков, подходов или аргументов по теме. Извлекайте конкретные факты/цифры из документа (со ссылками). Проверяйте на прочность — «каков самый сильный контраргумент против этого?»

Using ONLY the text I provide, summarize the key findings and quote the exact sentence supporting each one. If something isn't in the text, say "not stated." Text: """{paste}""" Скармливайте ему источники. Не просите его вспоминать факты из памяти для чего-либо важного — вставляйте материал или используйте инструмент, который его извлекает (RAG). Требуйте ссылок. «Процитируй предложение, которое подтверждает каждое утверждение.» Неподтверждённые утверждения становятся видны. Отделяйте факт от вывода. Просите его помечать, что заявлено, а что истолковано. Выдуманные ссылки — классическая ловушка Модели изобретают правдоподобно выглядящие статьи, авторов и URL. Проверяйте, что каждая ссылка существует, прежде чем на неё полагаться. См. Галлюцинации.

Соберите источники сами (или с помощью инструмента извлечения). Резюмируйте каждый с опорой на текст + ссылками. Синтезируйте их в тематическое сравнение. Выявите пробелы/расхождения и «и что с того». Выборочно проверьте критические факты по оригиналам.

Скопировать как Markdown Средний What you'll learn Separate the three jobs non-engineers actually use a coding agent for — only one of them is coding, and that mismatch is the whole story Find the real cost centre of a broad rollout: not seats, not tokens, but the review queue of the engineers who inherit the output Understand the micro-model problem — why a trader's 40-line position script can be a regulated model, and what US supervisory guidance now says Stop conflating the two 2026 bank AI bans: internal coding tools versus third-party agents touching customer accounts are different problems with different fixes Match the surface to the job instead of the person, using the capability ladder Deploy controls that actually enforce — and know why server-managed settings and the default audit trail do not Последняя проверка: 2026-11-09. The Goldman Sachs specifics below (dates, headcounts, who kept access) come from the November 2, 2026 Bloomberg report and its follow-ups, and from a named company spokesperson. Access policies change quietly and without announcements — treat the Goldman case as a worked example whose details may have moved, not as a live description of that firm. The mechanisms and the control surface are the durable part of this page. Сверьтесь с официальным источником.
documents.s: Rolling Out a Coding Agent to Non-Engineers

documents.t: In July 2026, Goldman Sachs CIO Marco Argenti publicly praised the "vibe coding" happening among the firm's non-technical staff: people who were not engineers built things with AI tools and handed their creations to one of the firm's roughly 12,000 engineers to finish. In October 2026 internal guidance reversed that. Claude Code and GitHub Copilot now sit with engineers and with "strats" — the hybrid trading/quant/engineering population — and were withdrawn from bankers and traders. A spokesperson framed it as the end of a trial: after assessing "a variety of factors including productivity and risk management," the firm put the tools in the hands of those best suited to use them long term. Bloomberg broke it on November 2; the Hacker News thread passed 780 points. The coverage mostly ran as a verdict on AI. It is more useful as a case study in rollout design, because the failure mode it illustrates is one that almost every organisation rolling out a coding agent beyond engineering will hit, and almost none of them price in advance.

Start with what the withdrawn users were reportedly doing. Three jobs come up consistently in the reporting: What traders used it for Is this coding? What it actually is Following how clients were trading No Data analysis over sensitive flow data Simulating shifts in markets and in their positions No Quantitative modelling Drafting text and visuals No Document and asset generation None of the three is software engineering. A coding agent was the delivery vehicle, not the job. That is the single most important thing to take from the episode, and it is the thing the "banks fear AI" framing obscures. This happens because a terminal coding agent is, accidentally, the most capable general-purpose analysis tool most firms have deployed. It can reach a database, write the Python, run it, and render the chart — in one loop, without a ticket. If the sanctioned analytics path requires a data request and a two-week queue, the coding agent wins on merit every time. People were not misusing it. They were routing around an internal bottleneck, which is what capable people do. The consequence is that you are not deciding whether non-engineers may code. You are deciding whether unversioned, unreviewed analysis may be built against production data by people whose output nobody downstream has agreed to maintain. Phrased that way, a lot of rollout debates resolve themselves.
documents.s: The three jobs, only one of which is coding

documents.t: Look again at the July description — non-technical staff built things and passed them to one of 12,000 engineers "to enhance." That handoff is the rollout's true unit economics, and it is invisible in the business case. The seat cost is visible. The token cost is visible, and there are hard spend caps for it. The engineering hours required to review, harden, own and maintain a stream of prototypes built by people who cannot read the code are not visible to whoever approved the seats, because they land on a different team's quarter. The arithmetic is unkind. Suppose 2,000 non-engineers each produce one artefact worth escalating per month — a conservative rate for an enthusiastic population. That is 2,000 items a month arriving at an engineering organisation that did not plan for them. At four hours each to review, harden and take ownership, that is 8,000 engineer-hours a month, or roughly 50 full-time engineers absorbed by intake. Against 12,000 engineers it is survivable; as a surprise it is not, and it buys nothing that appears on the engineering roadmap. Three properties make this queue worse than an ordinary backlog: Guided walkthrough1 of 3 1It is unrefusable in practice⌄ The artefact already works for its author, who is often senior to the reviewer and has already shown it to their desk. 'No' is now a political act rather than a triage decision. Backlogs you cannot refuse are not backlogs, they are obligations. ←PreviousNext→ 2The author cannot fix review findings⌄ Normal review is a conversation between two people who can both read the diff. Here, every finding converts into engineering work rather than author rework. The reviewer does not reduce their own load by reviewing well — they increase it. ←PreviousNext→ 3Ownership never transfers, it only accretes⌄ Once an engineer touches it, it is theirs. The original author keeps requesting changes and keeps depending on it, but the pager, the dependency upgrades and the incident belong to the team that 'helped'. Every escalated prototype is a permanent liability with no owner budget attached. ←PreviousNext→ If you take one action from this page, make it this one: before widening access, ask the engineering organisation that will inherit the output to agree to an intake rate, in writing, with a path for refusal. A rollout that cannot answer "who maintains what these people build, and what happens when they say no" is not a rollout, it is a deferred argument.
documents.s: The cost centre nobody budgets: the review queue

documents.t: For firms in regulated sectors there is a second, sharper issue, and it is the one most likely to end a rollout abruptly. A trader who asks an agent to "simulate how my book moves if the curve steepens 50bp" has not written a script. They have built a model — in the specific, load-bearing sense that financial supervisors use the word. Longstanding US supervisory guidance defines a model as a quantitative method, system or approach that applies statistical, economic, financial or mathematical theories to turn input data into quantitative estimates. A position-simulation script written in an afternoon fits that definition comfortably. So does an approval-routing helper that applies weighted criteria to flag a counterparty transaction, or an eligibility check that scores whether a customer qualifies for an offer. Models in that sense are supposed to live in a model inventory, with documentation, independent validation, and a change history. The practice of model risk management was built for a world where models were discrete, expensive and few — produced by identifiable quant teams on a release cycle slow enough for a validation function to keep up. A coding agent in the hands of 2,000 non-engineers inverts every one of those assumptions. The artefacts are cheap, numerous, undocumented, unversioned, and produced by people who do not know that the word "model" now applies to them. This is the micro-model problem: decision logic that meets the regulatory definition of a model, created faster than any validation function can inventory it, by authors who never asked the question. The governance gap is not that the output is bad. It is that nobody can enumerate what exists. The supervisory ground also moved in 2026, which matters for anyone citing chapter and verse. On April 17, 2026 the Federal Reserve issued SR 26-2, "Revised Guidance on Model Risk Management," superseding SR 11-7 (April 4, 2011) and SR 21-8 (April 9, 2021). If your internal policy, your vendor's compliance deck or a blog post you are relying on still cites SR 11-7 as current, it is out of date by more than six months. Последняя проверка: 2026-11-09. SR 26-2's existence, date and the letters it supersedes are confirmed against the Federal Reserve's own SR letter index. Several secondary write-ups make specific claims about how SR 26-2 treats generative and agentic AI in scope; we could not confirm those against the primary letter and have deliberately left them out. Read the letter and its attachment yourself before building a control on a scope claim, and have counsel do the same — nothing here is legal or compliance advice. Сверьтесь с официальным источником.

Search coverage of 2026 bank AI restrictions and you will get two stories blended into one. They are not the same problem and they do not share a fix. Internal coding agents Third-party agents on customer accounts Example Goldman Sachs restricting Claude Code and Copilot to engineers JPMorgan, Bank of America and Citi limiting outside AI agents' access to customer accounts Who is acting Your own employees, inside your perimeter Software acting for a customer, outside your perimeter The fear Unreviewed logic, data barriers, auditability of machine-written code Unauthorised transactions and credential-scoped access at scale — Jamie Dimon's "rogue agents," of which "there could be thousands" Typical control Access scoping, managed policy, review gates Read-only scoping at the API boundary — Meta's Muse, for instance, can read a Chase balance but not move money Where to read more This page Securing agents · Agent payments and x402 Bank of America's CEO said the firm hired 1,000 contractors to patch software against agent-exposed vulnerabilities — that is the second column, not the first. If you cite it in an internal memo about giving your analysts Claude Code, you have cited the wrong thing, and the first person to notice will spend your credibility. One more piece of context worth holding, because it cuts against the easy reading: Goldman Sachs is lead-left underwriter on Anthropic's IPO, with the S-1 filed October 26, 2026 and the roadshow expected the week of November 9, 2026. A firm narrowing internal access to a product while underwriting its public listing is not a contradiction. It is evidence that the decision was about deployment scope rather than a verdict on the tool — which is exactly how you should read any restriction like it, including your own.

The instinct after reading the above is to gate by job title. That is what Goldman did, and for a firm with 12,000 engineers and a supervisory examiner it is a defensible blunt instrument. It is usually the wrong first move for everyone else, because it removes the capability without removing the demand — and unmet demand for AI analysis does not evaporate, it moves to a personal account on a personal laptop where you have no telemetry at all. Gate by job instead. Most of what non-engineers want from a coding agent is available on a surface that generates no review queue and no micro-models. The job Right surface Why it is the right one Analyse a dataset, make a chart Claude app with file upload and its analysis tool Ephemeral, no repo, no artefact to maintain. See Data Analysis Draft documents, decks, visuals Claude app, Projects Never needed a coding agent. See Business & Strategy Query sanctioned systems Read-only MCP server you operate You control the schema, the scope and the log. See Securing MCP servers Reuse a recurring analysis A skill or saved prompt built by engineering once Turns 200 ad-hoc micro-models into one reviewed artefact. See Skills Prototype something that must become real software Coding agent, with a declared intake path The only rung that legitimately generates review work — so make the queue explicit Operate on production data or money Nothing self-serve See The trust ladder The ladder has a property worth noticing: the top rung is the only one that produces a maintenance obligation, and the five rungs below it absorb most of the real demand. Firms that skip the ladder and deploy a coding agent as their general AI offering are paying engineering-review prices for work that a chat surface handles for free.
documents.s: The capability ladder: match the surface to the job

documents.t: If you do run a coding agent across a wide population, the distinction below is the one that gets missed in rollout plans — including by people who have read the docs. Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Managed settings enforce. Server-managed settings are a convenience.⌄ A managed-settings.json deployed by your device-management tooling sits at the top of the precedence stack and cannot be overridden locally. Settings served from your claude.ai organisation only reach sessions that have already authenticated into your organisation — so they never reach the machine that logged in with a personal account, which is precisely the machine you were worried about. Anthropic's own documentation says to treat a server-managed list as a convenience for machines you cannot reach with device management, not as enforcement. Plan accordingly: MDM is the control, the server-side copy is the fallback. ←PreviousNext→ 2forceLoginOrgUUID is what closes the personal-account hole⌄ Without it, a developer can sign in with a personal claude.ai account and your organisation sees nothing: no telemetry, no policy, no audit trail, and your data leaving through a consumer account. Setting forceLoginMethod and forceLoginOrgUUID in managed settings makes Claude Code refuse a login belonging to any organisation you have not listed, and exit at startup if the credential in use belongs to one. This is the single highest-leverage key in the file. ←PreviousNext→ 3allowedProviders decides which services the machine may reach Claude through⌄ Separate concern from which account is used. It lists the permitted routes — the Anthropic API, Amazon Bedrock, a gateway — and refuses a session configured for anything else at startup, or on its next request if it switches mid-session. Requires Claude Code v2.1.285 or later. This is the key that stops traffic quietly detouring through an unapproved proxy; see [gray-market AI proxies](/docs/security/gray-market-ai-proxies) for why that matters. ←PreviousNext→ 4Environment credentials are refused, not merely discouraged⌄ Under these keys, Claude Code blocks sessions authenticating with ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN or apiKeyHelper — even when managed settings themselves supply them — because organisation membership cannot be verified for an environment credential. Useful to know before you discover it as a support ticket from every CI job you own. ←PreviousNext→ 5Permissions are a per-repo gate, not a population gate⌄ Allow and deny rules are the right tool for what an agent may do in a given project. They are the wrong tool for who may run an agent at all. Do not let a well-written deny list substitute for an access decision. See Permissions and the precedence stack in Settings. ←PreviousNext→ managed-settings.json — the enforcement floor, deployed by MDM CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ { "forceLoginMethod": "claudeai", "forceLoginOrgUUID": ["00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000"], "allowedProviders": ["anthropic", "bedrock"], "env": { "CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY": "1", "OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER": "otlp", "OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER": "otlp", "OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL": "grpc", "OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT": "http://collector.internal.example.com:4317", "OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS": "1" } } Replace the UUID with your own organisation ID from your admin settings, and the endpoint with your collector. Pinning the telemetry variables in the managed env block matters: a destination set there is locked, and Claude Code removes conflicting developer-set variables at startup. A destination a developer can change is not an audit trail.
documents.s: Controls that enforce, and controls that only look like they do

documents.t: This one is worth the price of admission, because it is the gap between what rollout plans claim and what the data contains. Claude Code exports a genuinely useful set of OpenTelemetry metrics — claude_code.session.count, claude_code.lines_of_code.count, claude_code.commit.count, claude_code.pull_request.count, claude_code.cost.usage, claude_code.code_edit_tool.decision, claude_code.active_time.total — carrying attributes including user.email, user.account_uuid and organization.id. Per-user cost attribution and per-user active time are both available out of the box. For the full picture see OpenTelemetry tracing and usage and cost analytics. But metrics and events are redacted by default, and the redaction is more aggressive than most people expect: MCP server and tool names appear as "custom" or "mcp" — with no tool name — unless OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS=1 is set. An organisation that believes it has a record of which internal systems its agents touched has, by default, a record that says mcp. Prompt content, assistant responses and system prompts require OTEL_LOG_USER_PROMPTS=1. Tool output — file reads, command output — requires OTEL_LOG_TOOL_CONTENT=1. Bash commands and file paths also sit behind OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS=1. There is no built-in admin dashboard. You export to your own observability backend and build the view yourself. Budget for that; it is the step that quietly does not happen. The default is the right default — it protects employees from casual surveillance, and claude_code.safety_event still records permission checks and blocks without exposing content. But it means the sentence "we have full auditability" is false on a default install, and the cheapest moment to discover that is now rather than during an examination. Turning the flags on is a decision with real privacy weight: tell people what you are logging, agree a retention period, and keep the content flags off unless a named obligation requires them. See what your agent uploads for the employee-side view of the same question.
documents.s: The audit-trail gotcha that will embarrass you in a review

documents.t: Not a maturity model. Five questions whose absence of an answer predicts a reversal four months later. Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Which of the three jobs are people actually asking for?⌄ Ask ten of them. If the answers are analysis, drafting and querying — and they usually are — a coding agent is the wrong rung of the ladder and you can skip most of this page. ←PreviousNext→ 2Who has agreed to inherit the output, at what rate, with what right of refusal?⌄ In writing, from the engineering leader whose team it lands on. If nobody has agreed, you have budgeted the seats and not the cost. ←PreviousNext→ 3Can you enumerate what gets built?⌄ If the artefacts live on laptops, the answer is no, and in a regulated setting no is a finding. A sanctioned repo or workspace per population is the minimum that makes enumeration possible at all. ←PreviousNext→ 4Is the policy enforced by MDM, or only published?⌄ Deployed managed-settings.json with forceLoginOrgUUID, or a wiki page. Only one of those survives a motivated user with a personal account. ←PreviousNext→ 5What does your telemetry actually contain?⌄ Not what the metric list offers — what your collector received last week. Query it before you claim it. If MCP tool names come back as 'mcp', you know which flag you have not set. ←PreviousNext→ Check yourself 0/6 Key takeaways The three jobs non-engineers bring to a coding agent — analysis, modelling, drafting — are not coding. Decide about those jobs, not about job titles. A coding agent often wins on merit because the sanctioned analytics path is slow. Fix the bottleneck or the routing-around continues after any ban. The rollout's real cost is the engineering review queue: unrefusable, non-delegable back, permanently accreting. Get a written intake rate and a right of refusal before widening access. Micro-model problem: ad-hoc position and eligibility logic can meet the supervisory definition of a model. The gap is not quality, it is that nobody can enumerate what exists. SR 26-2 (April 17, 2026) supersedes SR 11-7 and SR 21-8. Update any policy that still cites SR 11-7 as current — and verify scope claims against the primary letter. Internal coding tools and third-party agents on customer accounts are two different 2026 bank stories. Do not cite one as evidence about the other. Managed settings via MDM enforce; server-managed settings are explicitly a convenience. forceLoginOrgUUID is the key that closes the personal-account hole; allowedProviders pins the route. Telemetry is redacted by default — MCP tool names log as 'mcp'. Query your collector before claiming auditability, and treat the content flags as a privacy decision, not a checkbox.
documents.s: Five questions to answer before you widen access

documents.t: Techstrong.ai: Goldman Sachs cuts bankers, traders off from AI coding tools over risk concerns — the November 2, 2026 write-up of the Bloomberg scoop: the July-to-October reversal, the named spokesperson quote, the 12,000-engineer figure, and the governance concerns cited. PYMNTS: Goldman Sachs bars bankers from employing some AI tools — independent corroboration, and the Argenti "passed on their creations to one of the firm's 12,000 engineers to enhance" detail that the review-queue section is built on. Federal Reserve: SR letters index and SR 26-2, Revised Guidance on Model Risk Management — the primary source for the April 17, 2026 date and the superseded letters. Read the attachment for the model definition and the scope language. Axios: Unvetted AI agents are accessing U.S. bank accounts — the other 2026 bank AI story, the one about third-party agents at the customer-account boundary. Claude Code: monitoring usage — the authoritative list of metrics, events and attributes, the OTEL_LOG_* flags and exactly what each one reveals, and the statement that there is no built-in admin dashboard. Claude Code: authentication and IAM — forceLoginMethod, forceLoginOrgUUID, allowedProviders, the credential precedence list, and the rules on blocked environment credentials. Claude Code: managed settings and server-managed settings — the precedence stack, and the explicit "convenience, not enforcement" characterisation of server-managed lists. AILmanac companions: Settings & precedence · Permissions · CI/CD for agent-written code · Hard spend caps

CI/CD for Agent-Written Code — the downstream half of the review-queue problem: once the artefacts do reach your pipeline, the merge queue breaks before the runner budget does, and there is arithmetic for it. The Trust Ladder — the general version of the capability ladder above: how much autonomy to grant an agent, staged against what you can verify. Скопировать как Markdown Все уровни ИИ — феноменальный партнёр по письму, если им управлять. Цель не в том, чтобы нажать кнопку и опубликовать, — а в том, чтобы быстро пройти путь от чистого листа к сильному черновику в вашем голосе, а затем отточить.

Дайте бриф. Цель, аудитория, формат, объём, тон. («Вступление к блог-посту на 600 слов для начинающих основателей, ободряющее, без жаргона.») Сначала план для всего, что длиннее нескольких абзацев, — утвердите структуру до прозы. Черновик, затем редактирование в несколько проходов («сожми», «больше конкретных примеров», «убери разгон в начале»). Подберите ваш голос. Вставьте образец вашего письма: «match this voice». Это единственный самый мощный рычаг качества. Перепрофилируйте. Один материал → тред, врезка для рассылки, пост в LinkedIn, письмо.

Brief: blog intro, 150 words, for {audience}, tone {tone}. Hook in the first line. Here's my voice to match: """{paste a paragraph you wrote}""" Edit this for clarity and concision without changing meaning. Show a bullet list of the changes. Text: """{paste}"""

Не давайте ему выдумывать факты ИИ с радостью выдаст правдоподобные статистику, цитаты, имена и источники, которые ошибочны. Никогда не публикуйте фактическое утверждение, которое вы не проверили. Просите его помечать всё, что требует реального источника, с помощью [verify], и заполняйте это сами. См. Галлюцинации. Вы — редактор. Сохраняйте суждение, вкус и ответственность за собой. Избегайте шаблонного «голоса ИИ». Конкретика, примеры и реальный образец вашего стиля это исправляют. Раскрывайте факт использования ИИ там, где это важно.

Скопировать как Markdown Продвинутый Вы подправили промпт, и он кажется лучше — но так ли это? Без evals (оценок) вы летите вслепую: каждое изменение — это подбрасывание монетки, и вы узнаёте о поломке от рассерженного пользователя, а не от теста. Evals превращают «ощущения» в число, которому можно доверять, которое можно отстоять и отслеживать во времени. Это самое главное, что отличает любительские промпты от продакшен-уровня работы с Claude. What you'll learn Почему «мне это выглядит хорошо» — не тест, и что измерять вместо этого Постройте golden dataset из РЕАЛЬНЫХ сбоев (снизу вверх), а не из выдуманных Оценивайте кодом там, где можете, и LLM-as-judge там, где не можете Подключите evals в CI, чтобы изменение промпта или модели никогда не дало незаметную регрессию Последняя проверка: 2026-06-24. Инструментарий для evals и поведение моделей меняются быстро — перепроверяйте указанные руководства и перекалибровывайте судью всякий раз, когда меняете тестируемую модель. OWASP по-прежнему ставит ошибки в этом (и prompt injection) в число главных рисков LLM на 2026 год. Сверьтесь с официальным источником.

Три правила, которые вас спасут: Снизу вверх лучше, чем сверху вниз. Сначала собирайте реальные сбои, затем проектируйте метрику, чтобы их ловить. Eval, построенный на реальных поломках, предсказывает реальные поломки; eval, придуманный у доски, в основном измеряет ваше воображение. Число, которое можно перезапустить. Eval повторяем: одинаковые входы → сопоставимый результат. Именно это позволяет честно сравнить промпт v1 и v2 или claude-haiku-4-5 и claude-sonnet-5. Дёшево запускать — запускайте часто. Если на это у человека уходит полдня, этого не произойдёт. Автоматизируйте.

Ваш golden dataset — сердце любого eval: тщательно отобранный набор входов с известными правильными ожиданиями. Guided walkthrough1 of 4 1Сначала собирайте реальные сбои⌄ Начинайте с реальных плохих выводов: продакшен-трейсов, баг-репортов, тикетов поддержки. Именно эти случаи имеют значение. ←PreviousNext→ 2Закрепите 50–100 случаями, написанными вручную⌄ Вручную напишите случаи, покрывающие самые критичные и самые подверженные ошибкам сценарии. Это ваш стабильный опорный набор. ←PreviousNext→ 3Расширяйте до ~500+⌄ Добавляйте обезличенные продакшен-образцы (вычищайте PII) и синтетические случаи для недопредставленных сценариев. Не доверяйте агрегированным метрикам на крошечном наборе. ←PreviousNext→ 4Растите его каждую неделю⌄ Каждая новая продакшен-регрессия становится новым тест-кейсом. Golden dataset живой, а не замороженный. ←PreviousNext→

Тянитесь к самой дешёвой надёжной проверке в первую очередь. Программные (детерминированные) проверки — используйте их везде, где у ответа есть структура: точное совпадение / совпадение по ключевым словам, «валидный JSON по этой схеме», «вызвал ли он правильный инструмент с правильными аргументами», «меньше N токенов / меньше X мс». Быстро, бесплатно и никогда не флаки. LLM-as-judge — для размытых измерений (полезность, тон, верность источнику), которые сопротивляются коду. Дайте судье рубрику, а не ощущение, и откалибруйте его по человеческим разметкам, прежде чем доверять ему. У судей есть предвзятости LLM-судьи склоняются к более длинным ответам (предвзятость к многословию) и к тому варианту, который показан первым (позиционная предвзятость). Защита: строгая рубрика, попарное сравнение вместо абсолютной оценки, перестановка порядка ответов и перепроверка судьи на размеченном человеком срезе. Судья — это один слой, а не весь тест. Рубрика LLM-as-judge (стартовая) CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ You are a strict grader. You are given a QUESTION, a REFERENCE answer, and a MODEL answer. Score the MODEL answer from 1-5 on (a) faithfulness to the reference and (b) helpfulness. Output ONLY JSON, nothing else: {"score": <1-5>, "reason": "<one short sentence>"} QUESTION: {{question}} REFERENCE: {{reference}} MODEL: {{model_answer}}

Агент может прийти к правильному финальному ответу неправильным путём — зациклившись, вызвав разрушительный инструмент или прожигая ваш бюджет. Поэтому оценивайте путь, а не только пункт назначения: вызвал ли он правильные инструменты, в разумном порядке, без циклов, в рамках бюджета? Проверки корректности вызовов инструментов и траектории ловят сбои, которые eval только по финальному ответу никогда не увидит.
documents.s: Для агентов тестируйте ещё и траекторию

documents.t: Вот где evals окупаются: сделайте регрессии невозможными для мёрджа. Guided walkthrough1 of 3 1Запускайте golden set на каждом pull request⌄ Оценивайте программно, где возможно; запускайте судью на остальном. ←PreviousNext→ 2Валите сборку при падении⌄ Задайте порог (например, оценка не должна падать относительно main). Изменение промпта, ухудшающее качество, не сможет попасть в релиз. ←PreviousNext→ 3Замкните петлю в продакшене⌄ Когда судья помечает живой ответ, направляйте его в очередь человеческой проверки; ревьюер подтверждает, добавляет случай в golden set и перетестирует после исправления. ←PreviousNext→ Проверь себя 0/3 Key takeaways Нет eval = релиз «на ощущениях». Постройте его, прежде чем доверять промпту или агенту. Golden dataset из реальных сбоев; растите его каждую неделю на новых регрессиях. Сначала проверки на основе кода; LLM-as-judge (с рубрикой, откалиброванный) для размытых частей. Для агентов оценивайте траекторию, а не только вывод. Запускайте это в CI и валите сборку при падении — так качество перестаёт регрессировать.

LLM-as-a-Judge: ключевые техники и лучшие практики — DeepEval — рубрики, калибровка и предвзятость судьи. Руководство по оценке AI-агентов 2026 — инструменты тестирования, траектории и мониторинг — целевые объёмы golden dataset и интеграция в CI. LLM-as-a-Judge: 7 лучших практик и шаблонов — Monte Carlo — практичные шаблоны судьи и подводные камни. Оценка LLM: практические советы в Booking.com — уроки оценки продакшен-масштаба. Anthropic — разрабатывайте свои тесты / оценивайте — официальное руководство по построению эмпирических evals для Claude.

Скопировать как Markdown Средний What you'll learn See exactly what changed in July 2026 — categorized entries replace the daily summary in the app, and a new beta header rewires the API Learn how to view, edit, and delete individual entries in Settings without wiping everything Understand the four behavior changes the agent-memory-2026-07-22 header brings to memory_store endpoints, and why the old cursors stop working Meet the memory_store.* webhooks and Dreams — the parts nobody documents Apply five practical patterns for teaching Claude what to remember (and what to forget) For a year, "Claude's memory" meant a single evolving paragraph the model rewrote each day — good for a bio, bad for anything with structure. Between June and July 2026 Anthropic replaced that with an entry-based model: dozens of small, categorized notes Claude reads and writes in real time. Same idea powers the app and the Managed Agents memory API. This page connects them so you understand both surfaces from one mental model. Последняя проверка: 2026-07-24. The agent-memory-2026-07-22 beta header, the memory_store webhook events, and Dreams model support all changed within the last four weeks. Confirm current beta status and pricing on the platform release notes before shipping. Сверьтесь с официальным источником.
documents.s: Claude Memory 2026 — Categorized Entries, from App to API

documents.t: Both sides work the same way now: many small entries at named locations, each rewritable in isolation. The old model (one blob per user, rewritten wholesale) is gone in the app and has never been the API surface. Once you internalize "entries at paths, listed by prefix, edited one at a time", both surfaces stop feeling like separate features.
documents.s: The mental model that unifies both sides

documents.t: Guided walkthrough1 of 3 1July 9, 2026 — Monthly recap arrives⌄ A new Settings › Reflect surface starts showing topics you spent time on, your most active day, peak hour, and observations about how you work with Claude. Beta on Free, Pro, and Max (web + Claude Desktop). Requires memory enabled. ←PreviousNext→ 2July 10, 2026 — Categorized entries replace the daily summary⌄ Memory becomes a set of individual, categorized entries that Claude reads and updates during conversations, instead of one rolling daily summary. Announced in the Claude Apps release notes. ←PreviousNext→ 3Rollout — Free / Pro / Max, with Team & Enterprise following⌄ Third-party coverage places availability across Free, Pro, Max, Team, and Enterprise, but plan-by-plan wording shifts between Anthropic's help center and news posts. When it matters (compliance, audits), verify in-product for your plan. ←PreviousNext→

The old daily summary had a single failure mode: unrelated context leaked into each other. Fix a fact about your work project and Claude might overwrite something about your writing style. Small, categorized entries fix that structurally — each edit is scoped to one lane. Three consequences most users miss: Retrieval is now targeted, not associative. Claude can pull "your communication preferences" without dragging in the rest of your context. Prompts that used to need "remember I prefer X, not Y" to break through the summary now hit an existing entry directly. You can prune surgically. Delete a single wrong entry in Settings instead of wiping everything and re-teaching Claude who you are. The "burn it all down" tax on correcting one mistake is gone. Categories act as an invisible schema. When Claude decides where an entry belongs (e.g. "communication style" vs. "current project"), it's implicitly choosing whether that fact will be recalled in future personal chats, future work chats, or both. Naming things well up front nudges better recall later.

Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Open Settings › Memory⌄ You'll see entries grouped by category (professional context, communication preferences, ongoing projects, and similar buckets). ←PreviousNext→ 2Edit or delete individual entries⌄ Each entry has its own controls. Fix a wrong fact without touching the rest — the whole reason for the redesign. ←PreviousNext→ 3Steer writes in-chat⌄ Ask Claude to remember, forget, or update specific things ("remember I use Bun, not npm") and it will update the matching entry live. ←PreviousNext→ 4Use incognito for one-offs⌄ An incognito chat is excluded from memory writes and chat history. Use it for anything you don't want persisted — sensitive drafts, one-time explorations, credentials you'd rather not have summarized. ←PreviousNext→ 5Check the monthly recap⌄ Settings › Reflect surfaces what Claude has been talking to you about. Skim it to catch memory drift — if a topic you no longer care about keeps showing up, prune the entries. ←PreviousNext→ Watch out Memory is best-effort recall, not authoritative storage. Never treat it as a source of truth for anything you'd audit (contracts, credentials, medication, legal facts). Restate hard requirements in the prompt or in a Project's instructions.
documents.s: View and manage your own entries

documents.t: 1. Set standing preferences explicitly, once CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ Please remember these as standing preferences for our chats: - Language: Italian for prose, English for code and error strings. - Units: metric. - Coding style: TypeScript strict, no default exports. - Voice: direct, no filler, no closing "let me know if…". Store each as its own entry in the right category. 2. Correct a single fact without a wipe CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ Update the memory entry that says I use Vercel for hosting — I moved everything to Cloudflare Workers last month. Leave every other project fact alone. 3. Deliberately forget CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ Delete any memory entries about the "Project Nightingale" launch — that work is finished and I don't want it surfacing in future chats. 4. Audit what Claude thinks it knows CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ Before we start, list every memory entry you have about me, grouped by category. Flag anything that looks outdated so I can decide whether to keep or delete it. 5. Sandbox exploratory chats CopyCopied!Open in Claude↗ (Open the chat in Incognito.) Don't try to remember anything from this conversation — I'm just exploring a sensitive draft I don't want stored.

The Managed Agents platform exposes memory as memory stores — collections of memories addressed by path, listed with a path_prefix, and paged with cursors. On July 2, 2026 Anthropic shipped agent-memory-2026-07-22, a beta header that changes the semantics enough to break naive migrations. On July 22, 2026 the older managed-agents-2026-04-01 header adopted the same list behavior — so the "new" rules are now the only rules on memory-store endpoints.
documents.s: Part 2 — In the API: memory_stores and the new beta header

documents.t: # What changed Old behavior New behavior under agent-memory-2026-07-22 1 List order Client-controlled via order_by / order Stable, server-defined order. order_by and order are ignored — sorting client-side if you need it 2 depth parameter Free-form integer Accepts only 0, 1, or omitted. Any other value returns 400 3 path_prefix matching Substring match Must end with /, matches whole path segments only 4 Pagination cursors Interchangeable Cursors issued without the new header aren't valid with it. Restart from page 1 when you adopt it Two more gotchas: Header collision. On memory-store endpoints, agent-memory-2026-07-22 replaces managed-agents-2026-04-01. Sending both returns 400. Migrate the memory-store calls only; leave the other managed-agents endpoints on the original header. SDKs already switched. Python 0.116.0, TypeScript 0.110.0, Go 1.56.0, Java 2.48.0, Ruby 1.55.0, PHP 0.36.0, C# 12.35.0, and the CLI 1.16.0 all send agent-memory-2026-07-22 on memory-store calls automatically. If your code passes betas explicitly, replace managed-agents-2026-04-01 there — don't add both.
documents.s: The four behavior changes you must know

documents.t: Guided walkthrough1 of 6 1Bump the SDK⌄ Upgrade to at least Python 0.116.0 / TS 0.110.0 / Go 1.56.0 / Java 2.48.0 / Ruby 1.55.0 / PHP 0.36.0 / C# 12.35.0 (CLI 1.16.0). The header switch happens for you on memory-store calls. ←PreviousNext→ 2Drop dead parameters⌄ Remove order_by / order — the server ignores them. If your code sorts on the returned list order, move the sort client-side. ←PreviousNext→ 3Fix depth⌄ Replace any depth other than 0 or 1 with the value that best matches your intent, or omit the parameter. ←PreviousNext→ 4Normalize path_prefix⌄ Ensure every path_prefix ends with a slash. Remove any substring-style prefixes that relied on partial-segment matches — they will silently return fewer results now. ←PreviousNext→ 5Reset pagination⌄ On the first request after upgrade, don't reuse a stored cursor. Start from page 1 and re-derive the next cursor from the new response. ←PreviousNext→ 6Fix explicit betas⌄ If you pass betas manually, replace managed-agents-2026-04-01 on memory-store calls with agent-memory-2026-07-22 — never send both. ←PreviousNext→

Shipped July 22, 2026 alongside the header default: three memory_store.* webhook event types now cover the memory store's lifecycle, and four environment.* events cover the sandbox environment. This is the piece most integrators miss — you can now react to a memory store being created, updated, or removed by an agent run instead of polling GET /v1/memory_stores on a timer. Subscribe on the Managed Agents webhooks endpoint and route the events into your own audit trail or dashboard.
documents.s: Webhooks: react to memory-store lifecycle without polling

documents.t: Announced in the May 6, 2026 release notes and extended on July 10 to support Claude Fable 5 and Sonnet 5, Dreams is a research preview that reads an existing memory store plus past session transcripts and produces a reorganized output memory store: duplicates merged, stale entries replaced, new insights surfaced. Endpoints are gated by the dreaming-2026-04-21 beta header; access is by request. Treat it as the API-side analogue of the app's monthly recap — a scheduled reflection pass that keeps the store from silting up.
documents.s: Dreams: reorganize memory in the background

documents.t: Aspect Claude.ai app Managed Agents API Storage unit Categorized entry Memory at a path Grouping Category (professional context, communication preferences, ongoing projects, …) Path segments (/projects/acme/…) Read/write Live during chat Agent tool calls during a session Human-editable Yes, per entry in Settings › Memory Yes, via memory-store endpoints Wipe Per entry, or all Per memory, per prefix, or delete store Reflection Monthly recap (Settings › Reflect) Dreams (research preview) Isolation Incognito chat Per-agent, per-session memory-store selection Availability Free, Pro, Max, Team, Enterprise (verify per plan) Managed Agents (public beta) Where this lives in the rest of AILmanac: Memory & Context Editing — the client-side memory tool, a different beast: you implement the storage. Memory Across Chats — the beginner's overview of app memory. Agent Memory Architectures — the theory of episodic vs. semantic memory that makes sense of why categorized entries beat a rolling summary. Managed Agents — the harness that hosts the memory-store surface described here.

Pro tip Team and Enterprise: check whether admins can inspect entries. Treat the app memory as data classification 'internal', not 'confidential'. Never let Claude write API keys, tokens, or credentials into entries. If you paste one in a chat with memory on, delete both the message and any resulting entry. Use incognito for legal, medical, or financial one-offs. Nothing prevents the app from summarizing wording later if you don't. Audit periodically. Run the 'list every entry you have about me' prompt monthly and delete anything that no longer applies. On the API side, treat memory_stores as first-class data. Back them up, list-diff them before and after significant runs, and log memory_store.* webhook events to your audit trail.
